So shaken as we are, so wan with care, / Find we a time for frighted peace to pant, / And breathe short-winded accents of new broils / To be commenced in strands afar remote. / No more the thirsty entrance of this soil / Shall daub her lips with her own children's blood; / No more shall trenching war channel her fields, / Nor bruise her flowerets with the armed hoofs / Of hostile paces: those opposed eyes, / Which, like the meteors of a troubled heaven, / All of one nature, of one substance bred, / Did lately meet in the intestine shock / And furious close of civil butchery, / Shall now, in mutual well-beseeming ranks, / March all one way, and be no more opposed / Against acquaintance, kindred, and allies: / The edge of war, like an ill-sheathed knife, / No more shall cut his master. Therefore, friends, / As far as to the sepulchre of Christ— / Whose soldier now, under whose blessed cross / We are impressed and engaged to fight— / Forthwith a power of English shall we levy, / To chase these pagans in those holy fields / Over whose acres walk'd those blessed feet / Which fourteen hundred years ago were nail'd / For our advantage on the bitter cross. / But this our purpose now is twelvemonth old, / And bootless 'tis to tell you we will go: / Therefore we meet not now.—Then let me hear / Of you, my gentle cousin Westmoreland, / What yesternight our Council did decree / In forwarding this dear expedience.

Shaken and pale with worry as we are, let us find a moment for frightened peace to catch her breath, and speak, still panting, of new wars to be started in distant lands. No longer will this thirsty earth wet her lips with the blood of her own children. No longer will war carve trenches through her fields or crush her flowers under the hooves of enemy horses. Those eyes that faced each other in hostility, which, like meteors in a stormy sky, all of one nature and one birth, recently clashed in the shock and savage close of civil war, will now march together in orderly ranks, all one way, no longer set against friends, relatives and allies. The edge of war, like a knife in a badly made sheath, will no longer cut its own master. So, friends, we shall at once raise an English army and march as far as the tomb of Christ, whose soldier we now are, sworn to fight under his blessed cross, to chase the pagans out of those holy fields where his blessed feet walked, the feet that were nailed to the bitter cross for our sake fourteen hundred years ago. But this plan of ours is already a year old, and there's no point telling you that we will go; that's not why we're meeting now. Instead let me hear from you, my noble cousin Westmoreland, what the Council decided last night about speeding up this urgent expedition.

My liege, this haste was hot in question, / And many limits of the charge set down / But yesternight; when, all athwart, there came / A post from Wales loaden with heavy news; / Whose worst was, that the noble Mortimer, / Leading the men of Herefordshire to fight / Against th' irregular and wild Glendower, / Was by the rude hands of that Welshman taken; / A thousand of his people butchered, / Upon whose dead corpse' there was such misuse, / Such beastly, shameless transformation, / By those Welshwomen done, as may not be / Without much shame re-told or spoken of.

My lord, this business was being hotly debated, and many of the duties were assigned only last night, when suddenly a messenger arrived from Wales loaded with bad news. The worst of it was that the noble Mortimer, leading the men of Herefordshire against the lawless and wild Glendower, was captured by that rough Welshman. A thousand of his men were slaughtered, and their dead bodies were so savagely and shamelessly mutilated by the Welshwomen that it can't be described or even mentioned without great shame.
It seems, then, that the tidings of this broil / Brake off our business for the Holy Land.
It seems, then, that the news of this fighting interrupted our plans for the Holy Land.

This, match'd with other, did, my gracious lord; / For more uneven and unwelcome news / Came from the North, and thus it did import: / On Holy-rood day the gallant Hotspur there, / Young Harry Percy, and brave Archibald, / That ever-valiant and approved Scot, / At Holmedon met; / Where they did spend a sad and bloody hour, / As by discharge of their artillery, / And shape of likelihood, the news was told; / For he that brought them, in the very heat / And pride of their contention did take horse, / Uncertain of the issue any way.

This, together with other news, did, my lord. More troubling and unwelcome news came from the North: on Holy Cross Day the brave Hotspur, young Harry Percy, met the bold Archibald, that ever-brave and tested Scot, at Holmedon. They spent a grim and bloody hour there, as the messenger guessed from the sound of their guns and the way things looked. He rode off in the very heat of the battle, so he didn't know how it ended.

Here is a dear and true-industrious friend, / Sir Walter Blunt, new lighted from his horse, / Stain'd with the variation of each soil / Betwixt that Holmedon and this seat of ours; / And he hath brought us smooth and welcome news. / The Earl of Douglas is discomfited: / Ten thousand bold Scots, two-and-twenty knights, / Balk'd in their own blood, did Sir Walter see / On Holmedon's plains: of prisoners, Hotspur took / Mordake the Earl of Fife and eldest son / To beaten Douglas; and the Earls of Athol, / Of Murray, Angus, and Menteith. / And is not this an honourable spoil, / A gallant prize? ha, cousin, is it not?

Here is a dear and truly hard-working friend, Sir Walter Blunt, just off his horse and spattered with every kind of soil between Holmedon and here. He has brought us good and welcome news. The Earl of Douglas is defeated. Sir Walter saw ten thousand bold Scots and twenty-two knights lying heaped in their own blood on the plains of Holmedon. Hotspur took as prisoners Mordake, Earl of Fife and eldest son of the beaten Douglas, and the Earls of Athol, Murray, Angus and Menteith. Isn't that an honourable haul, a splendid prize? Well, cousin, isn't it?
Faith, 'tis a conquest for a prince to boast of.
Indeed, it's a victory a prince could boast of.

Yea, there thou makest me sad, and makest me sin / In envy that my Lord Northumberland / Should be the father to so blest a son,— / A son who is the theme of honour's tongue; / Amongst a grove, the very straightest plant; / Who is sweet Fortune's minion and her pride: / Whilst I, by looking on the praise of him, / See riot and dishonour stain the brow / Of my young Harry. O, that it could be proved / That some night-tripping fairy had exchanged / In cradle-clothes our children where they lay, / And call'd mine Percy, his Plantagenet! / Then would I have his Harry, and he mine: / But let him from my thoughts. What think you, coz, / Of this young Percy's pride? the prisoners, / Which he in this adventure hath surprised, / To his own use he keeps; and sends me word, / I shall have none but Mordake Earl of Fife.

Yes, and that's what makes me sad, and makes me sin by envying Lord Northumberland for being the father of such a blessed son, a son whom honour itself talks about, the straightest tree in the forest, Fortune's darling and pride. Meanwhile, when I look at the praise he earns, I see wild living and disgrace stain the face of my young Harry. Oh, if only it could be proved that some fairy roaming at night had swapped our children in their cradles, and named mine Percy and his Plantagenet! Then I would have his Harry, and he would have mine. But let me put my son out of my mind. What do you think, cousin, of young Percy's arrogance? He keeps for himself the prisoners he captured in this battle, and sends me word that I'll get none except Mordake, Earl of Fife.
This is his uncle's teaching, this is Worcester, / Malevolent to you in all aspects; / Which makes him prune himself, and bristle up / The crest of youth against your dignity.
That's his uncle Worcester's teaching. Worcester is hostile to you in every way, and he makes the young man preen himself and raise his crest against your royal authority.

But I have sent for him to answer this; / And for this cause awhile we must neglect / Our holy purpose to Jerusalem. / Cousin, on Wednesday next our Council we / Will hold at Windsor; so inform the lords: / But come yourself with speed to us again; / For more is to be said and to be done / Than out of anger can be uttered.

But I've sent for him to answer for this, and because of it we must set aside our holy expedition to Jerusalem for a while. Cousin, we will hold our Council at Windsor next Wednesday; tell the lords. But come back to me yourself quickly, because there is more to say and do than I can express while I am angry.
Now, Hal, what time of day is it, lad?
Now, Hal, what time of day is it, lad?

Thou art so fat-witted, with drinking of old sack, and / unbuttoning thee after supper, and sleeping upon benches / after noon, that thou hast forgotten to demand that truly which / thou wouldst truly know. What a devil hast thou to do with the / time of the day? unless hours were cups of sack, and minutes / capons, and the blessed Sun himself a fair hot wench in / flame-coloured taffeta, I see no reason why thou shouldst be / so superfluous to demand the time of the day.

You're so thick-headed from drinking old sherry, unbuttoning yourself after supper and sleeping on benches in the afternoon that you've forgotten how to ask properly for what you really want to know. What the devil do you care about the time of day? Unless hours were cups of sherry, minutes were roast chickens, and the blessed sun itself a pretty, hot girl in flame-coloured silk, I see no reason why you'd bother asking the time.

Indeed, you come near me now, Hal; for we that take purses go / by the Moon and the seven stars, and not by Phoebus,—he, that / wandering knight so fair. And I pr'ythee, sweet wag, when thou / art king,—as, God save thy Grace—Majesty I should say, for grace / thou wilt have none,—

Indeed, you've got me there, Hal. We who steal purses go by the moon and the seven stars, not by the sun, that wandering knight so fair. And please, sweet joker, when you are king, as God save your Grace (your Majesty, I should say, because grace you'll have none),
No, by my troth; not so much as will serve to be prologue / to an egg and butter.
No, I swear, not even enough to say a grace before a snack of egg and butter.
Well, how then? come, roundly, roundly.
Well, what then? Come on, out with it.

Marry, then, sweet wag, when thou art king, let not us that / are squires of the night's body be called thieves of the day's / beauty: let us be Diana's foresters, gentlemen of the shade, / minions of the Moon; and let men say we be men of good / government, being governed, as the sea is, by our noble and / chaste mistress the Moon, under whose countenance we steal.

Well then, sweet joker, when you are king, don't let us who are the night's bodyguards be called thieves who steal the day's beauty. Let us be called Diana's foresters, gentlemen of the shade, darlings of the moon. Let people say we are well-governed men, because, like the sea, we are governed by our noble and chaste mistress the moon, under whose face we steal.

Thou say'st well, and it holds well too; for the fortune of / us that are the Moon's men doth ebb and flow like the sea, / being governed, as the sea is, by the Moon. As, for proof, now: A / purse of gold most resolutely snatch'd on Monday night, and most / dissolutely spent on Tuesday morning; got with swearing Lay by, / and spent with crying Bring in; now ill as low an ebb as the foot / of the ladder, and by-and-by in as high a flow as the ridge of the / gallows.

You put it well, and it fits too, because the fortune of us moon's men ebbs and flows like the sea, since like the sea it is governed by the moon. For example: a purse of gold boldly snatched on Monday night and wildly spent on Tuesday morning; got by shouting "Hand it over!" and spent by shouting "Bring more drink!"; one moment at a low ebb at the foot of the ladder, and soon at high tide on top of the gallows.
By the Lord, thou say'st true, lad. And is not my hostess of the / tavern a most sweet wench?
By God, you're right, lad. And isn't the landlady of the tavern a very sweet woman?
As the honey of Hybla, my old lad of the castle. And is not a / buff jerkin a most sweet robe of durance?
As sweet as Sicilian honey, my old rogue of the castle. And isn't a leather jerkin a lovely thing to last you a long time?
How now, how now, mad wag! what, in thy quips and thy / quiddities? what a plague have I to do with a buff jerkin?
What's this, you mad joker? What, more of your jokes and quibbles? What the plague have I got to do with a leather jerkin?
Why, what a pox have I to do with my hostess of the tavern?
Well, what the pox have I got to do with the landlady of the tavern?
Well, thou hast call'd her to a reckoning many a time and oft.
Well, you've asked her for the bill many times.
Did I ever call for thee to pay thy part?
Did I ever call on you to pay your share?
No; I'll give thee thy due, thou hast paid all there.
No, I'll give you your due, you've paid for everything there.
Yea, and elsewhere, so far as my coin would stretch; / and where it would not, I have used my credit.
Yes, and elsewhere too, as far as my money would stretch, and where it wouldn't, I've used my credit.

Yea, and so used it, that, were it not here apparent that / thou art heir-apparent—But I pr'ythee, sweet wag, shall there be / gallows standing in England when thou art king? and / resolution thus fobb'd as it is with the rusty curb of old father / antic the law? Do not thou, when thou art king, hang a thief.

Yes, and used it so well that, if it weren't obvious that you're the heir to the throne... But please, sweet joker, will there still be gallows standing in England when you're king, and will courage still be cheated by the rusty bridle of that old clown, the law? When you are king, don't hang a thief.
Shall I? O rare! By the Lord, I'll be a brave judge.
Will I? Oh, wonderful! By God, I'll be a fine judge.
Thou judgest false already: I mean, thou shalt have the / hanging of the thieves, and so become a rare hangman.
You're judging wrongly already. I mean you'll have the job of hanging the thieves, and so become an excellent hangman.
Well, Hal, well; and in some sort it jumps with my humour; / as well as waiting in the Court, I can tell you.
Well, Hal, well, in a way that suits my temperament, as well as hanging around at Court, I can tell you.
Yea, for obtaining of suits, whereof the hangman hath no / lean wardrobe. 'Sblood, I am as melancholy as a gib-cat or a / lugg'd bear.
Yes, for the dead men's suits of clothes, of which the hangman has a big wardrobe. By God's blood, I'm as gloomy as a tomcat or a bear on a chain.
Or an old lion, or a lover's lute.
Or an old lion, or a lover's lute.
Yea, or the drone of a Lincolnshire bagpipe.
Yes, or the drone of a Lincolnshire bagpipe.
What say'st thou to a hare, or the melancholy of Moor-ditch?
What do you say to a hare, or the gloom of the Moorditch sewer?

Thou hast the most unsavoury similes, and art, indeed, the / most comparative, rascalliest, sweet young prince,—But, Hal, I / pr'ythee trouble me no more with vanity. I would to God thou and / I knew where a commodity of good names were to be bought. An old / lord of the Council rated me the other day in the street about you, / sir,—but I mark'd him not; and yet he talk'd very wisely,—but I / regarded him not; and yet he talk'd wisely, and in the street too.

You have the most unpleasant comparisons, and you're the most comparison-making, rascally, sweet young prince. But, Hal, please don't bother me any more with worldly nonsense. I wish to God you and I knew where we could buy a supply of good reputations. An old lord of the Council told me off in the street the other day about you, sir, but I paid him no attention; and yet he talked very wisely, but I ignored him; and yet he talked wisely, and in the street too.
Thou didst well; for wisdom cries out in the streets, and no man / regards it.
You did well, because wisdom cries out in the streets and no one listens to it.

O, thou hast damnable iteration, and art, indeed, able to corrupt / a saint. / Thou hast done much harm upon me, Hal; God forgive thee for it! / Before I knew thee, Hal, I knew nothing; and now am I, if a man / should speak truly, little better than one of the wicked. I must / give over this life, and I will give it over; by the Lord, an I do / not, I am a villain: I'll be damn'd for never a king's son in / Christendom.

Oh, you have a damnable way of quoting scripture, and you could corrupt a saint. You've done me a lot of harm, Hal, God forgive you for it! Before I knew you, Hal, I knew nothing of evil, and now, to tell the truth, I'm little better than one of the wicked. I must give up this life, and I will give it up. By God, if I don't, I'm a villain. I won't be damned for any king's son in Christendom.
Where shall we take a purse to-morrow, Jack?
Where shall we steal a purse tomorrow, Jack?
Zounds, where thou wilt, lad; I'll make one: an I do not, call / me villain, and baffle me.
By God's wounds, wherever you like, lad, I'll be one of the gang. If I'm not, call me a villain and disgrace me.
I see a good amendment of life in thee,—from praying to / purse-taking.
I see a fine reform in your life, from praying to purse-snatching.
Why, Hal, 'tis my vocation, Hal; 'tis no sin for a man to labour / in his vocation.
Why, Hal, it's my calling, Hal. It's no sin for a man to work at his calling.

—Pointz!—Now shall we know if Gadshill have set a match. O, if / men were to be saved by merit, what hole in Hell were hot enough / for him? This is the most omnipotent villain that ever cried / Stand! to a true man.

Poins! Now we'll find out if Gadshill has set up a robbery. Oh, if men were saved by what they deserved, what hole in hell would be hot enough for him? This is the most almighty villain that ever shouted "Stand!" to an honest man.

Good morrow, sweet Hal.—What says Monsieur Remorse? what / says Sir John Sack-and-sugar? Jack, how agrees the Devil and / thee about thy soul, that thou soldest him on Good-Friday last / for a cup of Madeira and a cold capon's leg?

Good morning, sweet Hal. What does Monsieur Remorse say? What does Sir John Sherry-and-Sugar say? Jack, how are you and the Devil getting on over your soul, which you sold him last Good Friday for a cup of Madeira and a cold chicken leg?
Sir John stands to his word,—the Devil shall have his bargain; / for he was never yet a breaker of proverbs,—he will give the / Devil his due.
Sir John keeps his word: the Devil will have his bargain. He has never broken a proverb, so he will give the Devil his due.
Then art thou damn'd for keeping thy word with the Devil.
Then you're damned for keeping your word to the Devil.
Else he had been damn'd for cozening the Devil.
Otherwise he'd be damned for cheating the Devil.

But, my lads, my lads, to-morrow morning, by four o'clock, / early at Gads-hill! there are pilgrims gong to Canterbury / with rich offerings, and traders riding to London with fat / purses: I have visards for you all; you have horses for / yourselves: Gadshill lies to-night in Rochester: I have bespoke / supper to-morrow night in Eastcheap: we may do it as secure as / sleep. If you will go, I will stuff your purses full of crowns; / if you will not, tarry at home and be hang'd.

But, lads, lads, tomorrow morning, by four o'clock, early, at Gad's Hill! There are pilgrims going to Canterbury with rich offerings and traders riding to London with fat purses. I have masks for you all; you have your own horses. Gadshill is staying in Rochester tonight. I have ordered supper for tomorrow night in Eastcheap. We can do it as safely as sleeping. If you come, I'll stuff your purses full of crowns; if you won't, stay home and be hanged.
Hear ye, Yedward; if I tarry at home and go not, I'll hang you / for going.
Listen, Edward, if I stay home and don't go, I'll have you hanged for going.
Hal, will you be one of us?
Who, I rob? I a thief? not I, by my faith.
Who, me rob? Me a thief? Not I, I swear.
There's neither honesty, manhood, nor good fellowship in thee, / nor thou camest not of the blood royal, if thou darest not stand / for ten shillings.
There's no honesty, courage or friendship in you, and you're not of royal blood, if you don't dare to stand up for ten shillings.
Well, then, once in my days I'll be a madcap.
Well then, once in my life I'll be a wild one.
Well, come what will, I'll tarry at home.
Well, come what may, I'll stay at home.
By the Lord, I'll be a traitor, then, when thou art king.
By God, then I'll be a traitor when you're king.
Sir John, I pr'ythee, leave the Prince and me alone: I will / lay him down such reasons for this adventure, that he shall go.
Sir John, please leave the Prince and me alone. I'll give him such reasons for this adventure that he'll come.

Well, God give thee the spirit of persuasion, and him the ears / of profiting, that what thou speakest may move, and what he / hears may be believed, that the true Prince may, for recreation- / sake, prove a false thief; for the poor abuses of the time want / countenance. Farewell; you shall find me in Eastcheap.

Well, may God give you the gift of persuasion and him ears that profit from it, so that what you say may move him and what he hears may be believed, so that the true Prince may, for fun's sake, turn out to be a false thief, since the petty crimes of these times need someone important to back them. Farewell; you'll find me in Eastcheap.
Farewell, thou latter Spring! farewell, All-hallown Summer!
Farewell, you late spring! Farewell, you Indian summer!

Now, my good sweet honey-lord, ride with us to-morrow: I / have a jest to execute that I cannot manage alone. Falstaff, / Bardolph, Peto, and Gadshill, shall rob those men that we have / already waylaid: yourself and I will not be there; and when they / have the booty, if you and I do not rob them, cut this head off / from my shoulders.

Now, my good sweet honey-lord, ride with us tomorrow. I have a joke to play that I can't manage alone. Falstaff, Bardolph, Peto and Gadshill will rob those men we've already set up as targets. You and I won't be there, and once they have the loot, if you and I don't rob them, cut this head off my shoulders.
But how shall we part with them in setting forth?
But how shall we get away from them when we set out?

Why, we will set forth before or after them, and appoint them / a place of meeting, wherein it is at our pleasure to fail; and / then will they adventure upon the exploit themselves; which they / shall have no sooner achieved but we'll set upon them.

Why, we'll set out before or after them and agree a meeting place, where we can choose not to turn up. Then they'll go ahead with the robbery by themselves, and as soon as they've done it, we'll attack them.
Ay, but 'tis like that they will know us by our horses, by our / habits, and by every other appointment, to be ourselves.
Yes, but they're likely to recognise us by our horses, our clothes and everything else we have.

Tut! our horses they shall not see,—I'll tie them in the wood; / our visards we will change, after we leave them; and, sirrah, I / have cases of buckram for the nonce, to immask our noted / outward garments.

Nonsense! They won't see our horses, I'll tie them up in the wood. We'll change our masks after we leave them, and, my friend, I have overalls of coarse cloth ready for the purpose to cover our well-known clothes.
But I doubt they will be too hard for us.
But I'm afraid they'll be too strong for us.

Well, for two of them, I know them to be as true-bred / cowards as ever turn'd back; and for the third, if he fight / longer than he sees reason, I'll forswear arms. The virtue of / this jest will be, the incomprehensible lies that this same fat / rogue will tell us when we meet at supper: how thirty, at least, / he fought with; what wards, what blows, what extremities he / endured; and in the reproof of this lies the jest.

Well, two of them I know to be as thorough-bred cowards as ever ran away, and as for the third, if he fights longer than he thinks sensible, I'll give up fighting for good. The beauty of this joke will be the huge lies this fat rogue will tell us when we meet at supper: how he fought at least thirty men, what defensive moves, what blows, what dangers he went through. And the joke lies in exposing those lies.
Well, I'll go with thee: provide us all things necessary and / meet me to-night in Eastcheap; there I'll sup. Farewell.
Well, I'll go with you. Get everything we need and meet me tonight in Eastcheap; I'll have supper there. Farewell.

I know you all, and will awhile uphold / The unyok'd humour of your idleness: / Yet herein will I imitate the Sun, / Who doth permit the base contagious clouds / To smother-up his beauty from the world, / That, when he please again to be himself, / Being wanted, he may be more wonder'd at, / By breaking through the foul and ugly mists / Of vapours that did seem to strangle him. / If all the year were playing holidays, / To sport would be as tedious as to work; / But, when they seldom come, they wish'd-for come, / And nothing pleaseth but rare accidents. / So, when this loose behaviour I throw off, / And pay the debt I never promised, / By how much better than my word I am, / By so much shall I falsify men's hopes; / And, like bright metal on a sullen ground, / My reformation, glittering o'er my fault, / Shall show more goodly and attract more eyes / Than that which hath no foil to set it off. / I'll so offend, to make offence a skill; / Redeeming time, when men think least I will.

I know you all, and for a while I'll go along with your unrestrained, idle ways. But in this I'll copy the sun, which lets the low, polluting clouds hide its beauty from the world, so that when it chooses to be itself again, being missed, it may be wondered at all the more for breaking through the foul and ugly mists that seemed to strangle it. If every day of the year were a holiday, playing would be as boring as working; but because holidays come rarely, they are longed for, and nothing pleases like the unusual. So, when I throw off this loose behaviour and pay the debt I never promised to pay, the better I turn out than people expected, the more I will prove their expectations wrong. And like bright metal against a dull background, my reformation, shining over my faults, will look finer and attract more attention than goodness that has nothing to set it off. I'll do wrong in such a way that I make wrongdoing into a clever tactic, making up for lost time when people least expect me to.

My blood hath been too cold and temperate, / Unapt to stir at these indignities, / And you have found me; for, accordingly, / You tread upon my patience: but be sure / I will from henceforth rather be myself, / Mighty and to be fear'd, than my condition, / Which hath been smooth as oil, soft as young down, / And therefore lost that title of respect / Which the proud soul ne'er pays but to the proud.

My temper has been too cold and mild, slow to react to these insults, and you have found that out; and so you walk all over my patience. But be sure that from now on I'll be what I truly am, a mighty king to be feared, rather than follow my natural disposition, which has been as smooth as oil and soft as a chick's down, and so has lost the respect that proud men only ever pay to the proud.
Our House, my sovereign liege, little deserves / The scourge of greatness to be used on it; / And that same greatness too which our own hands / Have holp to make so portly.
Our family, my sovereign lord, hardly deserves to have the whip of royal power used on it, and especially not that same power which our own hands helped to make so great.

Worcester, get thee gone; for I do see / Danger and disobedience in thine eye: / O, sir, your presence is too bold and peremptory, / And majesty might never yet endure / The moody frontier of a servant brow. / You have good leave to leave us: when we need / Your use and counsel, we shall send for you.

Worcester, go away, because I see danger and disobedience in your eyes. Oh, sir, your manner is too bold and overbearing, and royalty has never put up with a servant's sullen, frowning face. You have my permission to leave us; when we need your help and advice, we'll send for you.

Yea, my good lord. / Those prisoners in your Highness' name demanded, / Which Harry Percy here at Holmedon took, / Were, as he says, not with such strength denied / As is deliver'd to your Majesty: / Either envy, therefore, or misprision / Is guilty of this fault, and not my son.

Yes, my good lord. Those prisoners demanded in your Highness's name, which Harry Percy here took at Holmedon, were not, he says, refused as firmly as you were told. So either malice or a misunderstanding is to blame for this offence, not my son.

My liege, I did deny no prisoners. / But, I remember, when the fight was done, / When I was dry with rage and extreme toil, / Breathless and faint, leaning upon my sword, / Came there a certain lord, neat, trimly dress'd, / Fresh as a bridegroom; and his chin new reap'd / Show'd like a stubble-land at harvest-home: / He was perfumed like a milliner; / And 'twixt his finger and his thumb he held / A pouncet-box, which ever and anon / He gave his nose, and took't away again; / Who therewith angry, when it next came there, / Took it in snuff: and still he smiled and talk'd; / And, as the soldiers bore dead bodies by, / He call'd them untaught knaves, unmannerly, / To bring a slovenly unhandsome corse / Betwixt the wind and his nobility. / With many holiday and lady terms / He question'd me; amongst the rest, demanded / My prisoners in your Majesty's behalf. / I then, all smarting with my wounds being cold, / Out of my grief and my impatience / To be so pester'd with a popinjay, / Answer'd neglectingly, I know not what,— / He should, or he should not; for't made me mad / To see him shine so brisk, and smell so sweet, / And talk so like a waiting-gentlewoman / Of guns and drums and wounds,—God save the mark!— / And telling me the sovereign'st thing on Earth / Was parmaceti for an inward bruise; / And that it was great pity, so it was, / This villainous salt-petre should be digg'd / Out of the bowels of the harmless earth, / Which many a good tall fellow had destroy'd / So cowardly; and, but for these vile guns, / He would himself have been a soldier. / This bald unjointed chat of his, my lord, / I answered indirectly, as I said; / And I beseech you, let not his report / Come current for an accusation / Betwixt my love and your high Majesty.

My lord, I refused no prisoners. But I remember that when the fighting was over, when I was parched with rage and exhaustion, breathless and faint and leaning on my sword, a certain lord came along, neat and smartly dressed, as fresh as a bridegroom, his chin newly shaved so that it looked like a field of stubble after the harvest. He was perfumed like a dealer in fancy goods, and between his finger and thumb he held a little perfume box, which every so often he lifted to his nose and took away again, and the nose, offended, sniffed it up angrily when it came back. And all the time he smiled and chattered. When the soldiers carried dead bodies past, he called them ignorant, ill-mannered rascals for bringing a dirty, ugly corpse between the wind and his noble self. He questioned me in fancy, ladylike language, and among other things demanded my prisoners on your Majesty's behalf. Then I, smarting all over as my wounds cooled, in my pain and irritation at being pestered by this parrot, answered carelessly, I don't know what: he should have them, or he shouldn't. It made me mad to see him shine so smartly and smell so sweet, and talk like a lady's maid about guns and drums and wounds (God forgive the comparison!), telling me that the best thing on earth for an internal bruise was whale ointment, and that it was a great pity, so it was, that this wicked gunpowder should be dug out of the harmless earth, when it had killed many a fine brave fellow in such a cowardly way; and that, if it weren't for these awful guns, he'd have been a soldier himself. I answered his feeble, disjointed chatter offhandedly, my lord, as I said. And I beg you, don't let his report be accepted as an accusation that comes between my loyalty and your Majesty.

The circumstance consider'd, good my lord, / Whatever Harry Percy then had said / To such a person, and in such a place, / At such a time, with all the rest re-told, / May reasonably die, and never rise / To do him wrong, or any way impeach / What then he said, so he unsay it now.

Considering the circumstances, my good lord, whatever Harry Percy said to such a person, in such a place, at such a time, along with everything else reported, can reasonably be allowed to die and never rise again to harm him or to be used against him, as long as he takes it back now.

Why, yet he doth deny his prisoners, / But with proviso and exception, / That we at our own charge shall ransom straight / His brother-in-law, the foolish Mortimer; / Who, on my soul, hath wilfully betray'd / The lives of those that he did lead to fight / Against that great magician, damn'd Glendower, / Whose daughter, as we hear, the Earl of March / Hath lately married. Shall our coffers, then, / Be emptied to redeem a traitor home? / Shall we buy treason? and indent with fears / When they have lost and forfeited themselves? / No, on the barren mountains let him starve; / For I shall never hold that man my friend / Whose tongue shall ask me for one penny cost / To ransom home revolted Mortimer.

Why, he still refuses to hand over his prisoners, except on the condition that we pay the ransom at our own expense for his brother-in-law, that foolish Mortimer, who, I swear, deliberately threw away the lives of the men he led against that great magician, the damned Glendower, whose daughter, we hear, the Earl of March has recently married. Should our treasury be emptied to bring a traitor home? Should we pay for treason, and strike bargains with cowards who have lost themselves and their rights? No, let him starve on the barren mountains, because I will never consider any man my friend who asks me to spend one penny to ransom the rebel Mortimer.

Revolted Mortimer! / He never did fall off, my sovereign liege, / But by the chance of war: to prove that true / Needs no more but one tongue for all those wounds, / Those mouthed wounds, which valiantly he took, / When on the gentle Severn's sedgy bank, / In single opposition, hand to hand, / He did confound the best part of an hour / In changing hardiment with great Glendower. / Three times they breathed, and three times did they drink, / Upon agreement, of swift Severn's flood; / Who then, affrighted with their bloody looks, / Ran fearfully among the trembling reeds, / And hid his crisp head in the hollow bank / Blood-stained with these valiant combatants. / Never did base and rotten policy / Colour her working with such deadly wounds; / Nor never could the noble Mortimer / Receive so many, and all willingly: / Then let not him be slander'd with revolt.

Rebel Mortimer! He never turned against you, my sovereign lord, except by the fortune of war. To prove that, you need only one tongue for all those wounds, those gaping mouths of wounds, which he bravely received when, on the reedy bank of the gentle river Severn, in single combat, hand to hand, he spent the best part of an hour trading blows with the great Glendower. Three times they paused for breath, and three times, by agreement, they drank from the swift Severn, which, frightened by their bloody looks, ran fearfully among the trembling reeds and hid its curly-waved head in the hollow bank, stained with the blood of these brave fighters. Never did low and rotten scheming disguise itself with such deadly wounds, nor could the noble Mortimer have taken so many, and all willingly, if he were a traitor. So don't let him be slandered as a rebel.

Thou dost belie him, Percy, thou dost belie him; / He never did encounter with Glendower: / I tell thee, / He durst as well have met the Devil alone / As Owen Glendower for an enemy. / Art not ashamed? But, sirrah, henceforth / Let me not hear you speak of Mortimer: / Send me your prisoners with the speediest means, / Or you shall hear in such a kind from me / As will displease you.—My Lord Northumberland, / We license your departure with your son.— / Send us your prisoners, or you'll hear of it.

You're lying about him, Percy, you're lying about him. He never fought Glendower. I tell you, he would as soon have dared to face the Devil alone as have Owen Glendower for an enemy. Aren't you ashamed? But, sir, from now on don't let me hear you talk about Mortimer. Send me your prisoners as fast as possible, or you'll hear from me in a way you won't like. My Lord Northumberland, you have permission to leave, with your son. Send us your prisoners, or you'll hear about it.
An if the Devil come and roar for them, / I will not send them: I will after straight, / And tell him so; for I will else my heart, / Although it be with hazard of my head.
Even if the Devil comes and roars for them, I won't send them. I'll go after him at once and tell him so, because I must relieve my feelings, even if it costs me my head.
What, drunk with choler? stay, and pause awhile: / Here comes your uncle.
What, drunk with anger? Wait, stop for a moment. Here comes your uncle.

Speak of Mortimer! / Zounds, I will speak of him; and let my soul / Want mercy, if I do not join with him: / Yea, on his part I'll empty all these veins, / And shed my dear blood drop by drop i' the dust, / But I will lift the down-trod Mortimer / As high i' the air as this unthankful King, / As this ingrate and canker'd Bolingbroke.

Speak of Mortimer! By God's wounds, I will speak of him, and may my soul be denied mercy if I don't join forces with him. Yes, for his sake I'll empty all these veins and spill my precious blood drop by drop in the dust, but I'll raise the trampled Mortimer as high as this ungrateful King, this ungrateful and poisonous Bolingbroke.
[To Worcester] Brother, the King hath made your nephew mad.
Brother, the King has driven your nephew mad.
Who struck this heat up after I was gone?
Who stirred up this fury after I left?

He will, forsooth, have all my prisoners; / And when I urged the ransom once again / Of my wife's brother, then his cheek look'd pale, / And on my face he turn'd an eye of death, / Trembling even at the name of Mortimer.
He wants, if you please, all my prisoners. And when I pressed again for the ransom of my wife's brother, his cheek turned pale and he gave me a deadly look, trembling at the very name of Mortimer.
I cannot blame him: was not he proclaim'd / By Richard that dead is the next of blood?
I can't blame him. Wasn't Mortimer proclaimed next in line to the throne by Richard, who is now dead?

He was; I heard the proclamation: / And then it was when the unhappy King— / Whose wrongs in us God pardon!—did set forth / Upon his Irish expedition; / From whence he intercepted did return / To be deposed, and shortly murdered.

He was; I heard the proclamation. It was when the unlucky King (God pardon us for the wrongs we did him!) set off on his Irish expedition, from which he was called back to be deposed and soon afterwards murdered.
And for whose death we in the world's wide mouth / Live scandalized and foully spoken of.
And because of his death the whole world gossips about us, and we are disgraced and spoken of with contempt.
But, soft! I pray you; did King Richard then / Proclaim my brother Edmund Mortimer / Heir to the crown?
But wait, please. Did King Richard really proclaim my brother-in-law Edmund Mortimer heir to the crown?
He did; myself did hear it.
He did; I heard it myself.

Nay, then I cannot blame his cousin King, / That wish'd him on the barren mountains starve. / But shall it be, that you, that set the crown / Upon the head of this forgetful man, / And for his sake wear the detested blot / Of murderous subornation,—shall it be, / That you a world of curses undergo, / Being the agents, or base second means, / The cords, the ladder, or the hangman rather?— / O, pardon me, that I descend so low, / To show the line and the predicament / Wherein you range under this subtle King;— / Shall it, for shame, be spoken in these days, / Or fill up chronicles in time to come, / That men of your nobility and power / Did gage them both in an unjust behalf,— / As both of you, God pardon it! have done,— / To put down Richard, that sweet lovely rose, / And plant this thorn, this canker, Bolingbroke? / And shall it, in more shame, be further spoken, / That you are fool'd, discarded, and shook off / By him for whom these shames ye underwent? / No! yet time serves, wherein you may redeem / Your banish'd honours, and restore yourselves / Into the good thoughts of the world again; / Revenge the jeering and disdain'd contempt / Of this proud King, who studies day and night / To answer all the debt he owes to you / Even with the bloody payment of your deaths: / Therefore, I say,—

Well then, I can't blame his cousin the King for wishing him to starve on the barren mountains. But is it to be that you, who put the crown on the head of this ungrateful man and for his sake bear the hateful stain of being accessories to murder, is it to be that you suffer a world of curses as his agents, his low instruments, the ropes, the ladder, or rather the hangman? Oh, forgive me for sinking so low to show the rank and position you hold under this cunning King. Shall it be said in these times, to your shame, or written in history books to come, that men of your nobility and power pledged both to an unjust cause, as you both did, God forgive you, to put down Richard, that sweet lovely rose, and plant this thorn, this canker, Bolingbroke? And shall it be said, to your even greater shame, that you are fooled, thrown away and shaken off by the very man for whom you suffered these disgraces? No! There is still time for you to win back your banished honour and restore yourselves to the world's good opinion. Take revenge on the mocking, scornful contempt of this proud King, who thinks day and night about how to repay all he owes you with the bloody payment of your deaths. So, I say,

Peace, cousin, say no more: / And now I will unclasp a secret book, / And to your quick-conceiving discontent / I'll read you matter deep and dangerous; / As full of peril and adventurous spirit / As to o'er-walk a current roaring loud / On the unsteadfast footing of a spear.

Quiet, nephew, say no more. Now I'll open a secret book, and to your quick and angry mind I'll read out matters deep and dangerous, as full of danger and daring as walking across a roaring torrent on the shaky footing of a spear.

If we fall in, good night, or sink or swim! / Send danger from the east unto the west, / So honour cross it from the north to south, / And let them grapple. O, the blood more stirs / To rouse a lion than to start a hare!

If we fall in, goodnight, whether we sink or swim! Let danger run from east to west, as long as honour crosses it from north to south, and let them wrestle. Oh, the blood is stirred more by rousing a lion than by startling a hare!
Imagination of some great exploit / Drives him beyond the bounds of patience.
The thought of some great adventure is driving him beyond all patience.

By Heaven, methinks it were an easy leap, / To pluck bright honour from the pale-faced Moon; / Or dive into the bottom of the deep, / Where fathom-line could never touch the ground, / And pluck up drowned honour by the locks; / So he that doth redeem her thence might wear / Without corrival all her dignities: / But out upon this half-faced fellowship!

By heaven, it seems to me it would be an easy leap to pluck bright honour from the pale-faced moon, or to dive to the bottom of the sea, where no measuring line could ever reach the bed, and pull drowned honour up by her hair, so that the man who rescued her could wear all her glories without a rival. But away with this sharing of glory!
He apprehends a world of figures here, / But not the form of what he should attend.— / Good cousin, give me audience for a while.
He imagines a world of fancies here, but not the real business he should be attending to. Good nephew, listen to me for a while.
Those same noble Scots / That are your prisoners,—
Those noble Scots who are your prisoners,
I'll keep them all; / By God, he shall not have a Scot of them; / No, if a Scot would save his soul, he shall not: / I'll keep them, by this hand.
I'll keep them all. By God, he won't have a single Scot of them. No, not if a Scot could save his soul by it, he won't. I'll keep them, by this hand.
You start away, / And lend no ear unto my purposes. / Those prisoners you shall keep;—
You fly off and don't listen to what I'm proposing. You will keep those prisoners;

Nay, I will; that's flat. / He said he would not ransom Mortimer; / Forbade my tongue to speak of Mortimer; / But I will find him when he lies asleep, / And in his ear I'll holla Mortimer! / Nay, / I'll have a starling shall be taught to speak / Nothing but Mortimer, and give it him, / To keep his anger still in motion.

Yes, I will, and that's final. He said he wouldn't ransom Mortimer, forbade me even to speak of Mortimer, but I'll find him when he's asleep and shout "Mortimer!" in his ear. No, I'll get a starling taught to say nothing but "Mortimer" and give it to him, to keep his anger always on the boil.

All studies here I solemnly defy, / Save how to gall and pinch this Bolingbroke: / And that same sword-and-buckler Prince of Wales, / But that I think his father loves him not, / And would be glad he met with some mischance, / I'd have him poison'd with a pot of ale.

I solemnly reject every pursuit here except how to annoy and torment this Bolingbroke. And that brawling Prince of Wales, if I didn't think his father doesn't love him and would be glad if some accident befell him, I'd have him poisoned with a pot of ale.
Farewell, kinsman: I will talk to you / When you are better temper'd to attend.
Goodbye, nephew. I'll talk to you when you're in a better mood to listen.
Why, what a wasp-stung and impatient fool / Art thou, to break into this woman's mood, / Tying thine ear to no tongue but thine own!
Why, what an impatient fool you are, like a man stung by a wasp, to fly into this womanish temper, listening to no tongue but your own!

Why, look you, I am whipp'd and scourged with rods, / Nettled, and stung with pismires, when I hear / Of this vile politician, Bolingbroke. / In Richard's time,—what do you call the place?— / A plague upon't!—it is in Gloucestershire;— / 'Twas where the madcap Duke his uncle kept, / His uncle York;—where I first bow'd my knee / Unto this king of smiles, this Bolingbroke;— / When you and he came back from Ravenspurg.

Well, look, I feel whipped and beaten with rods, stung by nettles and bitten by ants, when I hear about this vile schemer Bolingbroke. In Richard's time, what do you call the place? Plague take it! It's in Gloucestershire. It was where that mad Duke his uncle lived, his uncle York, where I first bowed my knee to this king of smiles, this Bolingbroke, when you and he came back from Ravenspurgh.

You say true:— / Why, what a candy deal of courtesy / This fawning greyhound then did proffer me! / Look, when his infant fortune came to age, / And, Gentle Harry Percy, and kind cousin,— / O, the Devil take such cozeners!—God forgive me!— / Good uncle, tell your tale; for I have done.

You're right. Why, what a sugary load of courtesy this fawning greyhound offered me then! "Look, when my infant fortune comes of age," and "Gentle Harry Percy," and "Kind cousin." Oh, the Devil take such cheats! God forgive me! Good uncle, tell your story, I've finished.
Nay, if you have not, to't again; / We'll stay your leisure.
No, if you haven't, go on again. We'll wait until you're ready.

Then once more to your Scottish prisoners. / Deliver them up without their ransom straight, / And make the Douglas' son your only mean / For powers in Scotland; which, for divers reasons / Which I shall send you written, be assured, / Will easily be granted.— / [To Northumberland] You, my lord, / Your son in Scotland being thus employ'd, / Shall secretly into the bosom creep / Of that same noble prelate, well beloved, / Th' Archbishop.

Then back to your Scottish prisoners. Hand them over at once without ransom, and use Douglas's son as your only go-between for raising forces in Scotland, which, for various reasons I'll send you in writing, I assure you will easily be granted. You, my lord, while your son is busy in Scotland like this, will secretly worm your way into the confidence of that noble and well-loved churchman, the Archbishop.

True; who bears hard / His brother's death at Bristol, the Lord Scroop. / I speak not this in estimation, / As what I think might be, but what I know / Is ruminated, plotted, and set down, / And only stays but to behold the face / Of that occasion that shall bring it on.

Yes, who resents his brother Lord Scroop's death at Bristol. I don't say this as a guess about what might happen, but as something I know has been considered, planned and written down, and only waits to see the right moment to bring it about.
I smell't: upon my life, it will do well.
I can smell it. On my life, it will work well.
Before the game's a-foot, thou still lett'st slip.
You always let the hounds loose before the hunt has started.
Why, it cannot choose but be a noble plot:— / And then the power of Scotland and of York / To join with Mortimer, ha?
Why, it can't help being a noble plot. And then the forces of Scotland and of York join with Mortimer, eh?
In faith, it is exceedingly well aim'd.

And 'tis no little reason bids us speed, / To save our heads by raising of a head; / For, bear ourselves as even as we can, / The King will always think him in our debt, / And think we think ourselves unsatisfied, / Till he hath found a time to pay us home: / And see already how he doth begin / To make us strangers to his looks of love.

And there's good reason for us to hurry, to save our heads by raising an army. However carefully we behave, the King will always think he's in our debt, and think that we think ourselves unrewarded, until he finds a chance to pay us off for good. And look how he's already beginning to withhold his friendly looks from us.
He does, he does: we'll be revenged on him.
He is, he is. We'll have revenge on him.

Cousin, farewell: no further go in this / Than I by letters shall direct your course. / When time is ripe,—which will be suddenly,— / I'll steal to Glendower and Lord Mortimer; / Where you and Douglas, and our powers at once, / As I will fashion it, shall happily meet, / To bear our fortunes in our own strong arms, / Which now we hold at much uncertainty.

Nephew, goodbye. Go no further in this than I direct you in my letters. When the time is ripe, which will be soon, I'll slip away to Glendower and Lord Mortimer, where you and Douglas and all our forces will meet together, as I'll arrange it, to hold our fortunes in our own strong arms, which at present are very uncertain.
Farewell, good brother: we shall thrive, I trust.
Goodbye, good brother. We will succeed, I trust.
Uncle, adieu: O, let the hours be short, / Till fields and blows and groans applaud our sport!
Uncle, goodbye. Oh, let the hours be short until battlefields, blows and groans applaud our game!
Heigh-ho! an't be not four by the day, I'll be hang'd: / Charles' wain is over the new chimney, and yet our horse' not / pack'd.—What, ostler!
Heigh-ho! If it isn't four in the morning, I'll be hanged. The Plough constellation is over the new chimney, and our horse still isn't loaded. Hey, stable-boy!
I pr'ythee, Tom, beat Cut's saddle, put a few flocks in the / point; the poor jade is wrung in the withers out of all cess.
Please, Tom, soften Cut's saddle and put a bit of padding under the pommel. The poor nag's shoulders are rubbed raw beyond all measure.
Peas and beans are as dank here as a dog, and that is the / next way to give poor jades the bots; this house is turned / upside down since Robin ostler died.
The peas and beans here are as damp as a dog, and that's the quickest way to give poor horses worms. This inn has gone to pieces since Robin the stable-boy died.
Poor fellow! never joyed since the price of oats rose; it was / the death of him.
Poor man! He was never happy after the price of oats went up; it was the death of him.
I think this be the most villainous house in all London road / for fleas: I am stung like a tench.
I think this is the worst inn on the whole London road for fleas. I've been bitten so much I'm spotted like a tench.
Like a tench! by the Mass, there is ne'er a king in Christendom / could be better bit than I have been since the first cock.—What, / ostler! come away and be hang'd; come away.
Like a tench! By the Mass, no king in Christendom could have been better bitten than I've been since the first cock crowed. Hey, stable-boy! Come on, and be hanged, come on.
I have a gammon of bacon and two razes of ginger, to be / delivered as far as Charing-cross.
I have a leg of bacon and two roots of ginger to be delivered all the way to Charing Cross.

'Odsbody! the turkeys in my pannier are quite starved.—What, / ostler! A plague on thee! hast thou never an eye in thy head? / canst not hear? An 'twere not as good a deed as drink to break / the pate of thee, I am a very villain. Come, and be hang'd: / hast no faith in thee?

God's body! The turkeys in my basket are half starved. Hey, stable-boy! Plague on you! Haven't you got eyes in your head? Can't you hear? If cracking your skull wouldn't be as good a deed as having a drink, I'm a real villain. Come on, and be hanged! Have you no honesty in you?
Good morning, carriers. What time is it?
I think it be two o'clock.
I pr'ythee, lend me thy lantern, to see my gelding in the / stable.
Please lend me your lantern so I can look at my horse in the stable.
Nay, soft, I pray ye; I know a trick worth two of that, i'faith.
No, wait a minute. I know a trick worth two of that, I swear.
Ay, when? canst tell? Lend me thy lantern, quoth a? marry, I'll / see thee hang'd first.
Yes, when? Can you say? "Lend me your lantern," he says! By God, I'll see you hanged first.
Sirrah carrier, what time do you mean to come to London?
Fellow carrier, what time do you mean to reach London?
Time enough to go to bed with a candle, I warrant thee.— / Come, neighbour Muggs, we'll call up the gentlemen: they will / along with company, for they have great charge.
In good time to go to bed by candlelight, I promise you. Come on, neighbour Muggs, we'll wake the gentlemen. They want to travel in company, because they're carrying a lot of valuables.
That's even as fair as—at hand, quoth the chamberlain; for / thou variest no more from picking of purses than giving / direction doth from labouring; thou lay'st the plot how.
That's as good as "Right here," said the chamberlain, because you're no different from a pickpocket, just as giving orders is no different from doing the work: you plan how it's done.

Good morrow, Master Gadshill. It holds current that I told / you yesternight: there's a franklin in the wild of Kent hath / brought three hundred marks with him in gold: I heard him / tell it to one of his company last night at supper; a kind of / auditor; one that hath abundance of charge too, God knows what. / They are up already, and call for eggs and butter; they will away / presently.

Good morning, Master Gadshill. What I told you last night still holds. There's a rich farmer from the Weald of Kent who has brought three hundred marks in gold with him. I heard him tell one of his companions at supper last night, a sort of accountant, who's carrying plenty of valuables too, God knows what. They're up already and calling for eggs and butter; they'll be off soon.
Sirrah, if they meet not with Saint Nicholas' clerks, I'll give / thee this neck.
Friend, if they don't meet up with highwaymen, you can have my neck.
No, I'll none of it: I pr'ythee, keep that for the hangman; for / I know thou worshippest Saint Nicholas as truly as a man of / falsehood may.
No, I don't want it. Please save it for the hangman, because I know you worship Saint Nicholas, the patron of thieves, as faithfully as any dishonest man can.

What talkest thou to me of the hangman? if I hang, I'll make / a fat pair of gallows; for, if I hang, old Sir John hangs with / me, and thou know'st he is no starveling. Tut! there are other / Trojans that thou dreamest not of, the which, for sport-sake, / are content to do the profession some grace; that would, if / matters should be look'd into, for their own credit-sake, make / all whole. I am joined with no foot land-rakers, no long-staff / sixpenny strikers, none of these mad mustachio purple-hued / malt-worms; but with nobility and tranquillity, burgomasters and / great oneyers; such as can hold in, such as will strike sooner / than speak, and speak sooner than drink, and drink sooner than / pray: and yet, zwounds, I lie; for they pray continually to their / saint, the Commonwealth; or, rather, not pray to her, but prey on / her, for they ride up and down on her, and make her their boots.

Why are you talking to me about the hangman? If I hang, I'll make a fine fat pair of gallows, because if I hang, old Sir John hangs with me, and you know he's no skinny wretch. Nonsense! There are other fine fellows you don't dream of, who for fun are happy to lend our trade some dignity, and who, if things were looked into, would put everything right to protect their own reputations. I don't keep company with footpads, with petty muggers armed with long staffs, or with those wild, moustached, purple-faced beer drinkers, but with nobles and quiet gentlemen, mayors and great ones, men who can keep their mouths shut, who will strike before they speak, and speak before they drink, and drink before they pray. And yet, by God's wounds, I'm lying, because they pray constantly to their saint, the Commonwealth; or rather, they don't pray to her but prey on her, because they ride up and down on her and use her as their boots.
What, the Commonwealth their boots? will she hold out water / in foul way?
What, they use the Commonwealth as their boots? Will she keep the water out on a muddy road?
She will, she will; justice hath liquor'd her. We steal as in a / castle, cock-sure; we have the receipt of fernseed,—we walk / invisible.
She will, she will. Justice has greased her well. We steal as safely as if we were in a castle. We have the recipe for fern-seed: we walk invisible.
Nay, by my faith, I think you are more beholding to the night / than to fern-seed for your walking invisible.
No, I swear, I think you owe more to the darkness than to fern-seed for your walking invisible.
Give me thy hand: thou shalt have a share in our purchase, as / I am a true man.
Give me your hand. You'll have a share of our loot, as I'm an honest man.
Nay, rather let me have it, as you are a false thief.
No, I'd rather have it as you're a dishonest thief.
Go to; homo is a common name to all men. Bid the ostler / bring my gelding out of the stable. Farewell, you muddy knave.
Get away! "Man" is a name common to everyone. Tell the stable-boy to bring my horse out of the stable. Goodbye, you dirty rascal.
Come, shelter, shelter: I have remov'd Falstaff's horse, / and he frets like a gumm'd velvet.
Come on, hide, hide! I've moved Falstaff's horse, and he's fretting like cheap velvet stiffened with gum.
Pointz! Pointz, and be hang'd! Pointz!
Poins! Poins, and be hanged! Poins!
[Coming forward] Peace, ye fat-kidney'd rascal! what a brawling dost thou keep!
Quiet, you fat-guts rascal! What a racket you're making!
He is walk'd up to the top of the hill: I'll go seek him.
He's walked up to the top of the hill. I'll go and look for him.

I am accursed to rob in that thief's company: the rascal hath / removed my horse, and tied him I know not where. If I travel but / four foot by the squire further a-foot, I shall break my wind. / Well, I doubt not but to die a fair death for all this, if I 'scape / hanging for killing that rogue. I have forsworn his company hourly / any time this two-and-twenty year, and yet I am bewitch'd with the / rogue's company. If the rascal have not given me medicines to make / me love him, I'll be hang'd; it could not be else: I have drunk / medicines.— / Pointz!—Hal!—a plague upon you both!—Bardolph!—Peto!—I'll / starve, ere I'll rob a foot further. An 'twere not as good a deed as / drink, to turn true man, and to leave these rogues, I am the veriest / varlet that ever chewed with a tooth. Eight yards of uneven ground / is threescore and ten miles a-foot with me; and the stony-hearted / villains know it well enough: a plague upon't, when thieves cannot / be true one to another! / [They whistle] Whew!—A plague upon you all! Give me / my horse, you rogues; give me my horse, and be hang'd!

I'm cursed to be robbing in that thief's company. The rascal has moved my horse and tied him up I don't know where. If I walk even four more feet by the measuring rule, I'll run out of breath. Well, I'm sure I'll die a respectable death after all this, if I escape hanging for killing that rogue. I've sworn off his company every hour for the last twenty-two years, and yet I'm bewitched by the rascal. If he hasn't given me love potions to make me love him, I'll be hanged. It can't be anything else: I've drunk potions. Poins! Hal! A plague on both of you! Bardolph! Peto! I'll starve before I rob a foot further. If turning honest and leaving these rogues isn't as good a deed as drinking, I'm the worst scoundrel that ever chewed with a tooth. Eight yards of rough ground is seventy miles on foot to me, and the stony-hearted villains know it well enough. A plague on it, when thieves can't be honest with one another! Whew! A plague on you all! Give me my horse, you rogues, give me my horse, and be hanged!
[Coming forward] Peace! lie down; lay thine ear close to the / ground, and list if thou canst hear the tread of travellers.
Quiet! Lie down, put your ear close to the ground and listen whether you can hear travellers coming.
Have you any levers to lift me up again, being down? 'Sblood, I'll / not bear mine own flesh so far a-foot again for all the coin in thy / father's exchequer. What a plague mean ye to colt me thus?

Have you got any levers to lift me up again once I'm down? By God's blood, I won't carry my own flesh so far on foot again for all the money in your father's treasury. Why the plague are you tricking me like this?
Thou liest; thou art not colted, thou art uncolted.
You're lying; you're not tricked, you're un-horsed.
I pr'ythee, good Prince Hal, help me to my horse, good king's / son.
Please, good Prince Hal, help me to my horse, good king's son.
Out, ye rogue! shall I be your ostler?
Get away, you rogue! Am I supposed to be your stable-boy?

Go, hang thyself in thine own heir-apparent garters! If I be / ta'en, I'll peach for this. An I have not ballads made on you / all, and sung to filthy tunes, let a cup of sack be my poison. / When a jest is so forward, and a-foot too, I hate it.

Go and hang yourself with your own heir-apparent garters! If I'm caught, I'll turn informer about this. If I don't have ballads written about you all and sung to dirty tunes, let a cup of sherry be my poison. When a joke goes this far, and on foot too, I hate it.
So I do, against my will.
I'm doing that already, against my will.
O, 'tis our setter: I know his voice.
Oh, it's our scout; I know his voice.
Case ye, case ye; on with your visards: there's money of / the King's coming down the hill; 'tis going to the King's / exchequer.
Mask up, mask up, put your masks on. There's money of the King's coming down the hill; it's on its way to the King's treasury.
You lie, ye rogue; 'tis going to the King's tavern.
You're lying, you rogue; it's on its way to the King's tavern.
There's enough to make us all.
There's enough to make all our fortunes.
Sirs, you four shall front them in the narrow lane; Ned / Pointz and I will walk lower; if they 'scape from your / encounter, then they light on us.
Gentlemen, you four will confront them in the narrow lane. Ned Poins and I will wait further down. If they escape from you, they'll run into us.
How many be there of them?
How many of them are there?
Zwounds, will they not rob us?
By God's wounds, won't they rob us?
What, a coward, Sir John Paunch?
What, are you a coward, Sir John Paunch?
Indeed, I am not John of Gaunt, your grandfather; but yet / no coward, Hal.
Well, I'm not John of Gaunt, your grandfather, but I'm still no coward, Hal.
Well, we leave that to the proof.
Well, we'll leave that to be proved.
Sirrah Jack, thy horse stands behind the hedge: when thou / need'st him, there thou shalt find him. Farewell, and stand fast.
Jack, my friend, your horse is behind the hedge. When you need him, you'll find him there. Goodbye, and stand firm.
Now cannot I strike him, if I should be hang'd.
Now I can't hit him, even if I were to be hanged for not doing it.
[aside to POINTZ] Ned, where are our disguises?
[aside to PRINCE HENRY] Here, hard by: stand close.
Here, close by. Keep out of sight.
Now, my masters, happy man be his dole, say I: every man / to his business.
Now, gentlemen, good luck to every man, I say. Everyone to his job.
Come, neighbour: / The boy shall lead our horses down the hill; / We'll walk a-foot awhile and ease our legs.
Come, neighbour. The boy can lead our horses down the hill; we'll walk for a while and stretch our legs.
Strike; down with them; cut the villains' throats. Ah, / whoreson caterpillars! bacon-fed knaves! they hate us youth: / down with them; fleece them.
Strike! Down with them! Cut the villains' throats! Ah, you son-of-a-whore caterpillars, bacon-fed rascals! They hate us young folk. Down with them, fleece them!
O, we're undone, both we and ours for ever!
Oh, we're ruined, both we and our families, for ever!

Hang ye, gorbellied knaves, are ye undone? No, ye fat chuffs; / I would your store were here! On, bacons on! What, ye knaves! / young men must live. You are grand-jurors, are ye? we'll jure / ye, i'faith.

Hang you, you pot-bellied rascals, are you ruined? No, you fat misers, I wish all your wealth were here! Move, you pigs, move! What, you rascals, young men have to live. You're grand jurors, are you? We'll jury you, I swear.
The thieves have bound the true men. Now, could thou and I rob / the thieves, and go merrily to London, it would be argument for a / week, laughter for a month, and a good jest for ever.

The thieves have tied up the honest men. Now, if you and I could rob the thieves and ride merrily to London, it would be something to talk about for a week, to laugh about for a month, and a good joke for ever.
Stand close: I hear them coming.
Keep out of sight; I hear them coming.

Come, my masters, let us share, and then to horse before day. / An the Prince and Pointz be not two arrant cowards, there's no / equity stirring: there's no more valour in that Pointz than in a / wild duck.

Come on, gentlemen, let's share it out, and then to horse before daylight. If the Prince and Poins aren't two out-and-out cowards, there's no justice in the world. There's no more courage in that Poins than in a wild duck.

Got with much ease. Now merrily to horse: / The thieves are scatter'd, and possess'd with fear / So strongly that they dare not meet each other; / Each takes his fellow for an officer. / Away, good Ned. Fat Falstaff sweats to death, / And lards the lean earth as he walks along: / Were't not for laughing, I should pity him.

That was easily done. Now merrily to horse. The thieves are scattered and so gripped by fear that they don't dare meet up; each one thinks his friend is a constable. Come on, good Ned. Fat Falstaff is sweating himself to death and basting the lean earth with fat as he walks along. If I weren't laughing, I'd pity him.

—But, for mine own part, my lord, I could be well contented to / be there, in respect of the love I bear your House.—He could be / contented; why is he not, then? In respect of the love he bears / our House!—he shows in this, he loves his own barn better than he / loves our house. Let me see some more. The purpose you undertake / is dangerous;—Why, that's certain: 'tis dangerous to take a cold, / to sleep, to drink; but I tell you, my lord fool, out of this nettle, / danger, we pluck this flower, safety. The purpose you undertake is / dangerous; the friends you have named uncertain; the time itself / unsorted; and your whole plot too light for the counterpoise of so / great an opposition.— / Say you so, say you so? I say unto you again, you are a shallow, / cowardly hind, and you lie. What a lack-brain is this! By the Lord, / our plot is a good plot as ever was laid; our friends true and / constant: a good plot, good friends, and full of expectation; an / excellent plot, very good friends. What a frosty-spirited rogue is / this! Why, my Lord of York commends the plot and the general course / of the action. Zwounds! an I were now by this rascal, I could brain / him with his lady's fan. Is there not my father, my uncle, and / myself? Lord Edmund Mortimer, my Lord of York, and Owen Glendower? / is there not, besides, the Douglas? have I not all their letters to / meet me in arms by the ninth of the next month? and are they not / some of them set forward already? What a pagan rascal is this! an / infidel! Ha! you shall see now, in very sincerity of fear and cold / heart, will he to the King, and lay open all our proceedings. O, I / could divide myself, and go to buffets, for moving such a dish of / skimm'd milk with so honourable an action! / Hang him! let him tell the King: we are prepared. I will set / forward to-night.—

"But for my own part, my lord, I would be glad to be there, because of the love I bear your family." He would be glad to; then why isn't he? "Because of the love he bears our family!" He shows by this that he loves his own barn better than our house. Let me see some more. "The plan you are undertaking is dangerous." Well, that's certain: it's dangerous to catch a cold, to sleep, to drink. But I tell you, my lord fool, out of this nettle, danger, we pick this flower, safety. "The plan you are undertaking is dangerous, the friends you have named unreliable, the timing itself badly chosen, and your whole plot too weak to balance against such a great opposition." Is that what you say, is that what you say? I say to you again, you're a shallow, cowardly peasant, and you're lying. What a brainless fool this is! By God, our plot is as good a plot as was ever laid, our friends true and loyal: a good plot, good friends, and full of promise; an excellent plot, very good friends. What a cold-blooded rogue this is! Why, my lord of York approves of the plot and the whole course of action. By God's wounds, if I were next to this rascal now, I could brain him with his lady's fan. Aren't there my father, my uncle and myself? Lord Edmund Mortimer, my lord of York and Owen Glendower? And besides them, isn't there Douglas? Don't I have letters from all of them promising to meet me in arms by the ninth of next month? And haven't some of them set out already? What a godless rascal this is, an unbeliever! Ha! Now you'll see him, in pure fear and cowardice, go to the King and reveal everything we're doing. Oh, I could split myself in two and start punching myself, for trying to interest such a bowl of skimmed milk in such an honourable enterprise! Hang him! Let him tell the King, we're ready. I'll set out tonight.
How now, Kate! I must leave you within these two hours.
What's the matter, Kate? I must leave you within these two hours.

O, my good lord, why are you thus alone? / For what offence have I this fortnight been / A banish'd woman from my Harry's bed? / Tell me, sweet lord, what is't that takes from thee / Thy stomach, pleasure, and thy golden sleep? / Why dost thou bend thine eyes upon the earth, / And start so often when thou sitt'st alone? / Why hast thou lost the fresh blood in thy cheeks; / And given my treasures and my rights of thee / To thick-eyed musing and curst melancholy? / In thy faint slumbers I by thee have watch'd, / And heard thee murmur tales of iron wars; / Speak terms of manage to thy bounding steed; / Cry Courage! to the field! And thou hast talk'd / Of sallies and retires, of trenches, tents, / Of palisadoes, frontiers, parapets, / Of basilisks, of cannon, culverin, / Of prisoners ransomed, and of soldiers slain, / And all the 'currents of a heady fight. / Thy spirit within thee hath been so at war, / And thus hath so bestirr'd thee in thy sleep, / That beads of sweat have stood upon thy brow, / Like bubbles in a late-disturbed stream; / And in thy face strange motions have appear'd, / Such as we see when men restrain their breath / On some great sudden hest. O, what portents are these? / Some heavy business hath my lord in hand, / And I must know it, else he loves me not.

Oh, my good lord, why are you always alone like this? What have I done to be banished from my Harry's bed for this fortnight? Tell me, sweet lord, what is it that takes away your appetite, your pleasure and your precious sleep? Why do you keep your eyes fixed on the ground, and start so often when you sit alone? Why have you lost the fresh colour in your cheeks, and given away my treasures and my rights in you to dull-eyed brooding and bad-tempered gloom? As you slept fitfully, I've watched over you and heard you mutter stories of iron wars, give riding commands to your leaping horse, and shout "Courage! To the battlefield!" And you've talked of attacks and retreats, of trenches and tents, of fences of stakes, forts and parapets, of heavy guns, cannon and light cannon, of prisoners ransomed and soldiers killed, and all the events of a furious battle. Your spirit inside you has been so much at war, and has so stirred you up in your sleep, that beads of sweat have stood on your forehead like bubbles in a stream that has just been disturbed, and strange expressions have crossed your face, like those we see when men hold their breath at some great and sudden command. Oh, what do these signs mean? My lord has some serious business in hand, and I must know it, or else he doesn't love me.
Is Gilliams with the packet gone?
Has Gilliams gone with the letters?
He is, my lord, an hour ago.
He has, my lord, an hour ago.
Hath Butler brought those horses from the sheriff?
Has Butler brought those horses from the sheriff?
One horse, my lord, he brought even now.
He brought one horse just now, my lord.
What horse? a roan, a crop-ear, is it not?
What horse? A roan with clipped ears, isn't it?
That roan shall be my throne. / Well, I will back him straight: O esperance!— / Bid Butler lead him forth into the park.
That roan will be my throne. Well, I'll ride him at once. Oh, hope! Tell Butler to lead him out into the park.
What do you say, my lady?
What is it carries you away?
What is it that's carrying you away?
Why, my horse, my love, my horse.
Why, my horse, my love, my horse.

Out, you mad-headed ape! / A weasel hath not such a deal of spleen / As you are toss'd with. In faith, / I'll know your business, Harry, that I will. / I fear my brother Mortimer doth stir / About his title, and hath sent for you / To line his enterprise: but if you go,—

Get away, you mad-headed monkey! A weasel isn't as hot-tempered as you are. I swear I'll know your business, Harry, I will. I'm afraid my brother Mortimer is stirring up trouble about his claim to the throne and has sent for you to back his enterprise. But if you go,
So far a-foot, I shall be weary, love.
So far on foot, I'll get tired, love.
Come, come, you paraquito, answer me / Directly to this question that I ask: / In faith, I'll break thy little finger, Harry, / An if thou wilt not tell me true.
Come on, come on, you parrot, give me a straight answer to my question. I swear I'll break your little finger, Harry, if you won't tell me the truth.

Away, / Away, you trifler! Love? I love thee not, / I care not for thee, Kate: this is no world / To play with mammets and to tilt with lips: / We must have bloody noses and crack'd crowns, / And pass them current too.—Gods me, my horse!— / What say'st thou, Kate? what wouldst thou have with me?

Go away, go away, you time-waster! Love? I don't love you, I don't care about you, Kate. This is no time to play with dolls and joust with lips. We must have bloody noses and broken heads, and pass them around like coins too. God save me, my horse! What do you say, Kate? What do you want with me?
Do you not love me? do you not indeed? / Well, do not, then; for, since you love me not, / I will not love myself. Do you not love me? / Nay, tell me if you speak in jest or no.
Don't you love me? Don't you really? Well then, don't, because if you don't love me, I won't love myself. Don't you love me? No, tell me whether you're joking or not.

Come, wilt thou see me ride? / And when I am o' horseback, I will swear / I love thee infinitely. But hark you, Kate; / I must not have you henceforth question me / Whither I go, nor reason whereabout: / Whither I must, I must; and, to conclude, / This evening must I leave you, gentle Kate. / I know you wise; but yet no further wise / Than Harry Percy's wife; constant you are; / But yet a woman: and, for secrecy, / No lady closer; for I well believe / Thou wilt not utter what thou dost not know; / And so far will I trust thee, gentle Kate.

Come, will you watch me ride? And when I'm on horseback, I'll swear I love you infinitely. But listen, Kate, from now on you mustn't question me about where I'm going or why. Where I must go, I must go. And, to sum up, I must leave you this evening, gentle Kate. I know you're wise, but no wiser than Harry Percy's wife should be. You're faithful, but still a woman. And as for keeping secrets, no lady keeps them better, because I'm quite sure you won't reveal what you don't know. That's how far I'll trust you, gentle Kate.
Not an inch further. But hark you, Kate: / Whither I go, thither shall you go too; / To-day will I set forth, to-morrow you. / Will this content you, Kate?
Not an inch further. But listen, Kate: where I go, you'll go too. I'll set out today, you tomorrow. Will this satisfy you, Kate?
Ned, pr'ythee, come out of that fat room, and lend me thy / hand to laugh a little.
Ned, please come out of that stuffy room and help me laugh a little.

With three or four loggerheads amongst three or fourscore / hogsheads. I have sounded the very base-string of humility. / Sirrah, I am sworn brother to a leash of drawers; and can call / them all by their Christian names, as, Tom, Dick, and Francis. / They take it already upon their salvation, that though I be but / Prince of Wales, yet I am the king of courtesy; and tell me flatly / I am no proud Jack, like Falstaff, but a corinthian, a lad of mettle, / a good boy,—by the Lord, so they call me;—and, when I am King / of England, I shall command all the good lads in Eastcheap. They / call drinking deep, dying scarlet; and, when you breathe in your / watering, they cry hem! and bid you play it off.
