To conclude, I am / so good a proficient in one quarter of an hour, that I can drink with / any tinker in his own language during my life. I tell thee, Ned, thou / hast lost much honour, that thou wert not with me in this action. But, / sweet Ned,—to sweeten which name of Ned, I give thee this pennyworth / of sugar, clapp'd even now into my hand by an under-skinker; one that / never spake other English in his life than Eight shillings and sixpence, / and You are welcome; with this shrill addition, Anon, anon, sir! Score / a pint of bastard in the Half-moon,—or so. But, Ned, to drive away / the time till Falstaff come, I pr'ythee, do thou stand in some by-room, / while I question my puny drawer to what end he gave me the sugar; / and do thou never leave calling Francis! that his tale to me may be / nothing but Anon. Step aside, and I'll show thee a precedent.

With three or four blockheads among sixty or eighty barrels of wine. I've plucked the lowest string of humility. My friend, I'm sworn brother to a trio of barmen and can call them all by their first names, Tom, Dick and Francis. They already swear on their salvation that though I'm only Prince of Wales, I'm the king of courtesy, and tell me straight out that I'm no stuck-up fellow like Falstaff, but a good-time lad, a lad of spirit, a good boy (by God, that's what they call me), and that when I'm King of England I'll have all the good lads in Eastcheap at my command. They call heavy drinking "dyeing scarlet", and when you pause for breath while drinking, they cry "Hem!" and tell you to knock it back. In short, I learned so much in a quarter of an hour that I can drink with any tinker in his own slang for the rest of my life. I tell you, Ned, you lost a lot of honour by not being with me in this campaign. But, sweet Ned, to sweeten the name of Ned I give you this pennyworth of sugar, which a junior barman pushed into my hand just now, one who has never spoken any other English in his life than "Eight shillings and sixpence," and "You are welcome," with the shrill addition, "Coming, coming, sir! Put a pint of sweet wine on the Half-moon room's bill," or something like that. But, Ned, to pass the time till Falstaff comes, please stand in some side room while I ask my little barman why he gave me the sugar, and you keep calling "Francis!" so that all he can say to me is "Coming." Step aside, and I'll show you an example.
Anon, anon, sir.—Look down into the Pomegranate, Ralph.
Coming, coming, sir. Look in on the Pomegranate room, Ralph.
How long hast thou to serve, Francis?
How long have you got left of your apprenticeship, Francis?
Forsooth, five years, and as much as to—
Truly, five years, and as much as to...
Five year! by'r Lady, a long lease for the clinking of / pewter. But, Francis, darest thou be so valiant as to play / the coward with thy indenture and show it a fair pair of heels / and run from it?

Five years! By Our Lady, that's a long contract for clinking pewter pots. But, Francis, would you dare to be brave enough to play the coward with your contract, show it a clean pair of heels and run away from it?
O Lord, sir, I'll be sworn upon all the books in England, / I could find in my heart—
Oh Lord, sir, I'll swear on every Bible in England, I could find it in my heart...
Let me see,—about Michaelmas next I shall be—
Let me see, about next Michaelmas I'll be...
Anon, sir.—Pray you, stay a little, my lord.
Coming, sir. Please wait a moment, my lord.
Nay, but hark you, Francis: for the sugar thou gavest / me, 'twas a pennyworth, was't not?
No, but listen, Francis. That sugar you gave me, it was a pennyworth, wasn't it?
O Lord, sir, I would it had been two!
Oh Lord, sir, I wish it had been two!
I will give thee for it a thousand pound: ask me when / thou wilt, and thou shalt have it.
I'll give you a thousand pounds for it. Ask me whenever you like, and you'll have it.
Anon, Francis? No, Francis; but to-morrow, Francis; or, / Francis, a Thursday; or, indeed, Francis, when thou wilt. But, / Francis,—
Coming, Francis? No, Francis, but tomorrow, Francis; or Thursday, Francis; or, really, Francis, whenever you like. But, Francis,
—wilt thou rob this leathern-jerkin, crystal-button, / nott-pated, agate-ring, puke-stocking, caddis-garter, / smooth-tongue, Spanish-pouch,—
will you rob this leather-jacketed, crystal-buttoned, crop-haired, agate-ringed, dark-stockinged, cheap-gartered, smooth-talking, Spanish-pursed fellow?
O Lord, sir, who do you mean?
Oh Lord, sir, who do you mean?
Why, then, your brown bastard is your only drink; for, / look you, Francis, your white canvas doublet will sully: in / Barbary, sir, it cannot come to so much.
Why then, cheap brown wine is your only drink, because, look, Francis, your white canvas jacket will get dirty. In Barbary, sir, it can't come to so much.
Away, you rogue! dost thou not hear them call?
Go on, you rogue! Can't you hear them calling?
What, stand'st thou still, and hear'st such a calling? Look / to the guests within. [Exit Francis]—My lord, old Sir John, / with half-a-dozen more, are at the door: shall I let them in?
What, are you standing still when you hear such calling? Look after the guests inside. My lord, old Sir John and half a dozen others are at the door. Shall I let them in?
Let them alone awhile, and then open the door.
Let them wait a while, then open the door.
Sirrah, Falstaff and the rest of the thieves are at the / door: shall we be merry?
My friend, Falstaff and the rest of the thieves are at the door. Shall we have some fun?
As merry as crickets, my lad. But hark ye; what cunning / match have you made with this jest of the drawer? Come, / what's the issue?
As merry as crickets, my lad. But listen, what clever game were you playing with this joke on the barman? Come on, what's the point of it?
I am now of all humours that have showed themselves humours / since the old days of goodman Adam to the pupil age of this / present twelve o'clock at midnight.—What's o'clock, Francis?
I'm in the mood for every mood that has existed since the old days of good old Adam up to the young hour of this present midnight. What's the time, Francis?

That ever this fellow should have fewer words than a parrot, and / yet the son of a woman! His industry is up-stairs and down-stairs; / his eloquence the parcel of a reckoning. I am not yet of Percy's / mind, the Hotspur of the North; he that kills me some six or seven / dozen of Scots at a breakfast, washes his hands, and says to his wife, / Fie upon this quiet life! I want work. O my sweet Harry, says she, / how many hast thou kill'd to-day? Give my roan horse a drench, / says he; and answers, Some fourteen, an hour after,—a trifle, a / trifle. / I pr'ythee, call in Falstaff: I'll play Percy, and that damn'd / brawn shall play Dame Mortimer his wife. Rivo! says the drunkard. / Call in ribs, call in tallow.

To think that this fellow should know fewer words than a parrot, and yet be born of a woman! His work is running upstairs and downstairs, his eloquence is reading out a bill. I'm not yet in the same mood as Percy, the Hotspur of the North, who kills six or seven dozen Scots before breakfast, washes his hands and says to his wife, "Damn this quiet life! I want work." "Oh my sweet Harry," she says, "how many have you killed today?" "Give my roan horse a dose of medicine," he says, and answers, an hour later, "About fourteen. A trifle, a trifle." Please call in Falstaff. I'll play Percy, and that damned pig will play Lady Mortimer his wife. "Cheers!" says the drunkard. Call in the ribs, call in the lard.
Welcome, Jack: where hast thou been?
Welcome, Jack. Where have you been?

A plague of all cowards, I say, and a vengeance too! marry, and / amen!— / Give me a cup of sack, boy.—Ere I lead this life long, I'll sew / nether-stocks, and mend them and foot them too. A plague of all / cowards!— / Give me a cup of sack, rogue.—Is there no virtue extant?

A plague on all cowards, I say, and a curse on them too! Indeed, and amen! Give me a cup of sherry, boy. Before I lead this life much longer, I'll take up sewing stockings, mending them and putting new feet on them too. A plague on all cowards! Give me a cup of sherry, you rogue. Is there no courage left in the world?
Didst thou never see Titan kiss a dish of butter? pitiful-hearted / butter, that melted at the sweet tale of the Sun! if thou didst, / then behold that compound.
Did you ever see the sun kiss a dish of butter? Soft-hearted butter, which melted at the sun's sweet talk! If you did, look at that mixture there.

You rogue, here's lime in this sack too: there is nothing but roguery / to be found in villainous man: yet a coward is worse than a cup of / sack with lime in it, a villanous coward.—Go thy ways, old Jack: die / when thou wilt, if manhood, good manhood, be not forgot upon the face / of the Earth, then am I a shotten herring. There live not three good / men unhang'd in England; and one of them is fat, and grows old: God / help the while! a bad world, I say. / I would I were a weaver; I could sing psalms or any thing. A plague of / all cowards! I say still.

You rogue, there's lime in this sherry too. There's nothing but roguery to be found in villainous mankind. And yet a coward is worse than a cup of sherry with lime in it, a villainous coward. Go your way, old Jack, die when you like: if courage, real courage, isn't forgotten on the face of the earth, then I'm a spawned-out herring. There aren't three good men left unhanged in England, and one of them is fat and growing old. God help us! It's a bad world, I say. I wish I were a weaver; I could sing psalms or anything. A plague on all cowards, I still say.
How now, wool-sack? what mutter you?
What's up, you sack of wool? What are you muttering?

A king's son! If I do not beat thee out of thy kingdom with a dagger / of lath, and drive all thy subjects afore thee like a flock of / wild-geese, I'll never wear hair on my face more. You Prince of Wales!

A king's son! If I don't beat you out of your kingdom with a wooden dagger and drive all your subjects in front of you like a flock of wild geese, I'll never grow hair on my face again. You, Prince of Wales!
Why, you whoreson round man, what's the matter?
Why, you son-of-a-whore round man, what's the matter?
Are not you a coward? answer me to that:—and Pointz there?
Aren't you a coward? Answer me that. And Poins there?
Zwounds, ye fat paunch, an ye call me coward, by the Lord, I'll / stab thee.
By God's wounds, you fat belly, if you call me a coward, by God, I'll stab you.

I call thee coward! I'll see thee damn'd ere I call thee coward: / but I would give a thousand pound, I could run as fast as thou canst. / You are straight enough in the shoulders; you care not who sees your / back: call you that backing of your friends? A plague upon such / backing! give me them that will face me.—Give me a cup of sack: / I am a rogue, if I drunk to-day.

I call you a coward! I'll see you damned before I call you a coward. But I'd give a thousand pounds to be able to run as fast as you can. You've got nice straight shoulders, you don't care who sees your back. Do you call that backing up your friends? A plague on such backing! Give me men who will face me. Give me a cup of sherry. I'm a rogue if I've had a drink today.
O villain! thy lips are scarce wiped since thou drunk'st last.
Oh, you villain! Your lips are hardly wiped since your last drink.
All is one for that. A plague of all cowards! still say I.
It's all the same. A plague on all cowards, I still say.
What's the matter? there be four of us here have ta'en a thousand / pound this day morning.
What's the matter? There are four of us here who took a thousand pounds this morning.
Where is it, Jack? where is it?
Where is it, Jack? Where is it?
Where is it! taken from us it is: a hundred upon poor four of us!
Where is it! It's been taken from us. A hundred men attacked just the four of us!

I am a rogue, if I were not at half-sword with a dozen of them two / hours together. I have 'scaped by miracle. I am eight times thrust / through the doublet, four through the hose; my buckler cut through / and through; my sword hack'd like a hand-saw,—ecce signum! I never / dealt better since I was a man: all would not do. A plague of all / cowards! Let them speak: if they speak more or less than truth, / they are villains and the sons of darkness.

I'm a rogue if I wasn't at close quarters with a dozen of them for two hours. I escaped by a miracle. I've been stabbed eight times through my jacket and four through my breeches, my shield is cut right through, my sword is hacked like a handsaw, look, here's the proof! I never fought better since I became a man, and it was no use. A plague on all cowards! Let them tell you. If they say more or less than the truth, they're villains and sons of darkness.
Tell us, gentlemen, how did it happen?
We four set upon some dozen,—
We four attacked about a dozen,
No, no; they were not bound.
No, no, they weren't tied up.
You rogue, they were bound, every man of them; or I am a Jew / else, an Ebrew Jew.
You rogue, they were tied up, every one of them, or else I'm a Jew, a Hebrew Jew.
As we were sharing, some six or seven fresh men sea upon us,—
As we were sharing out the loot, six or seven fresh men attacked us,
And unbound the rest, and then come in the other.
And untied the rest, and then the others joined in.
What, fought you with them all?
What, did you fight with all of them?
All? I know not what you call all; but if I fought not with fifty / of them, I am a bunch of radish: if there were not two or three / and fifty upon poor old Jack, then am I no two-legged creature.
All? I don't know what you call all, but if I didn't fight fifty of them, I'm a bunch of radishes. If there weren't fifty-two or fifty-three against poor old Jack, then I'm no two-legged creature.
Pray God you have not murdered some of them.
I pray to God you haven't murdered some of them.

Nay, that's past praying for: I have pepper'd two of them; two I / am sure I have paid, two rogues in buckram suits. I tell thee what, / Hal, if I tell thee a lie, spit in my face, call me horse. / Thou knowest my old ward: here I lay, and thus I bore my point. / Four rogues in buckram let drive at me,—

No, it's too late to pray for that. I've peppered two of them. Two I've certainly finished off, two rogues in canvas suits. I'll tell you what, Hal, if I'm telling you a lie, spit in my face and call me a horse. You know my old fighting stance: here I stood, and this is how I held my sword. Four rogues in canvas came at me,
What, four? thou saidst but two even now.
What, four? You said only two just now.
Four, Hal; I told thee four.
Four, Hal; I told you four.
These four came all a-front, and mainly thrust at me. I made me no more / ado but took all their seven points in my target, thus.
These four came at me all from the front and thrust at me with all their might. I didn't make a fuss, I just took all their seven sword-points on my shield, like this.
Seven? why, there were but four even now.
Seven? Why, there were only four just now.
Seven, by these hilts, or I am a villain else.
Seven, by the hilt of this sword, or else I'm a villain.
[aside to Pointz] Pr'ythee let him alone; we shall have more / anon.
Please leave him alone; we'll have more in a minute.
Are you listening to me, Hal?
Ay, and mark thee too, Jack.
Yes, and taking note of you too, Jack.
Do so, for it is worth the listening to. These nine in buckram / that I told thee of,—
Do, because it's worth listening to. These nine in canvas that I told you about,
—began to give me ground: but I followed me close, came in foot / and hand; and with a thought seven of the eleven I paid.
began to give way. But I followed close, came in with foot and hand, and in a flash I finished off seven of the eleven.
O monstrous! eleven buckram men grown out of two!
Oh, monstrous! Eleven canvas men grown out of two!
But, as the Devil would have it, three misbegotten knaves in Kendal / Green came at my back and let drive at me; for it was so dark, Hal, / that thou couldst not see thy hand.
But, as the Devil would have it, three misbegotten rascals in Kendal green came up behind me and attacked me, because it was so dark, Hal, that you couldn't see your own hand.
These lies are like the father that begets them, gross as a mountain, / open, palpable. Why, thou nott-pated fool, thou whoreson, obscene / greasy tallow-keech,—
These lies are like the father who produces them, as huge as a mountain, open and obvious. Why, you thick-headed fool, you son of a whore, you obscene, greasy lump of lard,
What, art thou mad? art thou mad? is not the truth the truth?
What, are you mad? Are you mad? Isn't the truth the truth?
Why, how couldst thou know these men in Kendal green, when it was / so dark thou couldst not see thy hand? come, tell us your reason: / what sayest thou to this?
Why, how could you tell these men were in Kendal green when it was so dark you couldn't see your hand? Come on, give us your reason. What do you say to this?
Come, your reason, Jack, your reason.
Come on, your reason, Jack, your reason.

What, upon compulsion? No; were I at the strappado, or all the racks / in the world, I would not tell you on compulsion. Give you a reason on / compulsion! if reasons were as plentiful as blackberries, I would / give no man a reason upon compulsion, I.

What, under force? No. If I were being tortured on the strappado or all the racks in the world, I wouldn't tell you under force. Give you a reason under force! If reasons were as common as blackberries, I wouldn't give any man a reason under force, not I.
I'll be no longer guilty of this sin; this sanguine coward, this / bed-presser, this horse-back-breaker, this huge hill of flesh,—
I won't go on being guilty of this sin. This red-faced coward, this bed-breaker, this horse's-back-breaker, this huge hill of flesh,
Away, you starveling, you eel-skin, you dried neat's-tongue, you / stock-fish,— / O, for breath to utter what is like thee!—you tailor's-yard, you / sheath, you bow-case, you vile standing tuck,—

Get away, you starveling, you eel-skin, you dried ox-tongue, you dried cod! Oh, give me breath to say what you're like! You tailor's measuring stick, you sword sheath, you bow case, you vile upright rapier,
Well, breathe awhile, and then to it again: and, when thou hast / tired thyself in base comparisons, hear me speak but this:—
Well, take a breath, and then start again. And when you've worn yourself out with low comparisons, just listen to me say this.

—We two saw you four set on four; you bound them, and were masters of / their wealth.—Mark now, how a plain tale shall put you down.— / Then did we two set on you four; and, with a word, outfaced you from / your prize, and have it; yea, and can show it you here in the house: / and, Falstaff, you carried yourself away as nimbly, with as quick / dexterity, and roared for mercy, and still ran and roar'd, as ever I / heard bull-calf. What a slave art thou, to hack thy sword as thou / hast done, and then say it was in fight! / What trick, what device, what starting-hole canst thou now find / out to hide thee from this open and apparent shame?

We two saw you four attack four men. You tied them up and took their money. Now see how a plain story will defeat you. Then we two attacked you four, and with one word we scared you away from your loot and have it, yes, and can show it to you here in the inn. And, Falstaff, you carried your guts away as nimbly and quickly, roaring for mercy and still running and roaring, as any bull-calf I ever heard. What a wretch you are, to hack your sword the way you did and then say it was done in the fight! What trick, what device, what bolt-hole can you find now to hide you from this open and obvious shame?
Come, let's hear, Jack; what trick hast thou now?
Come on, let's hear it, Jack. What trick have you got now?

By the Lord, I knew ye as well as he that made ye. Why, hear ye, / my masters: / Was it for me to kill the heir-apparent? should I turn upon the / true Prince? why, thou knowest I am as valiant as Hercules: but / beware instinct; the lion will not touch the true Prince. / Instinct is a great matter; I was now a coward on instinct. / I shall think the better of myself and thee during my life; I for a / valiant lion, and thou for a true prince. But, by the Lord, lads, / I am glad you have the money.— / [To Hostess within] Hostess, clap-to the doors: watch / to-night, pray to-morrow.—Gallants, lads, boys, hearts of gold, / all the titles of good fellowship come to you! / What, shall we be merry? shall we have a play extempore?

By God, I knew you as well as the one who made you. Why, listen, gentlemen. Was it for me to kill the heir to the throne? Should I turn on the true Prince? Why, you know I'm as brave as Hercules, but beware of instinct: the lion won't touch the true prince. Instinct is a great thing; I was a coward on instinct. I'll think better of myself and of you for the rest of my life: of myself as a brave lion, and of you as a true prince. But, by God, lads, I'm glad you have the money. Landlady, shut the doors! Stay up tonight, pray tomorrow. Gallants, lads, boys, hearts of gold, may every title of good fellowship be yours! What, shall we have some fun? Shall we have an improvised play?
Content; and the argument shall be thy running away.
Agreed, and the plot will be your running away.
Ah, no more of that, Hal, an thou lovest me!
Ah, no more of that, Hal, if you love me!
O Jesu, my lord the Prince,—
Oh Jesus, my lord the Prince,
How now, my lady the hostess! What say'st thou to me?
Well, my lady the landlady! What do you have to say to me?
Marry, my lord, there is a nobleman of the Court at door would / speak with you: he says he comes from your father.
Well, my lord, there's a nobleman from the Court at the door who wants to speak to you. He says he comes from your father.
Give him as much as will make him a royal man, and send him back / again to my mother.
Give him enough to make him a royal man, and send him back to my mother.
What manner of man is he?
What sort of man is he?
What doth gravity out of his bed at midnight? Shall I give him / his answer?
What's an old greybeard doing out of bed at midnight? Shall I give him his answer?
Faith, and I'll send him packing.
Now, sirs:—by'r Lady, you fought fair;—so did you, Peto;—so did you, / Bardolph: you are lions, too, you ran away upon instinct, you will not / touch the true Prince; no,—fie!
Now, gentlemen, by Our Lady, you fought well. So did you, Peto, and so did you, Bardolph. You're lions too, you ran away on instinct, you won't touch the true prince. No, shame on you!
Faith, I ran when I saw others run.
Honestly, I ran when I saw others running.
Tell me now in earnest, how came Falstaff's sword so hack'd?
Now tell me seriously, how did Falstaff's sword get so hacked?
Why, he hack'd it with his dagger; and said he would swear truth out of / England, but he would make you believe it was done in fight; and / persuaded us to do the like.
Why, he hacked it with his dagger, and said he would swear truth right out of England but he'd make you believe it was done in the fight, and he persuaded us to do the same.

Yea, and to tickle our noses with spear-grass to make them bleed; / and then to beslubber our garments with it, and swear it was the / blood of true men. I did that I did not this seven year before; / I blush'd to hear his monstrous devices.

Yes, and to tickle our noses with spear-grass to make them bleed, and then smear our clothes with it and swear it was the blood of honest men. I did something I hadn't done for seven years: I blushed to hear his outrageous schemes.

O villain, thou stolest a cup of sack eighteen years ago, and wert / taken with the manner, and ever since thou hast blush'd extempore. / Thou hadst fire and sword on thy side, and yet thou rann'st away: / what instinct hadst thou for it?

Oh, you villain, you stole a cup of sherry eighteen years ago and were caught red-handed, and you've been blushing on the spot ever since. You had fire and sword on your side, and still you ran away. What instinct did you have for that?
My lord, do you see these meteors? do you behold these / exhalations?
My lord, do you see these meteors? Do you see these fiery vapours?
What do you think they mean?
Choler, my lord, if rightly taken.
Bad temper, my lord, if rightly understood.
No, if rightly taken, halter.—Here comes lean Jack, here comes / bare-bone.—
No, if rightly taken, the hangman's rope. Here comes lean Jack, here comes the bag of bones.
How now, my sweet creature of bombast! How long is't ago, Jack, / since thou saw'st thine own knee?
Well, my sweet creature stuffed with padding! How long is it, Jack, since you last saw your own knee?

My own knee! when I was about thy years, Hal, I was not an eagle's / talon in the waist; I could have crept into any alderman's thumb-ring: / a plague of sighing and grief! it blows a man up like a bladder. / There's villanous news abroad: here was Sir John Bracy from your / father; you must to the Court in the morning. / That same mad fellow of the North, Percy; and he of Wales, that gave / Amaimon the bastinado, and swore the Devil his true liegeman upon the / cross of a Welsh hook,—what a plague call you him?

My own knee! When I was about your age, Hal, I wasn't as thick as an eagle's claw round the waist; I could have crept through an alderman's thumb ring. A plague on sighing and grief! It blows a man up like a balloon. There's terrible news about. Sir John Bracy was here from your father; you must go to Court in the morning. That same madman from the North, Percy, and the Welshman who beat the demon Amaimon and swore the Devil in as his loyal subject on the cross of a Welsh pike, what the plague do you call him?
Owen, Owen,—the same; and his son-in-law Mortimer; and old / Northumberland; and that sprightly Scot of Scots, Douglas, that / runs o' horseback up a hill perpendicular,—
Owen, Owen, that's the one; and his son-in-law Mortimer, and old Northumberland, and that lively Scot of Scots, Douglas, who can ride his horse straight up a vertical hill,
He that rides at high speed and with his pistol kills a sparrow / flying.
The one who rides at full gallop and kills a flying sparrow with his pistol.
So did he never the sparrow.
He never hit the sparrow, though.
Well, that rascal hath good metal in him; he will not run.
Well, that rascal has good spirit in him; he won't run away.
Why, what a rascal art thou, then, to praise him so for running!
Why, what a rascal you are, then, to praise him so much for running!
O' horseback, ye cuckoo! but a-foot he will not budge a foot.
On horseback, you cuckoo! But on foot he won't budge an inch.

I grant ye, upon instinct. Well, he is there too, and one Mordake, / and a thousand blue-caps more: / Worcester is stolen away to-night; thy father's beard is turn'd / white with the news: you may buy land now as cheap as stinking / mackerel. / But, tell me, Hal, art not thou horrible afeard? thou being / heir-apparent, could the world pick thee out three such enemies again / as that fiend Douglas, that spirit Percy, and that devil Glendower? / art thou not horribly afraid? doth not thy blood thrill at it?

I grant you, on instinct. Well, he's there too, and one Mordake, and a thousand more blue-bonneted Scots. Worcester has slipped away tonight. Your father's beard has turned white at the news. You can buy land now as cheap as rotten mackerel. But tell me, Hal, aren't you horribly afraid? You, the heir to the throne, could the world find you three such enemies again as that fiend Douglas, that spirit Percy and that devil Glendower? Aren't you horribly afraid? Doesn't your blood run cold at it?
Not a whit, i'faith; I lack some of thy instinct.
Not a bit, honestly. I lack some of your instinct.
Well, thou wilt be horribly chid to-morrow when thou comest to / thy father. If thou love life, practise an answer.
Well, you'll get a terrible telling-off tomorrow when you go to your father. If you value your life, rehearse an answer.
Do thou stand for my father and examine me upon the particulars / of my life.
You stand in for my father and question me about the details of my life.
Shall I? content: this chair shall be my state, this dagger my / sceptre, and this cushion my crown.
Shall I? All right. This chair will be my throne, this dagger my sceptre and this cushion my crown.
Thy state is taken for a joint-stool, thy golden sceptre for a / leaden dagger, and thy precious rich crown for a pitiful bald crown.
Your throne looks like a stool, your golden sceptre like a lead dagger, and your precious rich crown like a pitiful bald head.

Well, an the fire of grace be not quite out of thee, now shalt / thou be moved.— / Give me a cup of sack, to make my eyes look red, that it may be / thought I have wept; for I must speak in passion, and I will do it / in King Cambyses' vein.

Well, if the fire of grace isn't completely out in you, now you'll be moved. Give me a cup of sherry to make my eyes look red, so it'll be thought I've been crying, because I must speak with emotion, and I'll do it in the style of King Cambyses in the old play.
And here is my speech.—Stand aside, nobility.
And here's my speech. Stand aside, nobles.
O Jesu, this is excellent sport, i faith!
Oh Jesus, this is great fun, honestly!
Weep not, sweet Queen; for trickling tears are vain.
Weep not, sweet Queen, for trickling tears are vain.
O, the Father, how he holds his countenance!
Oh, Father, how straight he keeps his face!
For God's sake, lords, convey my tristful Queen; / For tears do stop the floodgates of her eyes.
For God's sake, lords, lead away my sorrowful Queen, for tears are blocking the floodgates of her eyes.
O Jesu, he doth it as like one of these harlotry players as ever / I see!
Oh Jesus, he does it just like one of those rascally actors I've seen!

Peace, good pint-pot; peace, good tickle-brain.—Harry, I do not / only marvel where thou spendest thy time, but also how thou art / accompanied: for though the camomile, the more it is trodden on, / the faster it grows, yet youth, the more it is wasted, the sooner / it wears. That thou art my son, I have partly thy mother's word, / partly my own opinion; but chiefly a villainous trick of thine eye, / and a foolish hanging of thy nether lip, that doth warrant me. If, / then, thou be son to me, here lies the point: Why, being son to me, / art thou so pointed at? / Shall the blessed Sun of heaven prove a micher, and eat blackberries? / a question not to be ask'd. Shall the son of England prove a thief, / and take purses? a question to be ask'd. / There is a thing, Harry, which thou hast often heard of, and it is / known to many in our land by the name of pitch: this pitch, as / ancient writers do report, doth defile; so doth the company thou / keepest: for, Harry, now I do not speak to thee in drink, but in / tears; not in pleasure, but in passion; not in words only, / but in woes also. And yet there is a virtuous man whom I have / often noted in thy company, but I know not his name.

Quiet, good pint-pot; quiet, good brain-tickler. Harry, I wonder not only where you spend your time but also what company you keep. For though camomile grows faster the more it is trodden on, youth wears out sooner the more it is wasted. That you are my son, I have partly your mother's word and partly my own opinion, but mainly a nasty habit of your eye and a silly drooping of your lower lip that convinces me. So if you are my son, here's the point: why, being my son, are you pointed at so much? Should the blessed sun of heaven play truant and eat blackberries? That's a question not to be asked. Should the son of England turn out a thief and steal purses? That's a question to be asked. There is something, Harry, which you have often heard of, known to many in our land by the name of pitch. This pitch, as ancient writers tell us, makes you dirty; so does the company you keep. For, Harry, I'm not speaking to you now in drink but in tears, not in pleasure but in sorrow, not in words only but in griefs too. And yet there is a virtuous man whom I have often seen in your company, but I don't know his name.
What manner of man, an it like your Majesty?
What sort of man, if it please your Majesty?

A goodly portly man, i'faith, and a corpulent; of a cheerful look, / a pleasing eye, and a most noble carriage; and, as I think, his age / some fifty, or, by'r Lady, inclining to threescore; and now I / remember me, his name is Falstaff: if that man should be lewdly given, / he deceiveth me; for, Harry, I see virtue in his looks. / If, then, the tree may be known by the fruit, as the fruit by the tree, / then, peremptorily I speak it, there is virtue in that Falstaff: him / keep with, the rest banish. And tell me now, thou naughty varlet, tell / me where hast thou been this month?

A fine, stately man, honestly, and a plump one, with a cheerful look, a pleasing eye and a most noble bearing. I think his age is about fifty, or, by Our Lady, nearer sixty. And now I remember, his name is Falstaff. If that man is wicked, he deceives me, because, Harry, I see virtue in his looks. If, then, the tree can be known by its fruit, as the fruit by the tree, then I say firmly there is virtue in that Falstaff. Keep company with him, banish the rest. And now tell me, you wicked rascal, tell me where you've been this month.
Dost thou speak like a king? Do thou stand for me, and I'll play / my father.
Do you call that speaking like a king? You stand in for me, and I'll play my father.
Depose me! if thou dost it half so gravely, so majestically, both / in word and matter, hang me up by the heels for a rabbit-sucker or a / poulter's hare.
Depose me! If you do it half as seriously and majestically, in both words and content, hang me up by the heels like a baby rabbit or a hare in a poultry shop.
And here I stand.—Judge, my masters.
And here I stand. Judge us, gentlemen.
Now, Harry, where have you come from?
The complaints I hear of thee are grievous.
The complaints I hear about you are serious.
'Sblood, my lord, they are false.—Nay, I'll tickle ye for a / young prince, i'faith.
By God's blood, my lord, they're false. No, I'll entertain you as a young prince, I promise.

Swearest thou, ungracious boy? henceforth ne'er look on me. Thou art / violently carried away from grace: there is a devil haunts thee, in / the likeness of an old fat man,—a tun of man is thy companion. Why / dost thou converse with that trunk of humours, that bolting-hutch of / beastliness, that swollen parcel of dropsies, that huge bombard of / sack, that roasted Manningtree ox with the pudding in his belly, that / reverend Vice, that grey Iniquity, that father ruffian, that vanity / in years? Wherein is he good, but to taste sack and drink it? wherein / neat and cleanly, but to carve a capon and eat it? wherein cunning, but / in craft? wherein crafty, but in villany? wherein villainous, but in / all things? wherein worthy, but in nothing?

Are you swearing, you graceless boy? From now on never look at me. You've been dragged violently away from grace. A devil haunts you in the form of a fat old man; a barrel of a man is your companion. Why do you keep company with that trunk full of diseases, that sieve-bin of beastliness, that swollen bundle of dropsy, that huge leather jug of sherry, that roasted Manningtree ox with the stuffing in its belly, that respected Vice, that grey-haired Iniquity, that old ruffian, that aged emptiness? What is he good for except tasting sherry and drinking it? What is he neat and clean at except carving a chicken and eating it? What is he clever at except cunning? Cunning at what except villainy? Villainous in what? In everything. Worthy in what? In nothing.
I would your Grace would take me with you: whom means your Grace?
I wish your Grace would let me follow you. Whom does your Grace mean?
That villainous abominable misleader of youth, Falstaff, that old / white-bearded Satan.
That villainous, abominable misleader of youth, Falstaff, that old white-bearded Satan.
My lord, the man I know.
My lord, I know the man.

But to say I know more harm in him than in myself, were to say more / than I know. That he is old,—(the more the pity,—his white hairs do / witness it. If sack and sugar be a fault, God help the wicked! if to / be old and merry be a sin, then many an old host that I know is damn'd: / if to be fat be to be hated, then Pharaoh's lean kine are to be loved. / No, my good lord: banish Peto, banish Bardolph, banish Pointz; but, / for sweet Jack Falstaff, kind Jack Falstaff, true Jack Falstaff, / valiant Jack Falstaff, and therefore more valiant, being, as he is, old / Jack Falstaff, banish not him thy Harry's company, banish not him thy / Harry's company: banish plump Jack, and banish all the world.

But to say I know more harm in him than in myself would be to say more than I know. That he's old, more's the pity, his white hairs prove. But if sherry and sugar are a crime, God help the wicked! If being old and merry is a sin, then many an old innkeeper I know is damned. If being fat means being hated, then Pharaoh's thin cows in the Bible are to be loved. No, my good lord: banish Peto, banish Bardolph, banish Poins. But sweet Jack Falstaff, kind Jack Falstaff, loyal Jack Falstaff, brave Jack Falstaff, and all the braver for being old Jack Falstaff, don't banish him from your Harry's company, don't banish him from your Harry's company. Banish plump Jack, and you banish all the world.
O, my lord, my lord! the sheriff with a most monstrous watch is / at the door.
Oh, my lord, my lord! The sheriff is at the door with an enormous body of watchmen.
Out, ye rogue!—Play out the play: I have much to say in the / behalf of that Falstaff.
Get out, you rogue! Finish the play. I have a lot to say on behalf of that Falstaff.
O Jesu, my lord, my lord,—
Oh Jesus, my lord, my lord,
Heigh, heigh! the Devil rides upon a fiddlestick: what's the matter?
Hey, hey! The Devil's riding a fiddlestick. What's the matter?
The sheriff and all the watch are at the door: they are come to / search the house. Shall I let them in?
The sheriff and the whole watch are at the door. They've come to search the house. Shall I let them in?
Dost thou hear, Hal? never call a true piece of gold a counterfeit: / thou art essentially mad without seeming so.
Do you hear, Hal? Never call a genuine gold coin a fake. You're really mad without seeming so.
And thou a natural coward, without instinct.
And you're a born coward, without instinct.

I deny your major: if you will deny the sheriff, so; if not, let him / enter: if I become not a cart as well as another man, a plague on my / bringing up! I hope I shall as soon be strangled with a halter as / another.

I deny your premise. If you'll refuse to let the sheriff in, fine; if not, let him come in. If I don't look as good in the hangman's cart as any other man, a plague on my upbringing! I hope I'll be strangled with a rope as quickly as anyone else.
Go, hide thee behind the arras:—the rest walk, up above. Now, / my masters, for a true face and good conscience.
Go and hide behind the tapestry. The rest of you, go upstairs. Now, gentlemen, for an honest face and a clear conscience.
Both which I have had; but their date is out, and therefore I'll / hide me.
I've had both of those, but they've expired, so I'll hide.
Now, master sheriff, what's your will with me?
Now, Master Sheriff, what do you want with me?
First, pardon me, my lord. A hue-and-cry / Hath followed certain men unto this house.
First, pardon me, my lord. A public pursuit has followed certain men to this house.
One of them is well known, my gracious lord,— / A gross fat man.
One of them is well known, my gracious lord, a huge fat man.

The man, I do assure you, is not here; / For I myself at this time have employ'd him. / And, sheriff, I will engage my word to thee, / That I will, by to-morrow dinner-time, / Send him to answer thee, or any man, / For any thing he shall be charged withal: / And so, let me entreat you leave the house.

The man, I assure you, is not here, because I've sent him on an errand myself. And, sheriff, I give you my word that by lunchtime tomorrow I'll send him to answer to you, or to any man, for anything he's accused of. So please leave the house.
I will, my lord. There are two gentlemen / Have in this robbery lost three hundred marks.
I will, my lord. Two gentlemen have lost three hundred marks in this robbery.
It may be so: if he have robb'd these men, / He shall be answerable; and so, farewell.
That may be so. If he robbed these men, he'll answer for it. And so, goodbye.
I think it is good morrow, is it not?
I think it's good morning, isn't it?
Indeed, my lord, I think't be two o'clock.
Yes, my lord, I think it's two o'clock.
This oily rascal is known as well as Paul's. Go, call him forth.
This greasy rascal is as well known as Saint Paul's Cathedral. Go and call him out.
Falstaff!—fast asleep behind the arras, and snorting like a / horse.
Falstaff! He's fast asleep behind the tapestry, snorting like a horse.
Hark, how hard he fetches breath. Search his pockets.
Listen to how hard he's breathing. Search his pockets.
Let's see what they be: read them.
Let's see what they are. Read them.
[Reads] Item, A capon, 2s. 2d. / Item, Sauce, 4d. / Item, Sack two gallons, 5s. 8d. / Item, Anchovies and sack after supper, 2s. 6d. / Item, Bread, ob.

Item, a chicken, two shillings and twopence. Item, sauce, fourpence. Item, sherry, two gallons, five shillings and eightpence. Item, anchovies and sherry after supper, two shillings and sixpence. Item, bread, a halfpenny.

O monstrous! but one half-pennyworth of bread to this intolerable / deal of sack! What there is else, keep close; we'll read it at more / advantage: there let him sleep till day. / I'll to the Court in the morning. We must all to the wars, and thy / place shall be honourable. I'll procure this fat rogue a charge of / foot; and I know his death will be a march of twelve-score. The money / shall be paid back again with advantage. Be with me betimes in the / morning; and so, good morrow, Pointz.

Oh, monstrous! Only a halfpenny's worth of bread to this unbelievable amount of sherry! Keep the rest of the papers safe; we'll read them at a better time. Let him sleep there till daylight. I'll go to Court in the morning. We must all go to the wars, and you'll have an honourable position. I'll get this fat rogue command of a company of foot soldiers; I know a march of two hundred and forty yards will kill him. The money will be paid back with interest. Come to me early in the morning. And so, good morning, Poins.
These promises are fair, the parties sure, / And our induction full of prosperous hope.
These promises are good, our allies reliable, and our beginning full of hope of success.
Lord Mortimer,—and cousin Glendower,—Will you sit down?— / And uncle Worcester,—A plague upon it! I have forgot the map.
Lord Mortimer, and cousin Glendower, will you sit down? And uncle Worcester... A plague on it! I've forgotten the map.
No, here it is. / Sit, cousin Percy; sit, good cousin Hotspur; / For by that name as oft as Lancaster / Doth speak of you, his cheek looks pale, and with / A rising sigh he wisheth you in Heaven.
No, here it is. Sit, cousin Percy, sit, good cousin Hotspur, because whenever King Henry calls you by that name, his cheek turns pale, and with a rising sigh he wishes you were in heaven.
And you in Hell, as oft as he hears Owen Glendower spoke of.
And you in hell, whenever he hears Owen Glendower mentioned.
I cannot blame him: at my nativity / The front of heaven was full of fiery shapes, / Of burning cressets; ay, and at my birth / The frame and huge foundation of the Earth / Shaked like a coward.
I can't blame him. When I was born, the face of the sky was full of fiery shapes, of blazing torches; yes, and at my birth the frame and huge foundation of the earth shook like a coward.
Why, so it would have done at the same season, if your mother's / cat had but kitten'd, though yourself had never been born.
Why, it would have done that at the same time if your mother's cat had just had kittens, even if you'd never been born at all.
I say the Earth did shake when I was born.
I tell you the earth shook when I was born.
And I say the Earth was not of my mind, if you suppose as / fearing you it shook.
And I tell you the earth didn't agree with me, if you think it shook out of fear of you.
The Heavens were all on fire, the Earth did tremble.
The heavens were all on fire, the earth trembled.

O, then th' Earth shook to see the Heavens on fire, / And not in fear of your nativity. / Diseased Nature oftentimes breaks forth / In strange eruptions; oft the teeming Earth / Is with a kind of colic pinch'd and vex'd / By the imprisoning of unruly wind / Within her womb; which, for enlargement striving, / Shakes the old beldam Earth, and topples down / Steeples and moss-grown towers. At your birth, / Our grandam Earth, having this distemperature, / In passion shook.

Oh, then the earth shook to see the heavens on fire, not out of fear of your birth. Sick nature often breaks out in strange eruptions. Often the pregnant earth is griped and troubled with a kind of colic, caused by unruly wind trapped inside her womb, which, struggling to get out, shakes the old grandmother earth and topples steeples and moss-covered towers. At your birth our grandmother earth, suffering from this disorder, shook in a fit.

Cousin, of many men / I do not bear these crossings. Give me leave / To tell you once again, that at my birth / The front of heaven was full of fiery shapes; / The goats ran from the mountains, and the herds / Were strangely clamorous to the frighted fields. / These signs have mark'd me extraordinary; / And all the courses of my life do show / I am not in the roll of common men. / Where is he living,—clipp'd in with the sea / That chides the banks of England, Scotland, Wales,— / Which calls me pupil, or hath read to me? / And bring him out that is but woman's son / Can trace me in the tedious ways of art, / And hold me pace in deep experiments.

Cousin, there are not many men from whom I'll take such contradiction. Allow me to tell you once more that at my birth the face of the sky was full of fiery shapes, the goats ran down from the mountains and the herds made a strange noise in the frightened fields. These signs have marked me out as extraordinary, and the whole course of my life shows that I am not on the list of ordinary men. Where is the man living, anywhere within the sea that beats against the shores of England, Scotland and Wales, who can call me his pupil or say he has taught me? And show me any son of a woman who can follow me along the hard paths of magic and keep up with me in deep experiments.
I think there is no man speaks better Welsh.—I'll to dinner.
I don't think anyone speaks better Welsh. I'm going to dinner.
Peace, cousin Percy; you will make him mad.
Quiet, cousin Percy; you'll drive him mad.
I can call spirits from the vasty deep.
I can call up spirits from the vast deep.
Why, so can I, or so can any man; / But will they come when you do call for them?
Why, so can I, or so can anyone; but will they come when you call them?
Why, I can teach you, cousin, to command the Devil.
Why, I can teach you, cousin, to command the Devil.

And I can teach thee, coz, to shame the Devil / By telling truth: tell truth, and shame the Devil. / If thou have power to raise him, bring him hither, / And I'll be sworn I've power to shame him hence. / O, while you live, tell truth, and shame the Devil!

And I can teach you, cousin, to shame the Devil by telling the truth: tell the truth and shame the Devil. If you have the power to raise him, bring him here, and I swear I have the power to shame him away. Oh, as long as you live, tell the truth and shame the Devil!
Come, come, no more of this unprofitable chat.
Come on, come on, no more of this pointless talk.
Three times hath Henry Bolingbroke made head / Against my power; thrice from the banks of Wye / And sandy-bottom'd Severn have I sent / Him bootless home and weather-beaten back.

Three times Henry Bolingbroke has led an army against my forces; three times I have sent him back home from the banks of the Wye and the sandy-bottomed Severn, empty-handed and battered by the weather.
Home without boots, and in foul weather too! / How 'scaped he agues, in the Devil's name!
Home without boots, and in bad weather too! How in the Devil's name did he escape catching a fever?
Come, here's the map: shall we divide our right / According to our threefold order ta'en?
Come, here's the map. Shall we divide up what we're entitled to, according to our three-way agreement?

Th' archdeacon hath divided it / Into three limits very equally. / England, from Trent and Severn hitherto, / By south and east is to my part assign'd: / All westward, Wales beyond the Severn shore, / And all the fertile land within that bound, / To Owen Glendower:—and, dear coz, to you / The remnant northward, lying off from Trent. / And our indentures tripartite are drawn; / Which being sealed interchangeably,— / A business that this night may execute,— / To-morrow, cousin Percy, you, and I, / And my good Lord of Worcester, will set forth / To meet your father and the Scottish power, / As is appointed us, at Shrewsbury. / My father Glendower is not ready yet, / Nor shall we need his help these fourteen days:— / [To Glendower] Within that space you may have drawn together / Your tenants, friends, and neighbouring gentlemen.

The Archdeacon has divided it very equally into three parts. England, from the Trent and the Severn to here, to the south and east, is assigned to me. Everything westward, Wales beyond the Severn shore and all the fertile land within that boundary, goes to Owen Glendower. And to you, dear cousin, the rest to the north, lying beyond the Trent. Our three-way contracts are drawn up, and once they are sealed by each of us, which can be done tonight, tomorrow, cousin Percy, you, I and my good lord of Worcester will set out to meet your father and the Scottish forces at Shrewsbury, as arranged. My father-in-law Glendower isn't ready yet, and we won't need his help for a fortnight. In that time you can have gathered your tenants, friends and the gentlemen of your neighbourhood.

A shorter time shall send me to you, lords: / And in my conduct shall your ladies come; / From whom you now must steal, and take no leave, / For there will be a world of water shed / Upon the parting of your wives and you.

I'll come to you sooner than that, lords, and I'll escort your ladies. You must slip away from them now without saying goodbye, because there'll be an ocean of tears shed when you and your wives part.

Methinks my moiety, north from Burton here, / In quantity equals not one of yours. / See how this river comes me cranking in, / And cuts me from the best of all my land / A huge half-moon, a monstrous cantle out. / I'll have the current in this place damn'd up; / And here the smug and silver Trent shall run / In a new channel, fair and evenly: / It shall not wind with such a deep indent, / To rob me of so rich a bottom here.

It seems to me that my share, north from Burton here, isn't as big as either of yours. Look how this river comes winding in on me and cuts a huge half-moon, a monstrous chunk, out of the best of my land. I'll have the river dammed up at this point, and the smooth silver Trent will run here in a new channel, neatly and straight. It won't wind with such a deep curve to rob me of such a rich piece of valley here.
Not wind? it shall, it must; you see it doth.
Not wind? It will, it must; you can see it does.
Yea, but / Mark how he bears his course, and runs me up / With like advantage on the other side; / Gelding th' opposed continent as much / As on the other side it takes from you.
Yes, but look how it runs on and cuts back into my land with the same advantage on the other side, taking away as much from the land opposite as it takes from you on this side.
Yea, but a little charge will trench him here, / And on this north side win this cape of land; / And then he runneth straight and evenly.
Yes, but a little cost will dig him a new channel here and win this point of land on the north side, and then it will run straight and even.
I'll have it so: a little charge will do it.
I'll have it that way. A little cost will do it.
I will not have it alter'd.
Let me not understand you, then; speak it in Welsh.
Then make sure I don't understand you: say it in Welsh.

I can speak English, lord, as well as you; / For I was train'd up in the English Court; / Where, being but young, I framed to the harp / Many an English ditty lovely well, / And gave the tongue a helpful ornament, / A virtue that was never seen in you.

I can speak English, my lord, as well as you, because I was brought up at the English court, where, while still young, I set many English songs very beautifully to the harp and gave the language a helpful decoration, an accomplishment you've never shown.

Marry, and I am glad of it with all my heart: / I had rather be a kitten, and cry mew, / Than one of these same metre ballet-mongers; / I had rather hear a brazen canstick turn'd, / Or a dry wheel grate on the axletree; / And that would set my teeth nothing on edge, / Nothing so much as mincing poetry: / 'Tis like the forced gait of a shuffling nag.

Well, I'm glad of that with all my heart. I'd rather be a kitten and cry "miaow" than one of these verse ballad-sellers. I'd rather hear a brass candlestick being turned on a lathe, or a dry wheel grating on its axle; that wouldn't set my teeth on edge at all, nothing like as much as affected poetry. It's like the forced pace of a hobbling horse.
Come, you shall have Trent turn'd.
Come on, you shall have the Trent diverted.

I do not care: I'll give thrice so much land / To any well-deserving friend; / But in the way of bargain, mark ye me, / I'll cavil on the ninth part of a hair. / Are the indentures drawn? shall we be gone?

I don't care. I'll give three times as much land to any friend who deserves it; but when it comes to a bargain, mind you, I'll argue over the ninth part of a hair. Are the contracts drawn up? Shall we go?

The Moon shines fair; you may away by night: / I'll in and haste the writer, and withal / Break with your wives of your departure hence: / I am afraid my daughter will run mad, / So much she doteth on her Mortimer.

The moon is shining brightly; you can leave tonight. I'll go in and hurry up the clerk, and at the same time break the news of your departure to your wives. I'm afraid my daughter will go mad, she loves her Mortimer so much.
Fie, cousin Percy! how you cross my father!
Shame on you, cousin Percy! How you provoke my father-in-law!

I cannot choose: sometimes he angers me / With telling me of the moldwarp and the ant, / Of the dreamer Merlin and his prophecies, / And of a dragon and a finless fish, / A clip-wing'd griffin and a moulten raven, / A couching lion and a ramping cat, / And such a deal of skimble-skamble stuff / As puts me from my faith. I tell you what, / He held me last night at the least nine hours / In reckoning up the several devils' names / That were his lacqueys: I cried hum, and well, / But mark'd him not a word. O, he's as tedious / As a tired horse, a railing wife; / Worse than a smoky house: I had rather live / With cheese and garlic in a windmill, far, / Than feed on cates and have him talk to me / In any summer-house in Christendom.

I can't help it. Sometimes he makes me angry by telling me about the mole and the ant, about the dreamer Merlin and his prophecies, and about a dragon and a fish without fins, a griffin with clipped wings and a raven that's lost its feathers, a lion lying down and a cat rearing up, and such a load of rambling nonsense that it tries my patience. I'll tell you what: last night he kept me for at least nine hours listing the names of the various devils that were his servants. I said "hmm" and "very good", but didn't take in a word. Oh, he's as tiresome as a tired horse or a nagging wife, worse than a smoky house. I'd much rather live on cheese and garlic in a windmill far away than eat delicacies and have him talk to me in any fine country house in Christendom.

In faith, he is a worthy gentleman; / Exceedingly well-read, and profited / In strange concealments; valiant as a lion, / And wondrous affable, and as bountiful / As mines of India. Shall I tell you, cousin? / He holds your temper in a high respect, / And curbs himself even of his natural scope / When you do cross his humour; faith, he does: / I warrant you, that man is not alive / Might so have tempted him as you have done, / Without the taste of danger and reproof: / But do not use it oft, let me entreat you.

Honestly, he's a worthy gentleman, extremely well read and skilled in secret arts, as brave as a lion and wonderfully friendly, and as generous as the mines of India. Shall I tell you something, cousin? He has a great respect for your temperament, and he holds himself back from his natural freedom when you cross him; he really does. I promise you, there's no man alive who could have provoked him as you have without feeling danger and rebuke. But please don't do it often, I beg you.

In faith, my lord, you are too wilful-blunt; / And since your coming hither have done enough / To put him quite beside his patience. / You must needs learn, lord, to amend this fault: / Though sometimes it show greatness, courage, blood— / And that's the dearest grace it renders you,— / Yet oftentimes it doth present harsh rage, / Defect of manners, want of government, / Pride, haughtiness, opinion, and disdain; / The least of which haunting a nobleman / Loseth men's hearts, and leaves behind a stain / Upon the beauty of all parts besides, / Beguiling them of commendation.

Honestly, my lord, you're too stubborn and blunt, and since you came here you've done enough to drive him completely out of patience. You must learn to correct this fault, my lord. Although it sometimes shows greatness, courage and spirit, and that's the best credit it gives you, yet it often shows harsh anger, lack of manners and self-control, pride, arrogance, self-importance and scorn. Even the least of these, when it clings to a nobleman, loses him people's affection and leaves a stain on all his other good qualities, cheating them of praise.
Well, I am school'd: good manners be your speed! / Here come our wives, and let us take our leave.
Well, I've been taught my lesson. May good manners bring you success! Here come our wives; let's say goodbye.
This is the deadly spite that angers me, / My wife can speak no English, I no Welsh.
This is the cruel thing that annoys me: my wife can speak no English, and I no Welsh.
My daughter weeps: she will not part with you; / She'll be a soldier too, she'll to the wars.
My daughter's weeping; she won't part from you. She wants to be a soldier too and go to the wars.
Good father, tell her that she and my aunt Percy / Shall follow in your conduct speedily.
Good father, tell her that she and my aunt Percy will follow soon under your escort.
She's desperate here; a peevish self-will'd harlotry, / One that no persuasion can do good upon.
She's desperate here; a stubborn, self-willed hussy that no persuasion can do any good with.
I understand thy looks: that pretty Welsh / Which thou pour'st down from these swelling heavens / I am too perfect in; and, but for shame, / In such a parley should I answer thee.
I understand your looks. That pretty Welsh that you pour down from these brimming eyes, I understand only too well; and if I weren't ashamed, I'd answer you in the same language of tears.

I understand thy kisses, and thou mine, / And that's a feeling disputation: / But I will never be a truant, love, / Till I have learn'd thy language; for thy tongue / Makes Welsh as sweet as ditties highly penn'd, / Sung by a fair queen in a Summer's bower, / With ravishing division, to her lute.

I understand your kisses and you understand mine, and that's a conversation of feeling. But I'll never stop studying, love, until I've learned your language, because your tongue makes Welsh as sweet as finely written songs sung beautifully to her lute by a lovely queen in a summer bower.
Nay, if you melt, then will she run mad.
No, if you melt like that, she'll go mad.
O, I am ignorance itself in this!
Oh, I'm ignorance itself in this!

She bids you on the wanton rushes lay you down, / And rest your gentle head upon her lap, / And she will sing the song that pleaseth you, / And on your eyelids crown the god of sleep, / Charming your blood with pleasing heaviness; / Making such difference betwixt wake and sleep, / As is the difference betwixt day and night, / The hour before the heavenly-harness'd team / Begins his golden progress in the East.

She asks you to lie down on the soft rushes and rest your gentle head in her lap, and she'll sing the song you like and crown your eyelids with the god of sleep, enchanting your blood with a pleasant drowsiness, making the state between waking and sleeping like the twilight between day and night in the hour before the sun's heavenly team of horses begins its golden journey in the east.
With all my heart I'll sit and hear her sing: / By that time will our book, I think, be drawn.
With all my heart I'll sit and listen to her sing. By then, I think, our contract will be drawn up.
Do so: / An those musicians that shall play to you / Hang in the air a thousand leagues from hence, / And straight they shall be here: sit, and attend.
Do. And the musicians who will play for you are hanging in the air a thousand leagues from here, yet they'll be here at once. Sit down and listen.
Come, Kate, thou art perfect in lying down: come, quick, / quick, that I may lay my head in thy lap.
Come, Kate, you're perfect at lying down. Come on, quick, quick, so I can lay my head in your lap.
Now I perceive the Devil understands Welsh; / And 'tis no marvel he's so humorous. / By'r Lady, he's a good musician.
Now I see the Devil understands Welsh, and it's no wonder he's so moody. By Our Lady, he's a good musician.
Then should you be nothing but musical; for you are / altogether governed by humours. Lie still, ye thief, and hear / the lady sing in Welsh.
Then you should be nothing but musical, because you're completely ruled by your moods. Lie still, you thief, and listen to the lady sing in Welsh.
I had rather hear Lady, my brach, howl in Irish.
I'd rather hear my hound Lady howl in Irish.
Wouldst thou have thy head broken?
Do you want your head broken?
I won't do that either; it's a woman's fault.
Come, Kate, I'll have your song too.
Come, Kate, I'll have your song too.

Not yours, in good sooth! 'Heart! you swear like a / comfit-maker's wife. Not mine, in good sooth; and, As true / as I live; and, As God shall mend me; and, As sure as day; / And givest such sarcenet surety for thy oaths, / As if thou ne'er walk'dst further than Finsbury. / Swear me, Kate, like a lady as thou art, / A good mouth-filling oath; and leave in sooth, / And such protest of pepper-gingerbread, / To velvet-guards and Sunday-citizens. Come, sing.

"Not mine, truly"! By God's heart, you swear like a sweet-maker's wife. "Not mine, truly," and "As true as I live," and "As God shall save me," and "As sure as day." You give such flimsy silk guarantees for your oaths, as if you'd never walked further than Finsbury Fields. Swear like the lady you are, Kate, a good mouth-filling oath, and leave "truly" and such gingerbread protests to people in velvet-trimmed clothes and Sunday-best citizens. Come on, sing.
'Tis the next way to turn tailor, or be redbreast-teacher. / An the indentures be drawn, I'll away within these two hours; / and so, come in when ye will.
Singing is the quickest way to become a tailor or a teacher of robins. If the contracts are drawn up, I'll leave within two hours; and so come in when you like.
Come, come, Lord Mortimer; you are as slow / As hot Lord Percy is on fire to go. / By this our book's drawn; we'll but seal, and then / To horse immediately.
Come, come, Lord Mortimer, you're as slow as hot-tempered Lord Percy is on fire to go. By now our contract's drawn up; we'll just seal it, and then to horse at once.
Lords, give us leave; the Prince of Wales and I / Must have some private conference: but be near at hand, / For we shall presently have need of you.
Lords, leave us; the Prince of Wales and I must have a private conversation. But stay close by, because we'll need you shortly.

I know not whether God will have it so, / For some displeasing service I have done, / That, in His secret doom, out of my blood / He'll breed revengement and a scourge for me; / But thou dost, in thy passages of life, / Make me believe that thou art only mark'd / For the hot vengeance and the rod of Heaven / To punish my mistreadings. Tell me else, / Could such inordinate and low desires, / Such poor, such base, such lewd, such mean attempts, / Such barren pleasures, rude society, / As thou art match'd withal and grafted to, / Accompany the greatness of thy blood, / And hold their level with thy princely heart?

I don't know whether God wills it, for some offence I have committed, that in his secret judgement he will breed revenge and a punishment for me out of my own blood. But by the way you live your life you make me believe that you are marked out only as the burning vengeance and rod of heaven to punish my wrongdoings. Otherwise, tell me, how could such unruly and low desires, such poor, base, coarse and mean activities, such empty pleasures and rough company as you are joined and bound to, go along with the greatness of your blood and stand level with your princely heart?

So please your Majesty, I would I could / Quit all offences with as clear excuse / As well as I am doubtless I can purge / Myself of many I am charged withal: / Yet such extenuation let me beg, / As, in reproof of many tales devised / By smiling pick-thanks and base news-mongers,— / Which oft the ear of greatness needs must hear,— / I may, for some things true, wherein my youth / Hath faulty wander'd and irregular, / Find pardon on my true submission.

If it please your Majesty, I wish I could clear myself of all offences as plainly as I am sure I can clear myself of many I am accused of. Yet let me beg this much allowance: that, once I have disproved many stories invented by smiling flatterers and low gossips, which great men must often listen to, I may be pardoned, on my sincere submission, for the things that are true, in which my youth has wandered into faults and disorder.

God pardon thee! Yet let me wonder, Harry, / At thy affections, which do hold a wing / Quite from the flight of all thy ancestors. / Thy place in Council thou hast rudely lost, / Which by thy younger brother is supplied; / And art almost an alien to the hearts / Of all the Court and princes of my blood: / The hope and expectation of thy time / Is ruin'd; and the soul of every man / Prophetically does forethink thy fall. / Had I so lavish of my presence been, / So common-hackney'd in the eyes of men, / So stale and cheap to vulgar company, / Opinion, that did help me to the crown, / Had still kept loyal to possession, / And left me in reputeless banishment, / A fellow of no mark nor likelihood. / By being seldom seen, I could not stir / But, like a comet, I was wonder'd at; / That men would tell their children, This is he; / Others would say, Where, which is Bolingbroke? / And then I stole all courtesy from Heaven, / And dress'd myself in such humility, / That I did pluck allegiance from men's hearts, / Loud shouts and salutations from their mouths, / Even in the presence of the crowned King. / Thus did I keep my person fresh and new; / My presence, like a robe pontifical, / Ne'er seen but wonder'd at: and so my state, / Seldom but sumptuous, showed like a feast, / And won by rareness such solemnity. / The skipping King, he ambled up and down / With shallow jesters and rash bavin wits, / Soon kindled and soon burnt; carded his state, / Mingled his royalty, with capering fools; / Had his great name profaned with their scorns; / And gave his countenance, against his name, / To laugh at gibing boys, and stand the push / Of every beardless vain comparative; / Grew a companion to the common streets, / Enfeoff'd himself to popularity; / That, being daily swallow'd by men's eyes, / They surfeited with honey, and began / To loathe the taste of sweetness, whereof a little / More than a little is by much too much. / So, when he had occasion to be seen, / He was but as the cuckoo is in June, / Heard, not regarded; seen, but with such eyes / As, sick and blunted with community, / Afford no extraordinary gaze, / Such as is bent on sun-like majesty / When it shines seldom in admiring eyes; / But rather drowsed, and hung their eyelids down, / Slept in his face, and render'd such aspect / As cloudy men use to their adversaries, / Being with his presence glutted, gorged, and full. / And in that very line, Harry, stand'st thou; / For thou hast lost thy princely privilege / With vile participation: not an eye / But is a-weary of thy common sight, / Save mine, which hath desired to see thee more; / Which now doth that I would not have it do, / Make blind itself with foolish tenderness.

God pardon you! But let me wonder, Harry, at your tastes, which fly in a completely different direction from all your ancestors. You have rudely lost your place in the Council, which your younger brother has filled, and you are almost a stranger to the hearts of the whole Court and the princes of my blood. The hope and expectation of your future is ruined, and every man's soul is predicting your downfall. If I had been so free with my presence, so worn out in men's eyes like a hired horse, so stale and cheap in common company, public opinion, which helped me to the crown, would have stayed loyal to the king in possession and left me in disgraced exile, a fellow of no importance or prospects. By being seldom seen, I couldn't move without being wondered at like a comet, so that men would tell their children, "That's him," and others would say, "Where? Which one is Bolingbroke?" And then I stole every grace from heaven and dressed myself in such humility that I plucked loyalty from men's hearts and loud cheers and greetings from their mouths, even in the presence of the crowned King. In this way I kept myself fresh and new; my presence, like a bishop's robe, was never seen without being wondered at. And so my public appearances, rare but splendid, were like a feast and gained great dignity by being rare. The frivolous King Richard ambled up and down with shallow jesters and quick, brushwood wits, soon lit and soon burnt out. He watered down his majesty and mixed his royalty with capering fools, let his great name be soiled by their mockery, and, against the dignity of his title, lent his presence to laughing at jeering boys and putting up with the challenges of every beardless, empty mocker. He became a companion of the common streets and gave himself away to popularity, so that, being swallowed daily by men's eyes, they were sick of honey and began to hate the taste of sweetness, of which a little more than a little is far too much. So when he had to appear in public, he was like the cuckoo in June, heard but not noticed; seen, but with eyes that, tired and dulled by familiarity, gave him no special attention, such as is given to sun-like majesty when it shines rarely on admiring eyes. Instead they were drowsy, let their eyelids droop, slept in his face, and gave him the sort of look that sullen men give their enemies, being glutted, gorged and full of his presence. And you are in exactly that position, Harry, because you've lost your princely privilege by mixing with low company. There isn't an eye that isn't tired of the common sight of you, except mine, which has wanted to see more of you, and which now does what I don't want it to do: blinds itself with foolish, loving tears.
I shall hereafter, my thrice-gracious lord, / Be more myself.
From now on, my most gracious lord, I'll be more truly myself.

For all the world, / As thou art to this hour, was Richard then / When I from France set foot at Ravenspurg; / And even as I was then is Percy now. / Now, by my sceptre, and my soul to boot, / He hath more worthy interest to the state / Than thou, the shadow of succession; / For, of no right, nor colour like to right, / He doth fill fields with harness in the realm, / Turns head against the lion's armed jaws; / And, being no more in debt to years than thou, / Leads ancient lords and reverend bishops on / To bloody battles and to bruising arms. / What never-dying honour hath he got / Against renowned Douglas! whose high deeds, / Whose hot incursions, and great name in arms, / Holds from all soldiers chief majority / And military title capital / Through all the kingdoms that acknowledge Christ: / Thrice hath this Hotspur, Mars in swathing-clothes, / This infant warrior, in his enterprises / Discomfited great Douglas; ta'en him once, / Enlarged him, and made a friend of him, / To fill the mouth of deep defiance up, / And shake the peace and safety of our throne. / And what say you to this? Percy, Northumberland, / Th' Archbishop's Grace of York, Douglas, and Mortimer / Capitulate against us, and are up. / But wherefore do I tell these news to thee? / Why, Harry, do I tell thee of my foes, / Which art my near'st and dearest enemy? / Thou that art like enough,—through vassal fear, / Base inclination, and the start of spleen,— / To fight against me under Percy's pay, / To dog his heels, and curtsy at his frowns, / To show how much thou art degenerate.

For all the world, what you are at this moment, Richard was then, when I landed from France at Ravenspurgh; and just as I was then, Percy is now. Now, by my sceptre and my soul as well, he has a worthier claim to the state than you, the mere shadow of an heir. With no right, or anything that looks like right, he fills the fields of the kingdom with armour, turns to face the armed jaws of the lion, and, though he's no older than you, leads old lords and reverend bishops into bloody battles and bruising combat. What everlasting honour he has won against the famous Douglas, whose great deeds, fierce raids and great name in arms give him the highest rank and military title among all soldiers in every Christian kingdom! Three times this Hotspur, Mars in nappies, this infant warrior, has defeated great Douglas in his campaigns. He captured him once, set him free and made a friend of him, to swell the cry of deep defiance and shake the peace and security of our throne. And what do you say to this? Percy, Northumberland, his Grace the Archbishop of York, Douglas and Mortimer have made a pact against us and are in arms. But why do I tell you this news? Why, Harry, do I tell you about my enemies, when you are my closest and dearest enemy? You're quite likely, out of cowardly fear, low tendencies and a fit of bad temper, to fight against me in Percy's pay, to follow at his heels and bow when he frowns, to show how degenerate you are.

Do not think so; you shall not find it so: / And God forgive them that so much have sway'd / Your Majesty's good thoughts away from me! / I will redeem all this on Percy's head, / And, in the closing of some glorious day, / Be bold to tell you that I am your son; / When I will wear a garment all of blood, / And stain my favour in a bloody mask, / Which, wash'd away, shall scour my shame with it: / And that shall be the day, whene'er it lights, / That this same child of honour and renown, / This gallant Hotspur, this all-praised knight, / And your unthought-of Harry, chance to meet. / For every honour sitting on his helm, / Would they were multitudes, and on my head / My shames redoubled! for the time will come, / That I shall make this northern youth exchange / His glorious deeds for my indignities. / Percy is but my factor, good my lord, / T' engross up glorious deeds on my behalf; / And I will call him to so strict account, / That he shall render every glory up, / Yea, even the slightest worship of his time, / Or I will tear the reckoning from his heart. / This, in the name of God, I promise here: / The which if I perform, and do survive, / I do beseech your Majesty, may salve / The long-grown wounds of my intemperance: / If not, the end of life cancels all bands; / And I will die a hundred thousand deaths / Ere break the smallest parcel of this vow.

Don't think so; you won't find it so. And God forgive those who have turned your Majesty's good opinion so far away from me! I will make up for all this on Percy's head, and at the end of some glorious day I'll be bold enough to tell you that I am your son, when I'll wear a garment all of blood and stain my face with a bloody mask, which, when it is washed away, will scour my shame away with it. And that will be the day, whenever it comes, when this same child of honour and fame, this gallant Hotspur, this much-praised knight, and your disregarded Harry happen to meet. I wish every honour that sits on his helmet were multiplied many times, and my shames on my head doubled! Because the time will come when I'll make this northern youth exchange his glorious deeds for my disgraces. Percy is only my agent, my good lord, buying up glorious deeds on my behalf; and I'll call him to such a strict account that he'll hand over every glory, yes, even the smallest honour he has ever won, or I'll tear the account from his heart. This, in the name of God, I promise here. If I carry it out and survive, I beg your Majesty to let it heal the long-standing wounds of my wild behaviour. If not, the end of life cancels all debts, and I'll die a hundred thousand deaths before I break the smallest part of this vow.
A hundred thousand rebels die in this. / Thou shalt have charge and sovereign trust herein.—
A hundred thousand rebels die by this promise. You shall have a command and the highest trust in this war.
How now, good Blunt! thy looks are full of speed.
How now, good Blunt! You look full of haste.

So is the business that I come to speak of. / Lord Mortimer of Scotland hath sent word / That Douglas and the English rebels met / Th' eleventh of this month at Shrewsbury: / A mighty and a fearful head they are, / If promises be kept on every hand, / As ever offer'd foul play in a State.

So is the business I've come to tell you about. Lord Mortimer of Scotland has sent word that Douglas and the English rebels met at Shrewsbury on the eleventh of this month. If promises are kept on every side, they are as mighty and fearful an army as ever threatened rebellion in a state.

The Earl of Westmoreland set forth to-day; / With him my son, Lord John of Lancaster; / For this advertisement is five days old. / On Wednesday next you, Harry, shall set forward; / On Thursday we ourselves will march: / Our meeting is Bridgenorth: and, Harry, you / Shall march through Glostershire; by which account, / Our business valued, some twelve days hence / Our general forces at Bridgenorth shall meet. / Our hands are full of business: let's away; / Advantage feeds him fat, while men delay.

The Earl of Westmoreland set out today, and with him my son, Lord John of Lancaster, because this news is five days old. Next Wednesday, Harry, you'll set out; on Thursday we will march ourselves.
