Our meeting place is Bridgnorth. And, Harry, you will march through Gloucestershire; so, by my reckoning of what needs to be done, our whole army will meet at Bridgnorth in about twelve days. We have our hands full of business. Let's go. Opportunity feeds the enemy fat while men delay.

Bardolph, am I not fallen away vilely since this last action? do I / not bate? do I not dwindle? Why, my skin hangs about me like an / old lady's loose gown; I am withered like an old apple-John. / Well, I'll repent, and that suddenly, while I am in some liking; I / shall be out of heart shortly, and then I shall have no strength to / repent. / An I have not forgotten what the inside of a church is made of, I / am a peppercorn, a brewer's horse: the inside of a church! / Company, villainous company, hath been the spoil of me.

Bardolph, haven't I wasted away dreadfully since this last business? Am I not shrinking? Am I not dwindling? Why, my skin hangs on me like an old lady's loose gown; I'm as wrinkled as an old dried apple. Well, I'll repent, and quickly, while I'm still in good shape. I'll lose heart soon, and then I won't have the strength to repent. If I haven't forgotten what the inside of a church looks like, I'm a peppercorn, a brewer's cart-horse. The inside of a church! Company, villainous company, has been the ruin of me.
Sir John, you are so fretful, you cannot live long.
Sir John, you fret so much you can't live long.

Why, there is it: come, sing me a song; make me merry. I was as / virtuously given as a gentleman need to be; virtuous enough; swore / little; diced not above seven times a week; paid money that I borrowed / —three or four times; lived well, and in good compass: and now I live / out of all order, out of all compass.

Well, there it is. Come on, sing me a song, cheer me up. I was as virtuously inclined as a gentleman needs to be: virtuous enough; swore little; played dice no more than seven times a week; paid back money I borrowed three or four times; lived well and within bounds. And now I live in total disorder, beyond all bounds.
Why, you are so fat, Sir John, that you must needs be out of all / compass,—out of all reasonable compass, Sir John.
Well, you're so fat, Sir John, that you're bound to be out of all bounds, out of all reasonable bounds, Sir John.
Do thou amend thy face, and I'll amend my life: thou art our admiral, / thou bearest the lantern in the poop,—but 'tis in the nose of thee; / thou art the Knight of the Burning Lamp.
You mend your face, and I'll mend my life. You're our flagship, you carry the lantern at the stern, but in your case it's in your nose. You're the Knight of the Burning Lamp.
Why, Sir John, my face does you no harm.
Well, Sir John, my face does you no harm.

No, I'll be sworn; I make as good use of it as many a man doth of a / death's-head or a memento mori: I never see thy face but I think upon / hell-fire, and Dives that lived in purple; for there he is in his robes, / burning, burning. If thou wert any way given to virtue, I would swear / by thy face; my oath should be, By this fire, that's God's angel: but / thou art altogether given over; and wert indeed, but for the light in / thy face, the son of utter darkness. When thou rann'st up Gad's-hill in / the night to catch my horse, if I did not think thou hadst been an ignis / fatuus or a ball of wildfire, there's no purchase in money. O, thou art / a perpetual triumph, an everlasting bonfire-light! Thou hast saved me a / thousand marks in links and torches, walking with thee in the night / betwixt tavern and tavern: but the sack that thou hast drunk me would / have bought me lights as good cheap at the dearest chandler's in Europe. / I have maintain'd that salamander of yours with fire any time this / two-and-thirty years; God reward me for it!

No, I swear it doesn't. I make as good use of it as many men do of a skull or a reminder of death. I never see your face without thinking of hell-fire and the rich man in the Bible who lived in purple, because there he is in his robes, burning, burning. If you had any leaning towards virtue, I'd swear by your face; my oath would be "By this fire, which is God's angel." But you're completely lost to sin, and if it weren't for the light in your face, you'd be the son of utter darkness. When you ran up Gad's Hill in the night to catch my horse, if I didn't think you were a will-o'-the-wisp or a ball of fireworks, then money is worth nothing. Oh, you're a permanent torchlight parade, an everlasting bonfire! You've saved me a thousand marks in torches, walking with you at night from tavern to tavern. But the sherry you've drunk at my expense would have bought me lights just as cheaply at the dearest candle-maker's in Europe. I've kept that fire-eating salamander of yours supplied with fire for the last thirty-two years. God reward me for it!
'Sblood, I would my face were in your stomach!
By God's blood, I wish my face were in your stomach!
God-a-mercy! so should I be sure to be heart-burn'd.—
God have mercy! Then I'd be sure to get heartburn.
How now, Dame Partlet the hen! have you enquir'd yet who / pick'd my pocket?
How now, Dame Partlet the hen! Have you found out yet who picked my pocket?

Why, Sir John, what do you think, Sir John? do you think I / keep thieves in my house? I have search'd, I have inquired, / so has my husband, man by man, boy by boy, servant by servant: / the tithe of a hair was never lost in my house before.

Why, Sir John, what do you think, Sir John? Do you think I keep thieves in my house? I've searched, I've asked questions, and so has my husband, man by man, boy by boy, servant by servant. Not a tenth of a hair was ever lost in my house before.
Ye lie, hostess: Bardolph was shaved, and lost many a hair; and / I'll be sworn my pocket was pick'd. Go to, you are a woman, go.
You're lying, landlady. Bardolph was shaved and lost many a hair, and I'll swear my pocket was picked. Go on, you're a woman, go.
Who, I? no; I defy thee: God's light, I was never call'd so in / mine own house before.
Who, me? No, I defy you. By God's light, I was never called that in my own house before.
Go to, I know you well enough.
Go on, I know you well enough.
No, Sir John; you do not know me, Sir John. I know you, Sir John: / you owe me money, Sir John; and now you pick a quarrel to beguile me / of it: I bought you a dozen of shirts to your back.
No, Sir John, you don't know me, Sir John. I know you, Sir John. You owe me money, Sir John, and now you're picking a quarrel to cheat me out of it. I bought you a dozen shirts for your back.
Dowlas, filthy dowlas: I have given them away to bakers' wives, / and they have made bolters of them.
Coarse cloth, filthy coarse cloth. I've given them away to bakers' wives, and they've made flour sieves out of them.
Now, as I am a true woman, holland of eight shillings an ell. / You owe money here besides, Sir John, for your diet and by-drinkings, / and money lent you, four-and-twenty pound.
Now, as I'm an honest woman, they were fine linen at eight shillings a yard. You owe money here as well, Sir John, for your meals and drinks between meals, and money lent you, twenty-four pounds.
He had his part of it; let him pay.
He had his share of it; let him pay.
He? alas, he is poor; he hath nothing.
Him? Alas, he's poor; he has nothing.

How! poor? look upon his face; what call you rich? let / them coin his nose, let them coin his cheeks: I'll not pay a / denier. What, will you make a younker of me? shall I not take / mine ease in mine inn, but I shall have my pocket pick'd? I have / lost a seal-ring of my grandfather's worth forty mark.

What! Poor? Look at his face. What do you call rich? Let them make coins out of his nose and his cheeks. I won't pay a penny. What, are you treating me like a greenhorn? Can't I relax in my own inn without having my pocket picked? I've lost a signet ring of my grandfather's worth forty marks.
O Jesu, I have heard the Prince tell him, I know not how oft, / that that ring was copper!
Oh Jesus, I've heard the Prince tell him I don't know how often that that ring was copper!
How! the Prince is a Jack, a sneak-cup: 'sblood, an he were / here, I would cudgel him like a dog, if he would say so.—
What! The Prince is a rascal, a sneaky drinker. By God's blood, if he were here and said so, I'd beat him like a dog.
How now, lad? is the wind in that door, i'faith? must we all / march?
Well, lad? Is that the way the wind blows, really? Must we all march?
Yes, two by two, like prisoners going to Newgate.
My lord, I pray you, hear me.
My lord, please listen to me.
What say'st thou, Mistress Quickly? How doth thy husband? I love / him well; he is an honest man.
What do you say, Mistress Quickly? How's your husband? I like him very much; he's an honest man.
My good lord, listen to me.
Pr'ythee, let her alone, and list to me.
Please leave her alone and listen to me.
The other night I fell asleep here behind the arras, and had my / pocket pick'd: this house is turn'd bawdy-house; they pick pockets.
The other night I fell asleep here behind the tapestry and had my pocket picked. This house has turned into a brothel; they pick pockets.
Wilt thou believe me, Hal? three or four bonds of forty pound / a-piece and a seal-ring of my grandfather's.
Will you believe me, Hal? Three or four bonds worth forty pounds each, and a signet ring of my grandfather's.
A trifle, something worth about eightpence.
So I told him, my lord; and I said I heard your Grace say so; / and, my lord, he speaks most vilely of you, like a foul-mouth'd / man as he is; and said he would cudgel you.
That's what I told him, my lord, and I said I'd heard your Grace say so. And, my lord, he speaks most vilely of you, foul-mouthed man that he is, and said he would beat you.
There's neither faith, truth, nor womanhood in me else.
If he did not, there's no faith, truth or womanhood in me.

There's no more faith in thee than in a stew'd prune; nor no more / truth in thee than in a drawn fox; and, for woman-hood, Maid Marian / may be the deputy's wife of the ward to thee. Go, you thing, go.

There's no more faith in you than in a stewed prune, no more truth in you than in a hunted fox, and as for womanhood, Maid Marian would be a respectable alderman's wife compared with you. Go, you thing, go.
Say, what thing? what thing? I am an honest man's wife: and, / setting thy knighthood aside, thou art a knave to call me so.
Tell me, what thing? What thing? I'm an honest man's wife, and, knighthood aside, you're a rascal to call me that.
Setting thy womanhood aside, thou art a beast to say otherwise.
Womanhood aside, you're a beast to say otherwise.
Say, what beast, thou knave, thou?
Tell me, what beast, you rascal, you?
An otter, Sir John, why an otter?
An otter, Sir John? Why an otter?
Why, she's neither fish nor flesh; a man knows not where to have / her.
Why, she's neither fish nor flesh; a man doesn't know where to have her.
Thou art an unjust man in saying so; thou or any man knows where / to have me, thou knave, thou!
You're an unfair man to say so. You or any man knows where to have me, you rascal, you!
Thou say'st true, hostess; and he slanders thee most grossly.
You're right, landlady, and he slanders you most grossly.
So he doth you, my lord; and said this other day you ought him a / thousand pound.
And he slanders you too, my lord. He said the other day that you owed him a thousand pounds.
Sirrah, do I owe you a thousand pound?
My man, do I owe you a thousand pounds?
A thousand pound, Hal! a million: thy love is worth a million; / thou owest me thy love.
A thousand pounds, Hal? A million! Your love is worth a million; you owe me your love.
Nay, my lord, he call'd you Jack, and said he would cudgel you.
No, my lord, he called you a rascal and said he'd beat you.
Indeed, Sir John, you said so.
You did say so, Sir John.
Yea, if he said my ring was copper.
Yes, if he said my ring was copper.
I say 'tis copper: darest thou be as good as thy word now?
I say it's copper. Do you dare to keep your word now?
Why, Hal, thou know'st, as thou art but man, I dare; but as thou / art prince, I fear thee as I fear the roaring of the lion's whelp.
Why, Hal, you know that, as you're just a man, I dare; but as you're a prince, I fear you as I fear the roaring of a lion's cub.
And why not as the lion?
And why not as the lion?
The King himself is to be feared as the lion: dost thou think I'll / fear thee as I fear thy father? nay, an I do, I pray God my girdle / break.
The King himself is the one to be feared like the lion. Do you think I'll fear you as I fear your father? No, if I do, I pray God my belt breaks.

Sirrah, there's no room for faith, truth, nor honesty in this / bosom of thine; it is all fill'd up with midriff. / Charge an honest woman with picking thy pocket! why, thou whoreson, / impudent, emboss'd rascal, if there were anything in thy pocket but / tavern-reckonings, and one poor pennyworth of sugar-candy to make thee / long-winded,—if thy pocket were enrich'd with any other injuries but / these, I am a villain: and yet you will stand to it; you will not / pocket-up wrong. Art thou not ashamed!

My man, there's no room for faith, truth or honesty in that chest of yours; it's all filled up with guts. Accusing an honest woman of picking your pocket! Why, you son-of-a-whore, shameless, swollen rascal, if there was anything in your pocket except tavern bills and one poor pennyworth of sugar candy to give you breath, if your pocket was enriched with any other losses than these, I'm a villain. And yet you'll stick to your story; you won't pocket an insult. Aren't you ashamed?

Dost thou hear, Hal? thou know'st, in the state of innocency Adam fell; / and what should poor Jack Falstaff do in the days of villainy? / Thou see'st I have more flesh than another man; and therefore more / frailty. You confess, then, you pick'd my pocket?

Do you hear, Hal? You know that Adam fell in the state of innocence; so what can poor Jack Falstaff be expected to do in these days of wickedness? You can see I have more flesh than other men, and therefore more weakness. So you admit you picked my pocket?
It appears so by the story.
It looks like it, from the story.

Hostess, I forgive thee: go, make ready breakfast; love thy husband, / look to thy servants, cherish thy guests: thou shalt find me tractable / to any honest reason; thou see'st I am pacified.—Still? Nay, pr'ythee, / be gone.

Landlady, I forgive you. Go and get breakfast ready. Love your husband, look after your servants, take care of your guests. You'll find me ready to listen to any honest argument. You see I'm calmed down. Still here? No, please go.
Now, Hal, to the news at Court: for the robbery, lad, how is / that answered?
Now, Hal, the news from Court. About the robbery, lad, how has that been dealt with?
O, my sweet beef, I must still be good angel to thee: the money / is paid back again.
Oh, my sweet beef, I must always be your good angel: the money's been paid back.
O, I do not like that paying back; 'tis a double labour.
Oh, I don't like that paying back; it's twice the work.
I am good friends with my father, and may do any thing.
I'm on good terms with my father and can do anything.
Rob me the exchequer the first thing thou doest, and do it with / unwash'd hands too.
Then the first thing you do, rob the treasury for me, and do it without washing your hands, too.
I have procured thee, Jack, a charge of Foot.
I've got you a command of foot soldiers, Jack.

I would it had been of Horse. Where shall I find one that can steal / well? O, for a fine thief, of the age of two-and-twenty or thereabouts! / I am heinously unprovided. Well, God be thanked for these rebels; they / offend none but the virtuous: I laud them, I praise them.

I wish it had been cavalry. Where will I find someone who can steal well? Oh, for a fine thief of about twenty-two! I'm terribly short of supplies. Well, thank God for these rebels; they offend nobody but the virtuous. I applaud them, I praise them.
Go bear this letter to Lord John of Lancaster, / My brother John; this to my Lord of Westmoreland.—
Go and take this letter to Lord John of Lancaster, my brother John, and this one to my lord of Westmoreland.
Go, Pointz, to horse, to horse; for thou and I / Have thirty miles to ride yet ere dinner-time.—
Go, Poins, to horse, to horse, because you and I have thirty miles to ride before dinner.

Meet me to-morrow, Jack, i' the Temple-hall / At two o'clock in th' afternoon: / There shalt thou know thy charge; and there receive / Money and order for their furniture. / The land is burning; Percy stands on high; / And either they or we must lower lie.

Meet me tomorrow, Jack, in the Temple hall at two o'clock in the afternoon. There you'll learn what your command is and receive money and orders for equipping your men. The country is on fire; Percy stands high; and either they or we must be brought low.
Rare words! brave world!—Hostess, my breakfast; come:— / O, I could wish this tavern were my drum!
Fine words! Brave world! Landlady, my breakfast, come on! Oh, I wish this tavern were my drum!

Well said, my noble Scot: if speaking truth / In this fine age were not thought flattery, / Such attribution should the Douglas have, / As not a soldier of this season's stamp / Should go so general-current through the world. / By God, I cannot flatter; I defy / The tongues of soothers; but a braver place / In my heart's love hath no man than yourself: / Nay, task me to my word; approve me, lord.

Well said, my noble Scot. If telling the truth weren't taken for flattery in these refined times, Douglas would have such praise that no soldier of this generation would be so widely honoured throughout the world. By God, I can't flatter; I despise the tongues of flatterers. But no man has a higher place in my heart's love than you. No, hold me to my word; test me, my lord.
Thou art the king of honour: / No man so potent breathes upon the ground / But I will beard him.
You are the king of honour. There's no man alive so powerful that I won't defy him.
Do that, and all is well.
What letters hast thou there?—I can but thank you.
What letters have you got there? I can only thank you.
These letters come from your father.
These letters come from your father.
Letters from him! why comes he not himself?
Letters from him! Why doesn't he come himself?
He cannot come, my lord; he's grievous sick.
He can't come, my lord; he's seriously ill.
Zwounds! how has he the leisure to be sick / In such a justling time? Who leads his power? / Under whose government come they along?
By God's wounds! How does he have time to be ill at such a hectic time? Who's leading his army? Under whose command are they coming?
His letters bears his mind, not I, my lord.
His letters tell you his mind, not I, my lord.
I pr'ythee, tell me, doth he keep his bed?
Please tell me, is he in bed?
He did, my lord, four days ere I set forth, / And at the time of my departure thence / He was much fear'd by his physicians.
He was, my lord, four days before I set out, and when I left, his doctors were very worried about him.
I would the state of time had first been whole / Ere he by sickness had been visited: / His health was never better worth than now.
I wish our affairs had been settled before he fell ill. His health was never worth more than now.

Sick now! droop now! this sickness doth infect / The very life-blood of our enterprise; / 'Tis catching hither, even to our camp. / He writes me here, that inward sickness,— / And that his friends by deputation could not / So soon be drawn; nor did he think it meet / To lay so dangerous and dear a trust / On any soul removed, but on his own. / Yet doth he give us bold advertisement, / That with our small conjunction we should on, / To see how fortune is disposed to us; / For, as he writes, there is no quailing now, / Because the King is certainly possess'd / Of all our purposes. What say you to it?

Sick now! Failing now! This sickness infects the very lifeblood of our enterprise; it's spreading even here to our camp. He writes to me here that he has an internal illness, and that his allies could not be gathered so quickly by a deputy, nor did he think it right to put such a dangerous and precious trust in anyone but himself. Still, he boldly advises that we should go ahead with our small combined forces to see how fortune is inclined towards us, because, as he writes, there's no backing out now, since the King certainly knows all our plans. What do you say to that?
Your father's sickness is a maim to us.
Your father's illness is a crippling blow to us.

A perilous gash, a very limb lopp'd off:— / And yet, in faith, 'tis not; his present want / Seems more than we shall find it. Were it good / To set the exact wealth of all our states / All at one cast? to set so rich a main / On the nice hazard of one doubtful hour? / It were not good; for therein should we read / The very bottom and the soul of hope, / The very list, the very utmost bound / Of all our fortunes.

A dangerous gash, a limb cut right off. And yet, honestly, it's not. His absence now seems worse than it will turn out to be. Would it be wise to stake all our resources on one throw of the dice, to bet so much on the risky chance of one uncertain hour? It wouldn't, because then we'd be reaching the very bottom of our hope, the very edge, the utmost limit of all our fortunes.
Faith, and so we should; / Where now remains a sweet reversion; / And we may boldly spend upon the hope / Of what is to come in: / A comfort of retirement lives in this.
Indeed, so we would; whereas now we have something good in reserve, and we can boldly spend in the hope of what is still to come. There's the comfort of a place to retreat to in this.
A rendezvous, a home to fly unto, / If that the Devil and mischance look big / Upon the maidenhead of our affairs.
A meeting place, a home to run to, if the Devil and bad luck threaten the start of our venture.

But yet I would your father had been here. / The quality and hair of our attempt / Brooks no division: it will be thought / By some, that know not why he is away, / That wisdom, loyalty, and mere dislike / Of our proceedings, kept the earl from hence: / And think how such an apprehension / May turn the tide of fearful faction, / And breed a kind of question in our cause; / For well you know we of the offering side / Must keep aloof from strict arbitrement, / And stop all sight-holes, every loop from whence / The eye of reason may pry in upon us. / This absence of your father's draws a curtain, / That shows the ignorant a kind of fear / Before not dreamt of.

But still I wish your father had been here. The nature of our enterprise can't stand division. Some people who don't know why he's away will think that wisdom, loyalty and simple disapproval of what we're doing kept the Earl away. And think how such a belief could turn the tide among our nervous supporters and raise doubts about our cause. You know well that we who are the attackers must keep clear of close examination and block every peephole and every loophole through which the eye of reason might pry into us. This absence of your father's draws back a curtain that shows the ignorant a cause for fear they never dreamed of before.

Nay, you strain too far. / I, rather, of his absence make this use: / It lends a lustre and more great opinion, / A larger dare to our great enterprise, / Than if the earl were here; for men must think, / If we, without his help, can make a head / To push against the kingdom, with his help / We shall o'erturn it topsy-turvy down. / Yet all goes well, yet all our joints are whole.

No, you're going too far. I make this use of his absence instead: it gives more glory and a greater reputation, a bigger sense of daring, to our great enterprise than if the Earl were here. Because people will think that if we can raise an army without his help to attack the kingdom, with his help we'll turn it upside down. All is still well; all our limbs are still whole.
As heart can think: there is not such a word / Spoke in Scotland as this term of fear.
As well as the heart could wish. There's no such word as "fear" spoken in Scotland.
My cousin Vernon! welcome, by my soul.
My cousin Vernon! Welcome, by my soul.
Pray God my news be worth a welcome, lord. / The Earl of Westmoreland, seven thousand strong, / Is marching hitherwards; with him Prince John.
I pray to God my news deserves a welcome, my lord. The Earl of Westmoreland is marching this way, seven thousand strong, and Prince John with him.
No harm in that. What else?
And further, I have learn'd / The King himself in person is set forth, / Or hitherwards intended speedily, / With strong and mighty preparation.
And further, I've learned that the King himself has set out in person, or plans to come this way quickly, with a strong and mighty army.
He shall be welcome too. Where is his son, / The nimble-footed madcap Prince of Wales, / And his comrades, that daff the world aside, / And bid it pass?
He'll be welcome too. Where's his son, the nimble-footed madcap Prince of Wales, and his friends, who toss the world aside and tell it to go its way?

All furnish'd, all in arms; / All plumed like estridges that with the wind / Bate it; like eagles having lately bathed; / Glittering in golden coats, like images; / As full of spirit as the month of May / And gorgeous as the Sun at midsummer; / Wanton as youthful goats, wild as young bulls. / I saw young Harry—with his beaver on, / His cuisses on his thighs, gallantly arm'd— / Rise from the ground like feather'd Mercury, / And vault it with such ease into his seat, / As if an angel dropp'd down from the clouds, / To turn and wind a fiery Pegasus, / And witch the world with noble horsemanship.

All equipped, all in armour, all plumed like ostriches flapping their wings in the wind, like eagles that have just bathed, glittering in golden coats like statues of saints, as full of spirit as the month of May and as splendid as the sun at midsummer, as playful as young goats and as wild as young bulls. I saw young Harry, with his visor up and his thigh armour on, splendidly armed, rise from the ground like winged Mercury and vault into the saddle so easily that it was as if an angel had dropped from the clouds to turn and wheel a fiery Pegasus and enchant the world with noble horsemanship.

No more, no more: worse than the Sun in March, / This praise doth nourish agues. Let them come; / They come like sacrifices in their trim, / And to the fire-eyed maid of smoky war, / All hot and bleeding, will we offer them: / The mailed Mars shall on his altar sit / Up to the ears in blood. I am on fire / To hear this rich reprisal is so nigh, / And yet not ours.—Come, let me taste my horse, / Who is to bear me, like a thunderbolt, / Against the bosom of the Prince of Wales: / Harry and Harry shall, hot horse to horse, / Meet, and ne'er part till one drop down a corse.— / O, that Glendower were come!

No more, no more! Worse than the sun in March, this praise breeds fevers. Let them come. They come like sacrificial animals in their finery, and we will offer them, all hot and bleeding, to the fiery-eyed goddess of smoky war. Armoured Mars will sit on his altar up to his ears in blood. I'm on fire to hear that this rich prize is so near and not yet ours. Come, let me try out my horse, which is to carry me like a thunderbolt against the chest of the Prince of Wales. Harry and Harry will meet, hot horse against horse, and never part till one drops down a corpse. Oh, if only Glendower had come!
There is more news: / I learn'd in Worcester, as I rode along, / He cannot draw his power this fourteen days.
There's more news. I learned in Worcester, as I rode along, that he can't gather his army for a fortnight.
That's the worst tidings that I hear of yet.
That's the worst news I've heard so far.
Ay, by my faith, that bears a frosty sound.
Yes, by my faith, that has a chilling sound.
What may the King's whole battle reach unto?
How big might the King's whole army be?
Forty let it be: / My father and Glendower being both away, / The powers of us may serve so great a day. / Come, let us take a muster speedily: / Doomsday is near; die all, die merrily.
Let it be forty. With my father and Glendower both away, our forces will be enough for such a great day. Come, let's hold a roll-call quickly. Doomsday is near; if we all die, let's die merrily.
Talk not of dying: I am out of fear / Of death or death's hand for this one half-year.
Don't talk about dying. I'm free from the fear of death or death's hand for the next half-year.
Bardolph, get thee before to Coventry; fill me a bottle of / sack: our soldiers shall march through; we'll to Sutton-Co'fil' / to-night.
Bardolph, go on ahead to Coventry and fill me a bottle of sherry. Our soldiers will march through; we'll get to Sutton Coldfield tonight.
Will you give me money, captain?
Will you give me money, captain?
Pay for it yourself, pay for it yourself.
This bottle will make an angel, a ten-shilling coin.
An if it do, take it for thy labour; an if it make twenty, / take them all; I'll answer the coinage. Bid my lieutenant / Peto meet me at the town's end.
And if it does, take it for your trouble; and if it makes twenty, take them all, I'll vouch for the coins. Tell my lieutenant Peto to meet me at the edge of town.

If I be not ashamed of my soldiers, I am a soused gurnet. I have / misused the King's press damnably. I have got, in exchange of / a hundred and fifty soldiers, three hundred and odd pounds. I / press'd me none but good householders, yeomen's sons; inquired / me out contracted bachelors, such as had been ask'd twice on the / banns; such a commodity of warm slaves as had as lief hear the / Devil as a drum; such as fear the report of a caliver worse than / a struck fowl or a hurt wild-duck. I press'd me none but such / toasts-and-butter, with hearts in their bodies no bigger than / pins'-heads, and they have bought out their services; and now / my whole charge consists of ancients, corporals, lieutenants, / gentlemen of companies, slaves as ragged as Lazarus in the / painted cloth, where the glutton's dogs licked his sores; and / such as, indeed, were never soldiers, but discarded unjust / serving-men, younger sons to younger brothers, revolted tapsters, / and ostlers trade-fallen; the cankers of a calm world and a long / peace; ten times more dishonourable ragged than an old faced / ancient: and such have I, to fill up the rooms of them that have / bought out their services, that you would think that I had a / hundred and fifty tattered Prodigals lately come from / swine-keeping, from eating draff and husks. A mad fellow met me on / the way, and told me I had unloaded all the gibbets, and press'd / the dead bodies. / No eye hath seen such scarecrows. I'll not march through Coventry / with them, that's flat: nay, and the villains march wide betwixt / the legs, as if they had gyves on; for, indeed, I had the most of / them out of prison. There's but a shirt and a half in all my company; / and the half-shirt is two napkins tack'd together and thrown over the / shoulders like a herald's coat without sleeves; and the shirt, to say / the truth, stolen from my host at Saint Alban's, or the red-nose / innkeeper of Daventry. / But that's all one; they'll find linen enough on every hedge.

If I'm not ashamed of my soldiers, I'm a pickled fish. I've abused the King's power to conscript men damnably. In exchange for a hundred and fifty soldiers, I've got three hundred and something pounds. I conscripted nobody but well-off householders and farmers' sons; I sought out engaged bachelors whose wedding banns had been read twice, a whole load of comfortable cowards who would as soon hear the Devil as a drum, men who fear the bang of a musket more than a wounded bird or a hurt wild duck. I conscripted nobody but such milksops, with hearts no bigger than pinheads, and they've all bought themselves out of service. And now my whole company consists of standard-bearers, corporals, lieutenants and gentlemen of the ranks, wretches as ragged as Lazarus in the painted wall-hanging, where the glutton's dogs licked his sores; and men who were never really soldiers at all, but dishonest servants who've been sacked, younger sons of younger brothers, runaway barmen and stable-boys out of work, the cankers of a calm world and a long peace, ten times more dishonourably ragged than an old patched flag. And I've got such men to fill the places of those who bought themselves out that you'd think I had a hundred and fifty tattered Prodigal Sons just back from keeping pigs and eating swill and husks. A madman met me on the way and told me I'd emptied all the gallows and conscripted the dead bodies. No eye has ever seen such scarecrows. I won't march through Coventry with them, that's certain. And the villains march with their legs wide apart, as if they still had shackles on, because I got most of them out of prison. There's only a shirt and a half in my whole company, and the half-shirt is two napkins tacked together and thrown over the shoulders like a herald's sleeveless coat, and the shirt, to tell the truth, was stolen from my landlord at Saint Albans or the red-nosed innkeeper of Daventry. But that doesn't matter; they'll find plenty of linen drying on every hedge.
How now, blown Jack! how now, quilt!
How now, puffed-up Jack! How now, quilt!
What, Hal! how now, mad wag! what a devil dost thou in / Warwickshire?—My good Lord of Westmoreland, I cry you mercy: / I thought your honour had already been at Shrewsbury.
What, Hal! How now, mad joker! What the devil are you doing in Warwickshire? My good lord of Westmoreland, I beg your pardon. I thought your honour was already at Shrewsbury.
Faith, Sir John, 'tis more than time that I were there, and you too; / but my powers are there already. The King, I can tell you, looks for / us all: we must away all, to-night.
Honestly, Sir John, it's high time I was there, and you too; but my troops are there already. The King, I can tell you, is expecting us all. We must all move on tonight.
Tut, never fear me: I am as vigilant as a cat to steal cream.
Nonsense, don't worry about me. I'm as alert as a cat stealing cream.
I think, to steal cream, indeed; for thy theft hath already made thee / butter. But tell me, Jack, whose fellows are these that come after?
Stealing cream, indeed, I think, because your thieving has already turned you into butter. But tell me, Jack, whose men are these coming along behind?
I did never see such pitiful rascals.
I've never seen such pitiful wretches.
Tut, tut; good enough to toss; food for powder, food for powder; / they'll fill a pit as well as better: tush, man, mortal men, / mortal men.
Tut, tut, good enough to be tossed on a pike. Food for gunpowder, food for gunpowder. They'll fill a mass grave as well as better men. Nonsense, man, they're mortal men, mortal men.
Ay, but, Sir John, methinks they are exceeding poor and bare,—too / beggarly.
Yes, but, Sir John, I think they're extremely poor and thin, too beggarly.
Faith, for their poverty, I know not where they had that; and, / for their bareness, I am sure they never learn'd that of me.
Well, as for their poverty, I don't know where they got that; and as for their thinness, I'm sure they never learned that from me.
No, I'll be sworn; unless you call three fingers on the ribs / bare. But, sirrah, make haste: Percy is already in the field.
No, I'll swear to that, unless you call three fingers' thickness of fat on the ribs thin. But hurry up, man. Percy is already in the field.
What, is the King in camp?
He is, Sir John: I fear we shall stay too long.
He is, Sir John. I'm afraid we'll be too late.
Well, / To the latter end of a fray and the beginning of a feast / Fits a dull fighter and a keen guest.
Well, the end of a fight and the start of a feast suit a dull fighter and a keen guest.
Then you're giving him an advantage.
Why say you so? looks he not for supply?
Why do you say that? Isn't he expecting reinforcements?
His is certain, ours is doubtful.
His are certain, ours are doubtful.
Good cousin, be advised; stir not to-night.
Good nephew, take advice; don't move tonight.
You do not counsel well: / You speak it out of fear and cold heart.
You're not giving good advice. You say it out of fear and cowardice.

Do me no slander, Douglas: by my life,— / And I dare well maintain it with my life,— / If well-respected honour bid me on, / I hold as little counsel with weak fear / As you, my lord, or any Scot that this day lives: / Let it be seen to-morrow in the battle / Which of us fears.

Don't slander me, Douglas. By my life, and I dare defend it with my life, if honour properly considered calls me on, I take as little notice of weak fear as you do, my lord, or any Scot alive today. Let it be seen in tomorrow's battle which of us is afraid.

Come, come, it may not be. I wonder much, / Being men of such great leading as you are, / That you foresee not what impediments / Drag back our expedition: certain Horse / Of my cousin Vernon's are not yet come up: / Your uncle Worcester's Horse came but to-day; / And now their pride and mettle is asleep, / Their courage with hard labour tame and dull, / That not a horse is half the half himself.

Come, come, it can't be done. I'm amazed that men with such great experience of command as you don't see what obstacles hold back our advance. Some of my cousin Vernon's cavalry haven't arrived yet. Your uncle Worcester's cavalry only came today, and now their pride and spirit are asleep, their courage tamed and dulled by hard work, so that not one horse is a quarter of his usual self.
So are the horses of the enemy / In general, journey-bated and brought low: / The better part of ours are full of rest.
So are the enemy's horses, generally worn out by the journey and run down. Most of ours are well rested.
The number of the King exceedeth ours. / For God's sake, cousin, stay till all come in.
The King's army is bigger than ours. For God's sake, nephew, wait till everyone has arrived.
I come with gracious offers from the King, / If you vouchsafe me hearing and respect.
I come with generous offers from the King, if you will grant me a respectful hearing.

Welcome, Sir Walter Blunt; and would to God / You were of our determination! / Some of us love you well; and even those some / Envy your great deservings and good name, / Because you are not of our quality, / But stand against us like an enemy.

Welcome, Sir Walter Blunt; and I wish to God you were on our side! Some of us love you well, and even those of us who do resent your great merits and good name because you aren't one of us, but stand against us like an enemy.

And God defend but still I should stand so, / So long as out of limit and true rule / You stand against anointed majesty! / But to my charge: the King hath sent to know / The nature of your griefs; and whereupon / You conjure from the breast of civil peace / Such bold hostility, teaching his duteous land / Audacious cruelty. If that the King / Have any way your good deserts forgot, / Which he confesseth to be manifold, / He bids you name your griefs; and with all speed / You shall have your desires with interest, / And pardon absolute for yourself and these / Herein misled by your suggestion.

And God forbid that I should stand anywhere else, as long as you stand against the anointed King, outside the law and true allegiance! But to my message. The King has sent to find out the nature of your grievances, and why you summon up such bold hostility out of the heart of peace at home, teaching his dutiful country reckless cruelty. If the King has in any way forgotten your services, which he admits are many, he invites you to name your grievances, and you will quickly have what you want with interest, and a full pardon for yourself and those you have misled into this.

The King is kind; and well we know the King / Knows at what time to promise, when to pay. / My father and my uncle and myself / Did give him that same royalty he wears; / And—when he was not six-and-twenty strong, / Sick in the world's regard, wretched and low, / A poor unminded outlaw sneaking home— / My father gave him welcome to the shore: / And—when he heard him swear and vow to God, / He came but to be Duke of Lancaster, / To sue his livery and beg his peace, / With tears of innocence and terms of zeal— / My father, in kind heart and pity moved, / Swore him assistance, and performed it too. / Now, when the lords and barons of the realm / Perceived Northumberland did lean to him, / The more and less came in with cap and knee; / Met him in boroughs, cities, villages, / Attended him on bridges, stood in lanes, / Laid gifts before him, proffer'd him their oaths, / Give him their heirs as pages, follow'd him / Even at the heels in golden multitudes. / He presently—as greatness knows itself— / Steps me a little higher than his vow / Made to my father, while his blood was poor, / Upon the naked shore at Ravenspurg; / And now, forsooth, takes on him to reform / Some certain edicts and some strait decrees / That lie too heavy on the commonwealth; / Cries out upon abuses, seems to weep / Over his country's wrongs; and, by this face, / This seeming brow of justice, did he win / The hearts of all that he did angle for: / Proceeded further; cut me off the heads / Of all the favourites, that the absent King / In deputation left behind him here / When he was personal in the Irish war.

The King is kind, and we know well that the King knows when to promise and when to pay. My father, my uncle and I gave him the very crown he wears. And when he had fewer than twenty-six followers, out of favour with the world, wretched and low, a poor, ignored outlaw sneaking home, my father welcomed him ashore. And when he heard him swear and vow to God that he had come only to be Duke of Lancaster, to claim his inheritance and beg for peace, with innocent tears and passionate words, my father, moved by kindness and pity, swore to help him, and did so too. Now, when the lords and barons of the kingdom saw that Northumberland supported him, great and small came to him with caps off and knees bent, met him in towns, cities and villages, waited for him on bridges, stood in lanes, laid gifts before him, offered him their oaths, gave him their heirs as pages, and followed at his heels in glittering crowds. Immediately, as greatness becomes aware of itself, he went a step higher than the vow he made to my father, when he was weak, on the bare shore at Ravenspurgh. And now, if you please, he takes it on himself to reform certain laws and harsh decrees that weigh too heavily on the country, cries out against abuses, seems to weep over his country's wrongs; and with this face, this pretended look of justice, he won the hearts of everyone he was fishing for. He went further: cut off the heads of all the favourites whom the absent King had left behind here as his deputies when he was in person at the Irish war.
Tut, I came not to hear this.
Tut, I didn't come to hear this.

Then to the point: / In short time after, he deposed the King; / Soon after that, deprived him of his life; / And, in the neck of that, task'd the whole State: / To make that worse, suffer'd his kinsman March / (Who is, if every owner were well placed, / Indeed his king) to be engaged in Wales, / There without ransom to lie forfeited; / Disgraced me in my happy victories, / Sought to entrap me by intelligence; / Rated my uncle from the Council-board; / In rage dismiss'd my father from the Court; / Broke oath on oath, committed wrong on wrong; / And, in conclusion, drove us to seek out / This head of safety; and withal to pry / Into his title, the which now we find / Too indirect for long continuance.

Then to the point. Shortly afterwards he deposed the King, soon after that took his life, and straight after that taxed the whole country. To make it worse, he allowed his kinsman March (who, if everyone had his rightful place, is really his king) to be held hostage in Wales, left there without ransom. He belittled me in my lucky victories and tried to trap me with spies; scolded my uncle and drove him from the Council table, angrily dismissed my father from Court, broke oath after oath, committed wrong after wrong, and, in short, drove us to raise this army for our safety, and at the same time to look into his claim to the throne, which we now find too crooked to last long.
Shall I return this answer to the King?
Shall I take this answer back to the King?

Not so, Sir Walter: we'll withdraw awhile. / Go to the King; and let there be impawn'd / Some surety for a safe return again, / And in the morning early shall my uncle / Bring him our purposes: and so, farewell.

No, Sir Walter. We'll withdraw for a while. Go to the King, and let some hostage be pledged to guarantee my uncle's safe return, and early in the morning my uncle will bring him our intentions. And so goodbye.
I would you would accept of grace and love.
I wish you would accept his grace and love.
And may be so we shall.
I pray to God you do.

Hie, good Sir Michael; bear this sealed brief / With winged haste to the Lord Marshal; / This to my cousin Scroop; and all the rest / To whom they are directed. If you knew / How much they do import, you would make haste.

Hurry, good Sir Michael. Take this sealed letter with all speed to the Lord Marshal, this one to my cousin Scroop, and all the rest to those they are addressed to. If you knew how important they are, you would hurry.
My good lord, / I guess their tenour.
My good lord, I can guess what they say.

Like enough you do. / To-morrow, good Sir Michael, is a day / Wherein the fortune of ten thousand men / Must bide the touch; for, sir, at Shrewsbury, / As I am truly given to understand, / The King, with mighty and quick-raised power, / Meets with Lord Harry: and, I fear, Sir Michael, / What with the sickness of Northumberland, / Whose power was in the first proportion, / And what with Owen Glendower's absence thence, / Who with them was a rated sinew too, / And comes not in, o'er-rul'd by prophecies,— / I fear the power of Percy is too weak / To wage an instant trial with the King.

You very likely can. Tomorrow, good Sir Michael, is a day when the fortune of ten thousand men must be put to the test. For, sir, at Shrewsbury, as I am reliably told, the King, with a mighty army quickly raised, meets Lord Harry Percy. And I fear, Sir Michael, what with the illness of Northumberland, whose army was the largest, and what with the absence of Owen Glendower, who was also counted on as a main strength and isn't coming, held back by prophecies, I fear Percy's army is too weak for an immediate trial of strength with the King.
Why, my good lord, you need not fear; / There's Douglas and Lord Mortimer.
Why, my good lord, you needn't be afraid. There's Douglas and Lord Mortimer.
But there is Mordake, Vernon, Lord Harry Percy, / And there's my Lord of Worcester; and a head / Of gallant warriors, noble gentlemen.
But there's Mordake, Vernon, Lord Harry Percy, and my lord of Worcester, and a force of brave warriors, noble gentlemen.

And so there is: but yet the King hath drawn / The special head of all the land together; / The Prince of Wales, Lord John of Lancaster, / The noble Westmoreland, and warlike Blunt; / And many more corrivals and dear men / Of estimation and command in arms.

So there is. But the King has gathered the best of the whole country: the Prince of Wales, Lord John of Lancaster, the noble Westmoreland and warlike Blunt, and many more partners and valued men of reputation and command in war.
Doubt not, my lord, they shall be well opposed.
Don't doubt it, my lord, they'll be well matched.

I hope no less, yet needful 'tis to fear; / And, to prevent the worst, Sir Michael, speed: / For if Lord Percy thrive not, ere the King / Dismiss his power, he means to visit us, / For he hath heard of our confederacy; / And 'tis but wisdom to make strong against him: / Therefore make haste. I must go write again / To other friends; and so, farewell, Sir Michael.

I hope so, yet it's necessary to fear. And to prevent the worst, Sir Michael, hurry. If Lord Percy doesn't succeed, the King means to visit us before he disbands his army, because he has heard of our alliance, and it's only wise to prepare our defences against him. So hurry. I must go and write to other friends. And so goodbye, Sir Michael.
How bloodily the Sun begins to peer / Above yon busky hill! the day looks pale / At his distemperature.
How bloodily the sun is beginning to peep over that wooded hill! The day looks pale at its sickly look.
The southern wind / Doth play the trumpet to his purposes; / And by his hollow whistling in the leaves / Foretells a tempest and a blustering day.
The south wind is acting as trumpeter for its intentions, and by its hollow whistling in the leaves it foretells a storm and a blustery day.
Then with the losers let it sympathize, / For nothing can seem foul to those that win.—
Then let it share the mood of the losers, because nothing can seem bad to those who win.

How, now, my Lord of Worcester! 'tis not well / That you and I should meet upon such terms / As now we meet. You have deceived our trust; / And made us doff our easy robes of peace, / To crush our old limbs in ungentle steel: / This is not well, my lord, this is not well. / What say you to't? will you again unknit / This churlish knot of all-abhorred war, / And move in that obedient orb again / Where you did give a fair and natural light; / And be no more an exhaled meteor, / A prodigy of fear, and a portent / Of broached mischief to the unborn times?

Well, my lord of Worcester! It isn't right that you and I should meet on such terms as we meet on now. You have betrayed our trust and made us take off our comfortable robes of peace to squeeze our old limbs into harsh steel armour. This isn't right, my lord, this isn't right. What do you say to it? Will you untie this brutal knot of hated war again and move once more in that obedient orbit where you gave out a fair and natural light, and no longer be a meteor sucked up from the earth, a fearful omen, a sign of evil let loose on generations not yet born?
Hear me, my liege: / For mine own part, I could be well content / To entertain the lag-end of my life / With quiet hours; for I do protest, / I have not sought the day of this dislike.
Listen to me, my lord. For my own part, I would be glad to spend the last part of my life in quiet hours, because I swear I have not looked for this day of conflict.
You have not sought it! why, how comes it, then?
You haven't looked for it! Why, how has it come about, then?
Rebellion lay in his way, and he found it.
Rebellion lay in his path, and he found it.

It pleased your Majesty to turn your looks / Of favour from myself and all our House; / And yet I must remember you, my lord, / We were the first and dearest of your friends. / For you my staff of office did I break / In Richard's time; and posted day and night / To meet you on the way, and kiss your hand, / When yet you were in place and in account / Nothing so strong and fortunate as I. / It was myself, my brother, and his son, / That brought you home, and boldly did outdare / The dangers of the time. You swore to us,— / And you did swear that oath at Doncaster,— / That you did nothing purpose 'gainst the state; / Nor claim no further than your new-fall'n right, / The seat of Gaunt, dukedom of Lancaster: / To this we swore our aid. But in short space / It rain'd down fortune showering on your head; / And such a flood of greatness fell on you,— / What with our help, what with the absent King, / What with the injuries of a wanton time, / The seeming sufferances that you had borne, / And the contrarious winds that held the King / So long in his unlucky Irish wars / That all in England did repute him dead,— / And, from this swarm of fair advantages, / You took occasion to be quickly woo'd / To gripe the general sway into your hand; / Forgot your oath to us at Doncaster; / And, being fed by us, you used us so / As that ungentle gull, the cuckoo-bird, / Useth the sparrow; did oppress our nest; / Grew by our feeding to so great a bulk, / That even our love durst not come near your sight / For fear of swallowing; but with nimble wing / We were enforced, for safety-sake, to fly / Out of your sight, and raise this present head: / Whereby we stand opposed by such means / As you yourself have forged against yourself, / By unkind usage, dangerous countenance, / And violation of all faith and troth / Sworn to us in your younger enterprise.

Your Majesty chose to turn your favourable looks away from me and our whole family. And yet I must remind you, my lord, that we were the first and dearest of your friends. For your sake I broke my staff of office in Richard's time and rode day and night to meet you on the way and kiss your hand, when you were nowhere near as strong and fortunate in position and reputation as I was. It was I, my brother and his son who brought you home and boldly faced the dangers of the time. You swore to us, and you swore that oath at Doncaster, that you intended nothing against the state and claimed no more than your newly inherited right, the seat of Gaunt, the dukedom of Lancaster. To this we swore our help. But in a short time fortune rained down in showers on your head, and such a flood of greatness fell on you, what with our help, the King's absence, the wrongs of a disorderly time, the injuries you seemed to have suffered, and the contrary winds that kept the King so long in his unlucky Irish wars that everyone in England thought he was dead, that out of this swarm of advantages you let yourself be quickly persuaded to seize total power into your own hands, and forgot your oath to us at Doncaster. And after being fed by us, you treated us as that unkind gull, the cuckoo, treats the sparrow: you crushed our nest and grew so huge on our feeding that even our love didn't dare come near you for fear of being swallowed. So we were forced, for safety's sake, to fly out of your sight on quick wings and raise this army. And so we stand against you by means you yourself have forged against yourself, through unkind treatment, threatening looks, and the breaking of all the faith and promises you swore to us in your earlier enterprise.

These things, indeed, you have articulate, / Proclaim'd at market-crosses, read in churches, / To face the garment of rebellion / With some fine colour that may please the eye / Of fickle changelings and poor discontents, / Which gape and rub the elbow at the news / Of hurlyburly innovation: / And never yet did insurrection want / Such water-colours to impaint his cause; / Nor moody beggars, starving for a time / Of pellmell havoc and confusion.

These things, indeed, you have listed, proclaimed at market crosses and read out in churches, to trim the garment of rebellion with some fine colour that may please the eyes of fickle turncoats and poor malcontents, who gape and rub their elbows at the news of riotous change. And rebellion has never lacked such watercolours to paint over its cause, nor sullen beggars hungry for a time of chaos and confusion.

In both our armies there is many a soul / Shall pay full dearly for this encounter, / If once they join in trial. Tell your nephew, / The Prince of Wales doth join with all the world / In praise of Henry Percy: by my hopes, / This present enterprise set off his head, / I do not think a braver gentleman, / More active-valiant or more valiant-young, / More daring or more bold, is now alive / To grace this latter age with noble deeds. / For my part,—I may speak it to my shame,— / I have a truant been to chivalry; / And so I hear he doth account me too: / Yet this before my father's Majesty,— / I am content that he shall take the odds / Of his great name and estimation, / And will, to save the blood on either side, / Try fortune with him in a single fight.

In both our armies there are many souls who will pay very dearly for this encounter, once they meet in battle. Tell your nephew that the Prince of Wales joins with all the world in praising Henry Percy. By my hopes of heaven, if this present rebellion is not counted against him, I don't think there is a braver gentleman alive, more actively brave or more bravely young, more daring or more bold, to grace this modern age with noble deeds. For my part, I say it to my shame, I have been a truant from chivalry, and I hear that's how he regards me too. Yet I say this before my father's Majesty: I am willing to let him have the advantage of his great name and reputation, and, to save blood on both sides, I will try my fortune with him in single combat.

And, Prince of Wales, so dare we venture thee, / Albeit considerations infinite / Do make against it.—No, good Worcester, no; / We love our people well; even those we love / That are misled upon your cousin's part; / And, will they take the offer of our grace, / Both he, and they, and you, yea, every man / Shall be my friend again, and I'll be his: / So tell your cousin, and then bring me word / What he will do: but, if he will not yield, / Rebuke and dread correction wait on us, / And they shall do their office. So, be gone; / We will not now be troubled with reply: / We offer fair; take it advisedly.

And, Prince of Wales, we would dare to risk you in it, though countless considerations count against it. No, good Worcester, no, we love our people well; we love even those who are misled on your nephew's side. And if they will accept our offer of mercy, he, they and you, yes, every man, shall be my friend again, and I'll be his. So tell your nephew, and then bring me word what he will do. But if he won't give in, rebuke and fearful punishment wait at our command, and they will do their job. So go. We won't be troubled with a reply now. Our offer is fair; consider it wisely.
It will not be accepted, on my life: / The Douglas and the Hotspur both together / Are confident against the world in arms.
It won't be accepted, on my life. Douglas and Hotspur together are confident against the whole world in arms.
Hence, therefore, every leader to his charge; / For, on their answer, will we set on them: / And God befriend us, as our cause is just!
Away, then, every commander to his troops, because once they've answered, we'll attack them. And may God befriend us, since our cause is just!
Hal, if thou see me down in the battle, and bestride me, / so; 'tis a point of friendship.
Hal, if you see me down in the battle, stand over me to protect me. It's a point of friendship.
Nothing but a colossus can do thee that friendship. / Say thy prayers, and farewell.
Only a colossus could do you that kind of friendship. Say your prayers, and goodbye.
I would it were bedtime, Hal, and all well.
I wish it were bedtime, Hal, and all was well.
Why, thou owest God a death.
Why, you owe God a death.

'Tis not due yet; I would be loth to pay Him before His day. / What need I be so forward with him that calls not on me? / Well, 'tis no matter; honour pricks me on. Yea, but how if honour / prick me off when I come on? how then? Can honour set-to a leg? / no: or an arm? no: or take away the grief of a wound? no. Honour / hath no skill in surgery then? no. What is honour? a word. What / is that word, honour? air. A trim reckoning!—Who hath it? he that / died o' Wednesday. Doth he feel it? no. Doth he hear it? no. Is it / insensible, then? yea, to the dead. But will it not live with the / living? no. Why? detraction will not suffer it. Therefore I'll none / of it: honour is a mere scutcheon:—and so ends my catechism.

It isn't due yet; I'd hate to pay him before the day it's due. Why should I be so eager to meet someone who isn't calling on me? Well, it doesn't matter; honour spurs me on. Yes, but what if honour marks me off the list of the living when I come on? What then? Can honour set a broken leg? No. Or an arm? No. Or take away the pain of a wound? No. Honour has no skill in surgery, then? No. What is honour? A word. What is in that word "honour"? Air. A fine sum! Who has it? The man who died on Wednesday. Does he feel it? No. Does he hear it? No. So it can't be sensed? Yes, by the dead. But won't it live with the living? No. Why? Slander won't allow it. So I'll have none of it. Honour is just a painted coat of arms at a funeral. And so my catechism ends.
O no, my nephew must not know, Sir Richard, / The liberal-kind offer of the King.
Oh no, my nephew mustn't know about the King's generous and kind offer, Sir Richard.
It would be best if he did.

Then are we all undone. / It is not possible, it cannot be, / The King should keep his word in loving us; / He will suspect us still, and find a time / To punish this offence in other faults: / Suspicion all our lives shall be stuck full of eyes; / For treason is but trusted like the fox, / Who, ne'er so tame, so cherish'd, and lock'd up, / Will have a wild trick of his ancestors. / Look how we can, or sad or merrily, / Interpretation will misquote our looks; / And we shall feed like oxen at a stall, / The better cherish'd, still the nearer death. / My nephew's trespass may be well forgot: / It hath th' excuse of youth and heat of blood, / And an adopted name of privilege,— / A hare-brain'd Hotspur, govern'd by a spleen: / All his offences live upon my head / And on his father's: we did train him on; / And, his corruption being ta'en from us, / We, as the spring of all, shall pay for all. / Therefore, good cousin, let not Harry know, / In any case, the offer of the King.

Then we are all ruined. It isn't possible, it can't be, that the King will keep his word to love us. He'll always suspect us and find a time to punish this offence through other faults. All our lives suspicion will be watching us with a hundred eyes, because treason is trusted only like a fox, which, however tame, well cared for and locked up, will still have some wild trick of its ancestors. However we look, sad or merry, people will misread our looks, and we'll feed like oxen in a stall: the better looked after, the nearer to death. My nephew's offence may well be forgotten. It has the excuse of youth and hot blood, and a nickname that gives him licence, a hare-brained Hotspur, ruled by his temper. All his offences rest on my head and on his father's. We led him on, and since he caught his corruption from us, we, as the source of it all, will pay for all. So, good cousin, don't let Harry know about the King's offer in any circumstances.
Deliver what you will, I'll say 'tis so. / Here comes your cousin.
Tell him what you like; I'll say it's so. Here comes your nephew.
My uncle is return'd: deliver up / My Lord of Westmoreland.—Uncle, what news?
My uncle has returned. Release my lord of Westmoreland. Uncle, what news?
The King will bid you battle presently.
The King will offer you battle at once.
Defy him by the Lord Of Westmoreland.
Send him a challenge by the lord of Westmoreland.
Lord Douglas, go you and tell him so.
Lord Douglas, go and tell him so.
Marry, I shall, and very willingly.
Indeed I will, and very willingly.
There is no seeming mercy in the King.
There's no sign of mercy in the King.
Did you beg any? God forbid!
Did you beg for any? God forbid!

I told him gently of our grievances, / Of his oath-breaking; which he mended thus, / By new-forswearing that he is forsworn: / He calls us rebels, traitors; and will scourge / With haughty arms this hateful name in us.

I told him gently about our grievances and his oath-breaking, which he corrected by swearing falsely all over again that he hadn't broken his oath. He calls us rebels and traitors, and will punish this hateful name in us with proud arms.
Arm, gentlemen; to arms! for I have thrown / A brave defiance in King Henry's teeth, / And Westmoreland, that was engaged, did bear it; / Which cannot choose but bring him quickly on.
To arms, gentlemen, to arms! I've thrown a bold defiance in King Henry's teeth, and Westmoreland, who was our hostage, carried it, which is bound to bring him on quickly.
The Prince of Wales stepp'd forth before the King, / And, nephew, challenged you to single fight.
The Prince of Wales stepped out in front of the King and, nephew, challenged you to single combat.
O, would the quarrel lay upon our heads; / And that no man might draw short breath to-day / But I and Harry Monmouth! Tell me, tell me, / How show'd his tasking? seem'd it in contempt?
Oh, I wish the quarrel rested on our heads alone, and that no man would be out of breath today except me and Harry Monmouth! Tell me, tell me, how did his challenge sound? Did it seem scornful?

No, by my soul: I never in my life / Did hear a challenge urged more modestly, / Unless a brother should a brother dare / To gentle exercise and proof of arms. / He gave you all the duties of a man; / Trimm'd up your praises with a princely tongue; / Spoke your deservings like a chronicle; / Making you ever better than his praise, / By still dispraising praise valued with you; / And, which became him like a prince indeed, / He made a blushing cital of himself; / And chid his truant youth with such a grace, / As if he master'd there a double spirit, / Of teaching and of learning instantly. / There did he pause: but let me tell the world, / If he outlive the envy of this day, / England did never owe so sweet a hope, / So much misconstrued in his wantonness.

No, by my soul. I never in my life heard a challenge made more modestly, unless a brother were challenging a brother to a friendly bout of arms. He gave you every honour due to a man, decorated your praises with a princely tongue, listed your merits like a history book, always making you better than his praise by dismissing praise itself as inadequate compared with you. And, what really suited him like a true prince, he gave a blushing account of himself and scolded his truant youth so gracefully that it was as if he had a double gift, teaching and learning at the same moment. There he stopped. But let me tell the world, if he survives the hostility of this day, England never had so sweet a hope, so much misjudged in his wildness.

Cousin, I think thou art enamoured / Upon his follies: never did I hear / Of any prince so wild o' liberty. / But be he as he will, yet once ere night / I will embrace him with a soldier's arm, / That he shall shrink under my courtesy.— / Arm, arm with speed: and, fellows, soldiers, friends, / Better consider what you have to do / Than I, that have not well the gift of tongue, / Can lift your blood up with persuasion.

Cousin, I think you've fallen in love with his follies. I never heard of any prince so wildly free. But let him be what he likes, before night I'll embrace him with a soldier's arm so that he'll shrink under my courtesy. To arms, to arms, quickly! And, comrades, soldiers, friends, you'd better think for yourselves about what you have to do, because I don't really have the gift of words to stir up your blood with persuasion.
My lord, here are letters for you.
My lord, here are letters for you.

I cannot read them now.— / O gentlemen, the time of life is short! / To spend that shortness basely were too long, / If life did ride upon a dial's point, / Still ending at th' arrival of an hour. / An if we live, we live to tread on kings; / If die, brave death, when princes die with us! / Now, for our consciences, the arms are fair, / When the intent of bearing them is just.

I can't read them now. Oh gentlemen, life is short! But to spend that short time basely would be too long, even if life rode on the hand of a clock and ended when the hour came. If we live, we live to trample on kings; if we die, it's a fine death when princes die with us! Now, as for our consciences, the cause is fair when the reason for taking up arms is just.
My lord, prepare: the King comes on apace.
My lord, get ready. The King is advancing fast.

I thank him, that he cuts me from my tale, / For I profess not talking; only this, / Let each man do his best: and here draw I / A sword, whose temper I intend to stain / With the best blood that I can meet withal / In the adventure of this perilous day. / Now, Esperance! Percy! and set on. / Sound all the lofty instruments of war, / And by that music let us all embrace; / For, Heaven to Earth, some of us never shall / A second time do such a courtesy.

I thank him for cutting short my speech, because talking isn't my trade. Only this: let each man do his best. And here I draw a sword whose steel I mean to stain with the best blood I can meet in the adventure of this dangerous day. Now, Esperance! Percy! And charge! Sound all the lofty instruments of war, and to that music let us all embrace, because, heaven to earth, some of us will never do such a kindness a second time.
What is thy name, that in the battle thus / Thou crossest me? what honour dost thou seek / Upon my head?
What's your name, that you come at me like this in the battle? What honour are you looking for from my head?
Know, then, my name is Douglas, / And I do haunt thee in the battle thus / Because some tell me that thou art a king.
Know, then, my name is Douglas, and I hunt you like this in the battle because some people tell me you are a king.
The Lord of Stafford dear to-day hath bought / Thy likeness; for, instead of thee, King Harry, / This sword hath ended him: so shall it thee, / Unless thou yield thee as my prisoner.
The Lord of Stafford paid dearly today for looking like you, because this sword killed him instead of you, King Harry; and it will kill you, unless you surrender as my prisoner.
I was not born a yielder, thou proud Scot; / And thou shalt find a king that will revenge / Lord Stafford's death.
I wasn't born to surrender, you proud Scot, and you'll find a king who will avenge Lord Stafford's death.
O Douglas, hadst thou fought at Holmedon thus, / I never had triumphed o'er a Scot.
Oh Douglas, if you had fought like this at Holmedon, I would never have beaten a Scot.
All's done, all's won; here breathless lies the King.
It's all over, all won. Here lies the King, dead.
This, Douglas? no; I know this face full well: / A gallant knight he was, his name was Blunt; / Semblably furnish'd like the King himself.
This, Douglas? No, I know this face very well. He was a brave knight; his name was Blunt, dressed just like the King himself.
A fool go with thy soul, where're it goes! / A borrow'd title hast thou bought too dear: / Why didst thou tell me that thou wert a king?
May the name of fool go with your soul, wherever it goes! You've paid too much for a borrowed title. Why did you tell me you were a king?
The King hath many marching in his coats.
The King has many men marching in his coats of arms.
Now, by my sword, I will kill all his coats; / I'll murder all his wardrobe piece by piece, / Until I meet the King.
Now, by my sword, I'll kill all his coats. I'll murder his whole wardrobe piece by piece until I meet the King.
Up, and away! / Our soldiers stand full fairly for the day.
Up, and away! Our soldiers are well placed to win the day.

Though I could 'scape shot-free at London, I fear the shot / here; here's no scoring but upon the pate.—Soft! who are you? / Sir Walter Blunt: there's honour for you! here's no vanity! I am / as hot as molten lead, and as heavy too: God keep lead out of me! / I need no more weight than mine own bowels. I have led my / ragamuffins where they are peppered: there's not three of my / hundred and fifty left alive; and they are for the town's end, to / beg during life. But who comes here?

Though I could escape paying the bill in London, I'm afraid of the shot here; there's no chalking it up here except on your head. Wait! Who are you? Sir Walter Blunt. There's honour for you! That's no empty show! I'm as hot as molten lead, and as heavy too. God keep lead out of me! I need no more weight than my own guts. I've led my ragamuffins where they've been shot to pieces. There aren't three of my hundred and fifty left alive, and they're fit for nothing but begging at the town gates for the rest of their lives. But who's coming here?
What, stand'st thou idle here? lend me thy sword: / Many a nobleman lies stark and stiff / Under the hoofs of vaunting enemies, / Whose deaths are yet unrevenged: I pr'ythee, / Lend me thy sword.
What, are you standing idle here? Lend me your sword. Many a nobleman lies stark and stiff under the hooves of boasting enemies, and their deaths are not yet avenged. Please lend me your sword.
O Hal, I pr'ythee give me leave to breathe awhile. Turk / Gregory never did such deeds in arms as I have done this / day. I have paid Percy, I have made him sure.
Oh Hal, please let me get my breath for a while. Turk Gregory never did such deeds in battle as I've done today. I've paid Percy back; I've made sure of him.
He is indeed; and living to kill thee. / I pr'ythee, lend me thy sword.
He's sure indeed, and alive to kill you. Please lend me your sword.
Nay, before God, Hal, if Percy be alive, thou gett'st not / my sword; but take my pistol, if thou wilt.
No, before God, Hal, if Percy's alive, you won't get my sword. But take my pistol, if you like.
Give it me: what, is it in the case?
Give it to me. What, is it in the holster?
Ay, Hal. 'Tis hot, 'tis hot: there's that will sack a city.
Yes, Hal. It's hot, it's hot. There's something there that will sack a city.
What, is't a time to jest and dally now?
What, is this a time to joke and fool around?

Well, if Percy be alive, I'll pierce him. If he do come in my / way, so; if he do not, if I come in his willingly, let him make / a carbonado of me. I like not such grinning honour as Sir / Walter hath: give me life; which if I can save, so; if not, / honour comes unlooked for, and there's an end.

Well, if Percy's alive, I'll pierce him. If he comes my way, fine; if he doesn't, and I go into his way willingly, let him cut me up for grilling. I don't like the kind of grinning honour Sir Walter has. Give me life. If I can save it, fine; if not, honour comes without my asking for it, and that's the end of it.
I pr'ythee, / Harry, withdraw thyself; thou bleedest too much.— / Lord John of Lancaster, go you unto him.
Please, Harry, withdraw; you're bleeding too much. Lord John of Lancaster, go with him.
Not I, my lord, unless I did bleed too.
Not I, my lord, unless I were bleeding too.
I do beseech your Majesty, make up, / Lest your retirement do amaze your friends.
I beg your Majesty, go forward, in case your retreat alarms your friends.
I will do so.— / My Lord of Westmoreland, lead him to his tent.
I will. My lord of Westmoreland, lead him to his tent.
Come, my lord, I'll lead you to your tent.
Come, my lord, I'll lead you to your tent.

Lead me, my lord? I do not need your help: / And God forbid, a shallow scratch should drive / The Prince of Wales from such a field as this, / Where stain'd nobility lies trodden on, / And rebels' arms triumph in massacres!

Lead me, my lord? I don't need your help. God forbid that a shallow scratch should drive the Prince of Wales from such a battlefield as this, where noblemen lie trampled in blood and rebels' weapons triumph in slaughter!
We breathe too long:—come, cousin Westmoreland, / Our duty this way lies; for God's sake, come.
We're resting too long. Come, cousin Westmoreland, our duty lies this way. For God's sake, come.
By Heaven, thou hast deceived me, Lancaster; / I did not think thee lord of such a spirit: / Before, I loved thee as a brother, John; / But now I do respect thee as my soul.
By heaven, you've surprised me, Lancaster; I didn't think you had such spirit. Before, I loved you as a brother, John; but now I respect you as my own soul.
I saw him hold Lord Percy at the point / With lustier maintenance than I did look for / Of such an ungrown warrior.
I saw him hold Lord Percy off at sword's point with more vigorous resistance than I expected from such a young warrior.
O, this boy / Lends mettle to us all!
Oh, this boy gives us all courage!
Another king! they grow like Hydra's heads: / I am the Douglas, fatal to all those / That wear those colours on them.—What art thou, / That counterfeit'st the person of a king?
Another king! They grow like the Hydra's heads. I am Douglas, deadly to everyone who wears those colours. Who are you, pretending to be a king?

The King himself; who, Douglas, grieves at heart / So many of his shadows thou hast met, / And not the very King. I have two boys / Seek Percy and thyself about the field: / But, seeing thou fall'st on me so luckily, / I will assay thee; so, defend thyself.

The King himself, who is sorry at heart, Douglas, that you've met so many of his shadows and not the real King. I have two sons looking for Percy and you around the battlefield; but since you've fallen on me so luckily, I'll take you on. So defend yourself.
I fear thou art another counterfeit; / And yet, in faith, thou bear'st thee like a king: / But mine I'm sure thou art, whoe'er thou be, / And thus I win thee.
I'm afraid you're another fake; and yet, honestly, you carry yourself like a king. But whoever you are, I'm sure you're mine, and this is how I'll win you.

Hold up thy head, vile Scot, or thou art like / Never to hold it up again! the spirits / Of valiant Shirley, Stafford, Blunt are in my arms: / It is the Prince of Wales that threatens thee; / Who never promiseth but he means to pay.—

Hold your head up, you vile Scot, or you're likely never to hold it up again! The spirits of brave Shirley, Stafford and Blunt are in my arms. It's the Prince of Wales who threatens you, and he never promises without meaning to pay.
Cheerly, my lord: how fares your Grace? / Sir Nicholas Gawsey hath for succour sent, / And so hath Clifton: I'll to Clifton straight.
Cheer up, my lord. How is your Grace? Sir Nicholas Gawsey has sent for help, and so has Clifton. I'll go to Clifton at once.
Stay, and breathe awhile: / Thou hast redeem'd thy lost opinion; / And show'd thou makest some tender of my life, / In this fair rescue thou hast brought to me.
Stay and rest for a while. You've won back your lost reputation and shown that you value my life, by this fine rescue you've made.

O God, they did me too much injury / That ever said I hearken'd for your death! / If it were so, I might have let alone / Th' insulting hand of Douglas over you, / Which would have been as speedy in your end / As all the poisonous potions in the world, / And saved the treacherous labour of your son.

Oh God, those who said I was waiting for your death did me a great wrong! If that were so, I could have left Douglas's insulting hand alone over you, which would have ended you as quickly as all the poisons in the world, and saved your son the treacherous labour.
Make up to Clifton: I'll to Sir Nicholas Gawsey.
Go on to Clifton. I'll go to Sir Nicholas Gawsey.
If I mistake not, thou art Harry Monmouth.
If I'm not mistaken, you're Harry Monmouth.
Thou speak'st as if I would deny my name.
You speak as if I would deny my name.

Why, then I see / A very valiant rebel of the name. / I am the Prince of Wales; and think not, Percy, / To share with me in glory any more: / Two stars keep not their motion in one sphere; / Nor can one England brook a double reign, / Of Harry Percy and the Prince of Wales.

Why, then I see a very brave rebel of that name. I am the Prince of Wales; and don't think, Percy, that you'll share glory with me any longer. Two stars can't move in one sphere, nor can one England stand a double reign of Harry Percy and the Prince of Wales.
Nor shall it, Harry; for the hour is come / To end the one of us; and would to God / Thy name in arms were now as great as mine!
